Investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult.

After hosting a virtual investor meeting with management, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Devon, with a price target of $59. #2671. Reds Show Their Quality in Belgium as Liverpool Beat Club Brugge 3–0

After a strong win over Manchester United at the weekend, Liverpool produced another top-drawer and professional performance in Europe, securing an impressive 3–0 victory away to Club Brugge.

Andoni Iraola made several changes to his starting eleven, but the performance showed the strength developing within the squad. Liverpool had to work for the result, particularly during periods when the hosts enjoyed possession, but their quality in the final third ultimately proved decisive.

Club Brugge 0–1 Liverpool – Alexander Isak (Dominik Szoboszlai) 13'

Club Brugge 0–2 Liverpool – Florian Wirtz (Rio Ngumoha) 79'

Club Brugge 0–3 Liverpool – Alexander Isak (Alisson Becker) 83'

Possession – Club Brugge 54% | Liverpool 46%

Total Shots – Club Brugge 17 | Liverpool 13

Shots on Target – Club Brugge 5 | Liverpool 4

Liverpool started well and looked to exploit Club Brugge's tendency to overplay in possession. The Reds pressed with energy and purpose, forcing opportunities to turn possession into attacking situations.

The opening goal arrived after just 13 minutes. Szoboszlai drove forward and delivered an intelligent low cross for Isak, who showed his instincts inside the penalty area to finish clinically. It was exactly the sort of movement and attacking understanding Liverpool will want to see more regularly.

Club Brugge responded and enjoyed spells of possession, but Liverpool remained organised. The hosts had opportunities to threaten, although the defensive pairing of Jacquet and Araújo dealt well with much of what came their way.

Víctor Muñoz was forced off in the 40th minute following a collision, with Rio Ngumoha introduced. It was an unfortunate interruption, but the young winger would go on to make a significant impact.

Liverpool went into the interval with a narrow lead, having shown good intensity without completely controlling the contest.

The second period presented a more difficult challenge. Club Brugge continued to push forward and Liverpool were forced to defend for longer spells. The hosts created opportunities, while the Reds also spurned chances to extend their advantage.

There was a feeling that the game remained open and that Club Brugge could potentially find a way back into it. However, Liverpool's quality eventually settled the contest in emphatic fashion.

The second goal was an outstanding piece of individual and collective play. Wirtz recovered possession deep inside his own half before driving forward. Isak and Ngumoha combined brilliantly in the build-up, with the latter providing an excellent pass for Wirtz to finish from the edge of the penalty area, his effort finding the net via the post.

Four minutes later, Liverpool made it three. Alisson produced an excellent assist, finding Isak, who finished superbly to register his second of the evening. Two goals in a short spell completely changed the complexion of the contest and gave the scoreline a convincing look.

Iraola then used his remaining substitutions to manage the closing stages, bringing on further experience and energy as Liverpool saw out the victory.

This was a hugely encouraging European performance from Liverpool. A 3–0 away win in Belgium, following the impressive victory over Manchester United, gives Iraola's side further momentum at an important stage of the season.

There were plenty of positives. Isak looked sharp and clinical, Wirtz once again demonstrated why he is becoming such an important figure in the attacking structure, and the defensive pairing of Jacquet and Araújo provided a strong platform. Nyoni also deserves credit for another mature midfield display, while Ngumoha made an immediate impact after coming off the bench.

Alisson's contribution should not be overlooked either. His performance was assured throughout, and his assist for Isak's second goal was an excellent piece of goalkeeping.

Liverpool did not have everything their own way. Club Brugge enjoyed more possession, registered more shots and caused problems at different stages. However, the Reds defended well when required and showed the clinical edge that separates good performances from winning ones.

The most pleasing aspect is the growing understanding between the attacking players. Wirtz is increasingly becoming the creative hub, Isak is finding his rhythm, and the younger players are showing they can contribute at this level.

Iraola will be pleased with another three points and a clean sheet. Liverpool now have an opportunity to build on this result and carry their improving form into the next challenge.

#2670. Packers-Rams Final Score: Blake Corum takes control in 26-13 Rams win

The Green Bay Packers' playoff hopes are officially on life support. The team needed a win over the Los Angeles Rams on Wednesday of Thanksgiving week to stay in the NFC's 7th and final playoff position with six games to go in the 2026 regular season. Instead, another offensive collapse in the second half doomed the team, as Jordan Love and company ran just eight plays, held the football for barely three minutes, and picked up no first downs between the start of the second half and the midpoint of the fourth quarter.

Over that time, the Rams took a lead and extended it out to ten points, which was too much for Green Bay to overcome. Blake Corum ran the football more than 20 times in the second half as the Green Bay defense wore down, and the Rams running back finished with over 180 yards on the ground and scored the go-ahead touchdown early in the third quarter to help the Rams coast to a 26-13 win.

Micah Parsons' return for the Packers saw him record a sack, but it was spoiled by his teammates' inability to stop the run and the Packers' offensive miscommunications. Jordan Love threw two interceptions, both of which appeared to be partially due to receivers running the wrong routes. Tucker Kraft committed an early fumble as well, giving the Packers three turnovers for the second straight game. And all told, the Packers had fewer than 20 minutes of possession in the game and ran just 44 plays on offense.

The unit certainly suffered after Christian Watson left the game with an apparent concussion, while right guard Kevin Zeitler injured his ankle in his first start as a Packer. But the Packers' issues were well beyond any injury issues, and they once again point to more fundamental problems with this team as a whole. With the Rams getting the win — going up by a game in the standings and earning a big tiebreaker with the victory — the Packers' likelihood of making the postseason is now awfully slim.

The Packers went 3-and-out on the game's opening drive, and the Rams immediately took advantage of a bad call, with Brandon Cisse getting flagged for a long pass interference penalty. That put them in field goal range quickly, but Xavier McKinney snuffed out a swing pass on 3rd down to force a 3-point attempt from former Packer Brandon McManus, who hit from 43 yards out to give the Rams an early lead.

Despite a running game that lost six carries on its first two carries, the Packers offense got moving on their second drive. Jordan Love hit Kaleb Johnson for 19 yards out of the backfield for the initial first down of the game, but after he found Tucker Kraft for another first down, the tight end coughed up the football as Nate Landman forced a fumble for the game's first turnover. Another inexplicable penalty on the ensuing drive helped the Rams drive deep into Packers territory, as Devonte Wyatt was called for an absurd roughing the passer penalty. Micah Parsons made his presence known for the first time with a pressure on Matthew Stafford, however, helping to limit the Rams to another field goal.

After another run for negative yardage by Johnson, Love hit Watson for a big 25-yard gain on a crossing route over the middle to get the Packers quickly across midfield. Trey Smack cut the Rams' lead to 6-3 a few plays later, hitting a bomb from 54 yards out to get Green Bay on the board.

The Rams responded with a touchdown drive, picking apart the Packers' secondary with short and intermediate. Stafford went 5 of 6 for 60 yards on the drive, with his longest play going to Konata Mumpfield for 24 yards, but it was Kyren Williams who finished it off, finding the end zone from seven yards out for a score. That gave them a 13-3 lead early on in the second quarter.

Love came up with back-to-back explosive plays on the first two snaps of the next drive, however, as the Packers answered. An end-around flea flicker from Savion Williams back to Love went for a gain of 21 to Watson, then Love hit Matthew Golden for a catch-and-run of 39 yards. A Chris Brooks run of 4 yards and a Love scramble for 7 set up goal to go and two plays later from the 7, Love drifted back and found Watson crossing left to right for a touchdown. Watson's 8th score of the season brought Green Bay back to within three points.

After forcing the Rams to punt for the first time all game, the Packers drove into field goal range once again. They did so thanks to Savion Williams picking up a 3rd-and-short on a dive when lined up as a tailback and Jordan Love finding MarShawn Lloyd for a nice gain out of the backfield for another first down. Matt LaFleur kept the offense on the field for a 4th-and-1 at the 30-yard line, and it proved to be a costly decision.

Love lofted a good pass to Watson up the right sideline for a gain of 15 yards, but Kamren Kinchens was ejected for a hit to Watson's head. Watson walked off on his own power, but the penalty and the catch were erased, offset by an offensive pass interference penalty on Matthew Golden. Watson walked to the locker room under his own power, but he would not return to the game.

Instead of sending the offense out again, Trey Smack came on for a 48-yard field goal attempt and he hit it, tying the game with just under two minutes left in the first half. Micah Parsons then got his first sack of the season on first down of the Rams' next drive, scuttling any real chance for Los Angeles to score before the half as the game went into the break tied at 13.

Coming out of the break, the Rams got cruising on the ground. Blake Corum picked up chunks of yardage as Stafford found Mumpfield for a couple of 3rd down conversions to get inside the Packers' 10. On 3rd-and-2, Mumpfield appeared to have a touchdown, but he was ruled to have bobbled the ball and the play was ruled incomplete. That appeared to set up a 4th down attempt, but instead the Packers were called for defensive holding on the play anyway, giving the Rams a 1st-and-goal from the one. After Corum got stopped on his first rushing attempt, he barely snuck over the goal line on second down to give the Rams a seven-point lead.

The Packers' offense got bailed out on the next sequence with the game hanging in the balance, but then gave the ball right back. After going three-and-out following the Rams' 8-minute drive, Los Angeles looked to put together a long drive again but Ty'Ron Hopper dropped into zone coverage and intercepted a Stafford pass, setting up Love and company in a great spot. However, he and Matthew Golden were not on the same page; Golden appeared to run the wrong route and Love's deep pass to the middle of the field got picked off near the goal line to return the favor.

Corum continued to run the ball effectively into the early fourth quarter, even as they saw a pair of starting offensive linemen and tight end Tyler Higbee leave the game with injuries. Finally, however, the Packers managed to get a stop with the Rams at the 40-yard line, leading to a surprising punt rather than a long field goal attempt.

The Packers still could not move the chains, however, failing to pick up a first down for the third time in three second half drives. Tucker Kraft came up a yard and a half short on 3rd-and-9, and Matt LaFleur called for a punt from deep in Rams territory. Corum gave the Packers a big jab on 2nd-and-long with a 13-yard reception, then delivered a knockout blow with a 35-yard run up the gut on 3rd-and-1. That set up another McManus field goal, making it a two-possession game at 23-13.

Green Bay finally started to mount a bit of a rally, picking up their first first downs of the second half with under six minutes to go in the game. Love picked up a 4th-and-8 from near midfield, but he got crossed up once again on a route, this time with Bo Melton, and threw his third interception of the game to truly put the game on ice. Los Angeles ran out all but the last 30 seconds or so of clock on the ground, adding a short field goal for the game's final points.

The win gave Sean McVay his first victory over his friend and former protege, as Matt LaFleur had been 5-0 against LA heading in. Green Bay now likely needs to run the table to make a run at the playoffs, or at least get a significant amount of help, now that they have fallen out of playoff position.

#2668. “Hasn’t really recovered”: Peter Schmeichel pinpoints where it has all gone wrong for Senne Lammens at Man United

Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens had a disastrous evening for the club in their 2-2 draw with Sporting CP.

The Red Devils made another poor start in Europe, conceding the first goal for the fourth European match in a row.

Lammens had actually been the hero moments earlier when he had managed to save Luis Suarez's penalty but was the villain of the piece just seconds later.

The Belgian came charging out of his goal and brought down the Sporting attacker, giving the referee an easy call to make.

Speaking to CBS Sports (via The Sun), he explained that he doesn't think taking Lammens out of the team would have any real benefit.

He explained, "yeah, I don't know when that point is. Pochettino has come in, he's brought his own staff, that means he's got a new goalkeeping coach. Maybe that is something that can change it for him."

The Dane continued to state, "in the World Cup he came on against Spain and made a mistake. Merino scored and they got knocked out and I feel like he's lost confidence from that mistake, hasn't really recovered. As a goalkeeper, when you're not on your best form you need your defenders in front of you to help you out and they haven't been able to do that and that just makes it so much worse and today was not a great day for him."

#2667. LeBron James records first triple-double with 76ers: Where he ranks on all-time list

In case you forgot, LeBron James is great.

The NBA's all-time leading scorer notched his first triple-double with the Philadelphia 76ers Wednesday, Nov. 25 in an NBA Cup matchup against the Miami Heat.

He completed the feat with 1:43 left in the fourth quarter, when he scooped his 10th rebound. With Joel Embiid sidelined to start the game and Jaylen Brown getting banged up just seconds before the end of the first half, James took over. He erupted in the second quarter, burying 3-pointer after 3-pointer. During one stretch in the second period, he scored 14 consecutive points for the 76ers.

"It's not my job to dominate every night for this ball club," James told reporters after the game. "We have a Finals MVP (Jaylen Brown), a regular season MVP (Joel Embiid), an up-and-coming superstar point guard (Tyrese Maxey), a young fella in VJ (Edgecombe), who is up and coming as well. My dues is paid in what I've done, but if they need me to dust off the cape from time to time, I can still accomplish that. But it's not my job. I don't think it's my job, but if they need it, I can do it."

James finished the game with 25 points on 9-of-15 shooting, adding 12 assists and those 10 rebounds. His point and assist totals were both season highs.

This is the 126th triple-double in James' career, which has now reached an NBA-record 24 seasons. Russell Westbrook holds the record for most triple-doubles in NBA history with 209. James ranks fifth behind Westbrook, Nikola Jokic, Oscar Robertson and Magic Johnson. No other player in NBA history had recorded a triple-double after turning 41 years old; James has now done it four times.

In fact, James now has more triple-doubles than Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and Larry Bird — combined.

James was ranked the 19th-best player in the league in USA TODAY's preseason rankings of the top 100 players.

The four-time MVP and NBA champion joined the 76ers this offseason as a free agent after leaving the Los Angeles Lakers.

"We all know, and everybody always says it, but Father Time wins," Heat coach Erik Spoelstra said. "But right now, he's giving Father Time hell."

#2665. Steelers could try to not pay Aaron Rodgers the balance of his $22 million salary

If/when the Steelers release quarterback Aaron Rodgers, they’ll have to decide whether to willingly pay the balance of his $22 million base salary, or whether to fight.

With his Week 12 paycheck already vested, the question becomes Week 13 through Week 18. Six weeks, totaling $7.33 million.

It won’t be easy to cut him off. First, the Steelers would have to release him for reasons unrelated to skill, injury, or salary cap. The argument, if the Steelers make it, would be that Rodgers’s appearance on Pat McAfee’s show constitutes personal conduct detrimental to the interests of the team.

A grievance would undoubtedly be filed, if the Steelers pursue that approach.

But even without the guarantee, Rodgers’s presence on the Week 1 roster qualifies him for the balance of his base salary as “termination pay” under the Collective Bargaining Agreement. To circumvent that, the Steelers would have to show that Rodgers has become ineligible for termination pay.

Here’s the key language, from Article 30, Section 3(b) of the CBA: “An otherwise qualified player will not be entitled to Termination Pay if (i) the Club terminated the player’s contract for Conduct Detrimental to the Club, and (ii) the Non-Injury Grievance Arbitrator determines that the player’s conduct was so severe that the maximum discipline for Conduct Detrimental of a fine equal to one week’s salary and suspension without pay for four weeks, pursuant to Article 42, Section 1(b)(xvii) of this Agreement (regardless of whether the Club imposed any such discipline prior to terminating the player’s contract), constitutes an inadequate remedy for the player’s conduct.”

It won’t be easy to satisfy that standard. But there’s language in the CBA that potentially applies to Rodgers’s public comments from Wednesday.

Here’s Article 6, titled “Public Statements": “The NFLPA and the Management Council agree that each will use reasonable efforts to curtail public comments by Club personnel or players which express criticism of any club, its coach, or its operation and policy, or which tend to cast discredit upon a Club, a player, or any other person involved in the operation of a Club, the NFL, the Management Council, or the NFLPA.”

That’s the same clause that fueled the NFL’s attack against the NFL Players Association’s report cards. The process constitutes comments from the NFLPA that express criticism of the teams, their coaches, the operations, and their policies.

None of this means the Steelers will attempt to cut off his final $7.33 million. But it’s an option. And it’s something to be considered as the Steelers try to figure out the next move.

#2664. Ollie Bassett: Packington to Toronto and life as a professional footballer in Canada

In the latest instalment of GOAL's 'Brits Abroad' series, a man that has played in both hemispheres talks futsal, life Down Under, growing tired of plane travel and what to do in Canada

There was a time not all that long ago when British footballers plying their trade abroad were rarer than hen's teeth. Individual reluctance to leave geographical comfort zones led to collective wings being clipped.

This is, however, a brave new world, with cultural advancement meaning that no corner of the planet should be considered too far-flung. Flying the nest and enjoying a different way of life is now an experience to be embraced, rather than feared.

Of course there are challenges - professional and personal hurdles that need to be cleared on the way - but why not embrace those instead of shying away from them? More and more players are adopting that mindset.

Taking that into account, and as we are forever told that travel broadens the mind, GOAL will be helping to tell the story of some of the intrepid explorers that have broken down barriers and found themselves in a position to impart both sporting and holidaying wisdom.

Next up is Ollie Bassett, a man who has taken the scenic route from Leicestershire in the East Midlands to the vibrant Canadian city of Toronto…

Aston Villa started Bassett's development process

"I started kicking a ball when I was extremely young, probably three or four. Then I joined my local team that my dad used to coach and manage, with my dad's best friend. They would coach together, so I played for them. When I was about seven or eight, we had a tournament - like a summer event - and there were scouts there. There was a Villa scout. He came over after one of the games and spoke to my dad and his mate about my situation. I joined the academy at Villa when I was seven, but I couldn't properly sign until I was eight because the lowest age group was U8. I trained with them for a little bit and as soon as I signed for the academy, obviously I stopped playing with all my mates. I was at Villa from eight until 16."

"Southampton was kind of a weird story about how it happened. I left Villa when they decided on the scholarships - I didn't get offered one. Then I went to, it wasn't Southampton's actual academy, they call it a second chance programme. They were based down in Bath, and alongside that I was doing college. That was meant to be a two-year programme, like two years for your scholarship. The whole purpose of that programme was to promote players into the Southampton academy. But Southampton at the time thought they weren't generating enough players into their full academy, so they knocked it on the head. That was meant to be two years, but they knocked it on the head after a year. We were like, 'well, we've signed a two-year deal, what are we going to do for the second year?'

"It just happened that at the time, because we were based down in Bath, Yeovil Town never used to have an academy. As they cancelled the second chance programme, Yeovil Town restarted their academy with a youth team, underneath the first team. So all the second year scholars from the Southampton thing went and did their second year with Yeovil. I'm still studying at this point, I'm still at college. I'm still living in Bath, but traveling to Yeovil to train. I went there and after two or three months, I started training with the first team. A month later, I made my debut. And then a month after that, I signed my first pro deal, which took me to the end of that year, plus the whole of the second year - an 18-month thing."

Heavier ball helps to improve technical ability

"I loved futsal. I still love it. I must have started when I was like 10. I played that alongside being at Villa. I did it on the side, just here and there. As I got older, about 14 or 15, and after I got released from Villa, I played futsal a lot more. I used to play that all the time. Every Friday night we were in a league. We trained maybe once a week. I was playing that alongside the academy. And then after I got released, I was playing a lot more until I went to the Southampton thing. I feel like when you shift to 11-a-side from playing small-sided, you don't naturally get as many touches. In futsal, the ball is not designed to be pinged 60, 70 yards in the air. It's obviously a lot heavier and it doesn't bounce as much, so the ball is always on the floor. That helped me massively. The technical side of my game, I think, is good. I feel a lot of it, or a good portion of it, was because I played a lot of futsal growing up."

Nuneaton Borough provided a brief pitstop

"My contract finished in Yeovil. At the time, the last six to eight months of that second year at Yeovil, I just wasn't enjoying it at all, to be honest. I understand the politics in football and all that sort of stuff, but as a kid, that was my first year as a pro and I wasn't playing. Sometimes I'd travel to not even be on the bench - just sit in the stand! I was like, 'I just don't really want to stay here'. I knew that they weren't going to renew my contract. I was happy at the time because I just didn't want to stay. Even though it was League Two, I just didn't want to stay. And after that, I was like, 'OK, I'm only 18, I'm going to try and find a club with a reserve team'. Obviously, Yeovil only had youth teams, so after 18 you're either playing first team football or you're not. There were no U21s in that.

"I went on trial at Barnsley and Burton Albion. I didn't get offered anything for their reserves. I ended up dropping down to play non-league in England. I was like, I've literally got no choice. I played non-league, which I think at the time was the league below the Conference North. So, it would be step three in the non-league pyramid. I'm a small midfielder, so the ball's just constantly going over my head! At this point, I'm not really enjoying playing football. The game's not suited to how I like to play. Then a coach from New Zealand reached out and was asking about me through the head of recruitment at Burton Albion. He put me in contact with him.

"Originally, I didn't really go to New Zealand to play football. I just went because I needed to figure out what I'm actually going to do. If I'm not going to play football, if I'm not enjoying playing football, then what am I going to do? So, I went there. I travelled for a little bit and then started training again with a local team. From there, I went to the National League of New Zealand. For me, it was just about getting the enjoyment back for playing. If I didn't have that, then I wasn't going to force myself to keep playing.

"I started enjoying it again and was like, 'okay, this is obviously what I want to do'. It was then a case of, how do I get back into playing full-time? I spoke to a few people over there. One of the boys connected me with his agent, who's still my agent to this day, who works in Canada. My thing was, can I get to the CPL? Because it was a new professional league. It was full-time. It's still developing. But the way they promote players, if you do well, it gives you a decent platform to go somewhere else. I tried to go there for the 2020 season from New Zealand. At the time, my agent was sending my clips. I think he spoke to three clubs in the CPL. All of them were just like, 'yeah, we don't really respect the New Zealand league, it's not professional, we're not looking to scout players from there'. This would have been mid-2019, end of 2019. I wanted to go for the 2020 season. So, I'm like, 'okay, I'll just forget about it, it's not going to happen, at least I tried'.

"That's when I decided to go from New Zealand to Australia for the start of 2020. I'm enjoying football and the Australian NPL league is better than the New Zealand league, you can earn more money there. I went at the start of 2020. I was playing and that, obviously, was the COVID year. The season wasn't even postponed, it just got straight up cancelled! At that time, New Zealand and Australia were the strictest countries in the world when it came to restrictions around COVID. We're all in lockdown, the season's been cancelled and there's no talk about it restarting. That's when I was like, 'I'm just going to go back to the UK, back to my parents, wait for this to die down a little bit and then just see what happens'.

"I went back to the UK mid-2020 and ended up signing for another step three team, Nuneaton Borough. I played for them for a little bit and then had an offer for the start of 2021 to go and play in the top division of Iceland. I was keen because it was full-time. But it wasn't professional. It was more like three, four times a week, training in the evening. It's classed as a professional league, but it's still similarly structured to non-league in England. All the other players probably have jobs during the day. I was set on going there because I didn't have anything else.

"And then, two or three days after Christmas at the end of 2020, the coach from Pacific, Pa-Modou Kah, who's now coaching in the USL Championship, called my agent. He was like, 'listen, I've seen his clips'. I didn't know this until later on, but he told me when I got there that my agent had sent a 10-minute highlights video. He just watched the first 30 seconds - the ball came to me, I dropped my shoulder and chopped a guy, and he decided that he wanted me. This is what I wanted back in 2020. I said to my agent, 'don't even ask'. At that point, I didn't really care if it was a one-year contract, five-year contract, if the money was good, if the money was bad. I just said, 'put me on a salary, give me my accommodation and get me there'. I knew that once I was there, I was playing full-time, playing professionally, I knew that I would do well. That's how the whole thing unfolded from New Zealand to the CPL."

Auckland was Bassett's first landing spot in New Zealand

"When I first moved to New Zealand, I moved to Auckland. Played a season there. Then the second season in the National League, I went to Wellington. They were one of the best teams in the New Zealand National League. So, I was like, 'okay, I'm going to be playing for a better team, if I want to move somewhere after this, I need to be scoring or making assists and winning - even if it is only New Zealand, I need to be doing well'. Football's obviously not their main sport. It's still part-time, semi-professional. So, I was working jobs as well. I worked in a few bars, worked construction with one of my close mates. It's funny to look back. It was just part of the journey.

"It is a beautiful country, though, the scenery and the people. If I was later on in my career and I wanted to go somewhere to retire and work after, that'd be pretty high on the list just because of how relaxed it is and how nice everyone is. But, I was 19, 20 at the time and in my head, when I started enjoying it again, I was like, 'I'm going to use this to get to whatever professional league I can'."

There is always plenty going on in Melbourne

"Melbourne is an incredible city. It's similar to New Zealand because they're obviously so close, but there's just so much more going on. The city's so big, lively and vibrant. Any day of the week, people are out. The NPL, I think, is a better league standard-wise than New Zealand. Even CPL clubs now are probably looking at Oz a little bit more because some NPL players are doing well and getting moves to the A-League. At that time, back in 2020, it wasn't like that. I think people probably just saw it as being similar. But having played in both, the NPL is a lot more competitive. And there was always talk around players in that football world of Australia.

"Australia is also better because you get paid more - you earn three, four, five times more than you would playing football in New Zealand. It's still part-time, it's still just two training sessions a week and a game on the weekend. You can work during the day, play football, but you earn significantly more money than you would in New Zealand. That's the attraction for a lot of players who probably aren't looking to go pro, or can't go pro, they can pick Australia over New Zealand because financially it makes more sense."

Vancouver Island lies on Canada's Pacific Coast

"My first team in Canada was Pacific in 2021. You've got Vancouver, then you've got Vancouver Island. I was on a small island, not a crazy amount going on. But again, another beautiful place. If you were a little bit older and you wanted to go somewhere in Canada, people would go there because it is nice. When my agent told me about the team, I didn't really do much research or find out where it was. For me it was literally, I don't care what team it is, where I live or where I go, it was just the opportunity to be back playing professionally and full time. I tried to use it as a stepping stone to go somewhere else or to get a better contract in the league.

"The CPL is one of those leagues where, because it's still new and there's not that many teams, everyone knows everyone. All the players know each other. You play against each other so much, the coaches know you, so, if you do well and you've proven yourself within the league, then you're always going to have teams that are interested in you. I feel like the majority of clubs will bring in internationals from outside but some of them hit and some of them completely miss. For clubs, it's important that you've proven what you can do in the league, that you're reliable. They know what they're going to get. That's the mentality that I went in with - just go, be back playing full time and then try and make the most of the opportunity."

Ottawa felt like home for a couple of years

"I'd say Ottawa started to feel like home. I moved there at the start of the 2022 season. That's the longest I've stayed at one club since I left Yeovil. That definitely felt like a second home away from home. I was really comfortable there. Towards the end of 2024, I'd been there three years. We reached the final in 2022. Individually, I'd won awards and stuff. We won the regular season in 2022. The only thing we didn't win was the play-offs. By the time the end of 2024 came, I just wanted to try something new. I wanted to have a new challenge and test myself in a different league. So, that was the reason why I left. But for the most part, that's the most comfortable I've felt away from football."

Warmer climes were experienced when arriving in Florida

"Tampa (Bassett joined Tampa Bay Rowdies in January 2025) happened because the USL (The United Soccer League) was always something that I was extremely interested in for the longest time. Even when I was in the CPL, the first few years were about doing well and proving myself. As I started growing and developing, getting better and producing more goals and assists, I was like, 'okay, can I look at the USL as a viable option?' I had a few offers at the end of 2023 to go there, but I was under contract with Ottawa. They were asking for money that USL clubs just weren't willing to pay at the time. They were like, 'we'll just wait one year and take him on a free'. Going into 2024, I didn't tell the club, but they kind of probably knew that this would be my last year. I was even telling my agent going into that 2024 season that he can start speaking to clubs midway through the season because I'm out of contract at the end of the year. That's what he did. He started speaking to a couple of clubs in the USL and we went back and forth with Tampa a few times.

"I ended up actually signing for Tampa in July of 2024, which was when I could sign a pre-contract. From there, I knew that once my season was done in Canada, I would be off to the USL. I feel like it's a step up from the CPL. I think it is a better league than the CPL. But it's very similar in the sense where if you do well in the league and you produce, then you can earn. Financially, you can better yourself. And also, clubs know what you can do so it's easier to stay in the league. It's similar to the CPL in that sense but I think the quality and the environments, it's a more complete league. It's more competitive. There's more teams, two conferences. That's why I decided to go there."

Inter Toronto showed faith after unfortunate injury issues

"I'll be honest, midway through when I was in the USL with Tampa, I was like, 'okay, I'm here now, I'm going to prove what I can do and I want to stay, whether it's with Tampa or someone else'. Then I got a crazy, weird injury that just wouldn't go away. I didn't play from the end of July until the end of the season. I didn't play another game for Tampa by the end of July. Then the end of the season comes and they don't take my option - because I had an option on my contract with Tampa and they don't take it because I'm injured and they don't know what's going on.

"I'm saying to my agent, 'I know I'm injured but I want to stay in the USL, I want to stay here, so we need to start speaking to clubs and see if that's going to be possible'. He was speaking to clubs and they were asking about my injury. A lot of clubs got put off by it because it was a really weird, strange injury that just wouldn't get better. It was a really deep core injury, to the point where getting out of bed was painful, twisting was painful, couldn't pass a ball, couldn't sprint, none of it. Clubs were put off by that. Toronto came in around October-November time. They offered me a contract and I just thought, 'you know what, maybe I need to go back to the CPL for now, get back fit and playing and doing well again'.

"Even after signing for them, I went into pre-season not fixed, I was still injured. It wasn't until I got checked by the medical department and got an injection for the injury that it started to get better. I was only really fully fit from June-July this year, because I was still dealing with it even after the injection. It's an injury that I've probably carried for 10, 11 months and just couldn't shake off. Looking back, I'm happy in Toronto, I like it as a city. We didn't have a great year this year, but as a city, it's nice. I'm looking forward to next season. I think in hindsight, if I was fully fit at the time, coming to the end of my year with Tampa, I probably would have had a lot more interest from the USL. It is what it is."

Bassett has mastered the art of packing a suitcase and racked up air miles

"Packing does still annoy me! Now, at the end of the season, I'm going home in two weeks for the off-season. I'll probably come back at the end of January or start of February for pre-season. It does get repetitive and boring after a while. So now, I travel extremely light. I'm not one of those people who bring three or four suitcases and take everything just in case they need to wear this certain piece of clothing. I generally just take one big suitcase, one small one and a backpack. I know at the end of the year I've got to repack everything! The packing side of it and the moving, it's obviously tedious and a little bit annoying.

"Canada as well, our season finished at the end of October and we won't start training again until the start of pre-season, which will probably be the end of January or the start of February. The season won't start until the first or second week of April. The off-season in Canada is extremely long. Which is obviously fine, everyone's under contract, but you have a long period of time where you're not playing and not training. I get a lot of time at home off the back of a CPL season. The packing and the moving and the flying… I'm over the flying! I don't know how many flights I've taken over the last eight years, but it's a lot!"

FIFA's flagship event passed through Toronto in 2026

"Toronto is a top city. A lot of people in Canada say it's between Toronto and Vancouver for the two best cities. I've not spent enough time in Vancouver to know but being in Toronto, I can understand why people like it. A lot of people are drawn to coming here. I never really fully experienced it when I was in Ottawa, because that's only a five-hour drive away from Toronto. Every time we would play Toronto, we would drive the night before and then as soon as the game's done, we would drive back. I never got to experience it. Everyone that I'd spoken to said it's a great city, and I can see why.

"I feel like this year was probably a lot better because we had the World Cup as well. Toronto was one of the host cities, so while that was going on it was unbelievable - to be in and around it was incredible. There's a mix and lots of different cultures. I feel like Victoria, my first year in Canada, out on the island, that's very Canadian. But Toronto's obviously a bigger city, so lots of different people, lots of different cultures. The food scene in Toronto especially is unbelievable. Any type of food you want, you just search it online and they've got it. It's just a big, popular city. We live close to downtown and it's easy to get around. It's just a lot of fun."

Life in big cities around the world is rarely cheap

"I feel like Canada's expensive. That's one thing I noticed when I went to Pacific, and then even Ottawa, I just feel like Canada is expensive. Toronto, obviously, the cost of living is expensive as well because it's a big city. You go out to eat and you pay your tax and then you've got a tip and that stuff. It all adds up. It's obviously expensive, but I think I'd compare Toronto to Melbourne in terms of cost of living-wise. It's probably very similar. You can understand why people want to go there and move there and live there because there's just so much going on. But it's definitely not cheap."

Playing chess helps to keep the mind sharp

"Over the last few weeks, me and one of my boys from back home, we're going to start a little coaching business. We're trying to use this off-season to get it up and running. And then next year when I come back, hopefully we've built it up enough to offer one-on-one and small group sessions. If I'm not doing that, I love cooking. Obviously we get breakfast and lunch provided by the club, so I'll eat that, but in the evenings I like to put some music on and cook, and chill. I play a lot of chess. No-one else on the team plays! One of the strength and conditioning coaches plays but no-one other than that. I play a lot online. Sometimes my dad will send me requests for a random game so I'll play against him.

"Obviously I go to the gym and stuff - that's not mandatory, but I feel like that's part of being a footballer, to stay healthy. This year was good because all of the international guys, the lads from outside of Toronto, we all lived in the same apartment building. Everyone had their own unit and lived by themselves, but in the same building. Outside of training we would go for coffee and hang out.

"That's one thing I've learned a lot over my career, being a footballer is unbelievable - it's the best job in the world - but you train in the morning, get home by 12:30-1 o'clock and you have got the rest of the day doing nothing. For me, you have to do stuff that keeps you stimulated or busy, just do something. That's why I learned to cook, because it kills time and you are eating good food. If you don't, every day looks the same and feels the same, you don't do anything. I think it's important to stay busy. On the weekends, if we are at home then we're here, if not then we are flying and coming back so that breaks your week up a little bit. For the most part, staying busy is super important."

The iconic Niagara Falls lie on the Canada-United States border

"If you're in Toronto, I'd say go to an NBA basketball game - something different from football. We have an MLS team here, but I'd look to catch an NBA game if they're in season, or baseball or hockey. Hockey's huge in Canada. It's not somewhere that I've been yet, I probably will go next year, but Niagara Falls isn't far from Toronto. Ice skating is very Canadian, they love it. When I was in Ottawa - this was pretty cool to be fair - they have a canal that runs all the way through Ottawa, a big lake. During the winter, when it would get cold enough, it would freeze over. People would, instead of driving or taking the train to work, they would skate from wherever they are on the canal up to wherever their offices are, change their skates and go to work. When I heard about that, I was like, that's crazy!"

Heavy snowfall is common when temperatures plummet

"The weather gets so cold during the winter. I'm lucky because we miss most of it because I'm gone at the end of November and not back until the start of February. I miss December and January, which are the worst two months. But I remember coming back at the end of 2022 in December, just before Christmas to see some of my mates when I was in Ottawa. I think at that time it was minus 25 or minus 30 - snow up to your knees and hip! That's one thing that everyone says about it - during the winter, it's seasonal depression for sure because it's just way too cold. No one's doing anything during the winter."

Trips to Las Vegas are more exciting than most away days

"A lot of players now don't get trapped, but they just want to stay at home or stay local. I understand it because not everyone's the same. If you're playing at a good level back home, then of course it doesn't make any sense to leave. But if you find yourself dropping down to another league, like what I did, then I've always had a passion for travelling. From when I was young, I always said I'd love to play abroad one day. When the opportunity came up, I was always going to take it. I just think it's an amazing thing to do. You can better your career from it. If you build a career, a successful career playing in the USL championship, then you've done really well.

"I feel like you learn a lot about yourself. You're moving away from home for the first time. You're putting yourself in situations that are uncomfortable, that you have to deal with. From that, the only way you deal with it is by growing through it. I've always encouraged people to do it. It's not an easy thing to do, but if you can get through the difficult times, you get to see different parts of the world, you give yourself opportunities through football to experience different markets in the world. I've seen players move from Canada and the US to top divisions in Southeast Asia and Asia. Those opportunities will never happen if you're playing in the lower leagues in England. You can be comfortable playing back home, but I feel like the doors that can open from playing overseas are massive. I would encourage anyone to do it if they've been thinking about it.

"Ever since I made the decision to move to New Zealand, football's taken me to places that I would never have visited in my life. I was in Auckland, Wellington, and Melbourne, and New Zealand, Australia. I was in Victoria, Ottawa, Toronto, Tampa. Even the cities that you go and play in, when you're playing away in the USL, we had Vegas first away game of the season in Tampa! It's places like that where you can go on holiday, but going there through being able to play football is crazy. Even the people you meet as well. My friend from back home that I'm really close with, he was traded to Detroit halfway through last season. I was staying with him for a few weeks. It's not a glamorous place and I would never have chosen to visit, but one of my close friends ended up there. I went for 10, 11 days to visit him. That's the whole point, you meet people and you travel to different cities that you would never have gone to through football or through playing in England. You're away from home but I think it's amazing, honestly. I wouldn't have changed any of it."

Bassett is not ruling out more far-flung adventures

"I've got a year left on my deal here in Toronto. This year was up and down. Second half of the season, I was back fit and I was playing and I wasn't injured. I was good, felt good. But this year as a whole was a bit disrupted with injuries. I've got a year left so I'll be back for the 2027 season. After that, who knows? I couldn't see myself going back to playing in England, I'll be honest. I don't see myself playing in England and retiring there. I see the rest of my career probably in Canada or the US.

"I've always been interested and intrigued about playing in Asia one day. That's always been something that's been in the back of my mind. Whether that happens or not, I have no idea. Cambodia is pretty, not popular, but a few players go there. The one that interests me is Indonesia. I don't know why, but I've had friends who played there and they said they're crazy about football. They love their football over there. So, just playing in an environment like that, I feel would be completely different. That's something I've thought about, but not something that has actually happened yet. And whether it does happen or not, I don't know. I don't think I want to go back to play in the UK any time soon."

How life in Canada ranks across five important areas

Weather: 8/10. "During the summer, eight or nine, but during the winter, one or two!"

Food: 9/10. "You can get anything you want - any type of food, they've got it."

People: 7/10. "That's a difficult one, because obviously it's a big city and you're not going to know everyone."

Things to do: 7/10. "There's a few things. If you want to travel outside of Toronto, like to Niagara Falls, if you're willing to travel - drive one, two, three hours - then there's plenty."

Cost of living: 4/10. "It's definitely not London prices, but it's expensive."

Access to Ollie was provided courtesy of Eikon Sports Group.

#2663. 49ers activate Nate Hobbs, re-sign Brandin Cooks to practice squad

Cornerback Nate Hobbs has not played in a game since signing with the 49ers in March, but that could change against the Seahawks this weekend.

Hobbs was activated from injured reserve on Wednesday as part of a handful of roster moves announced by the team. Hobbs landed on the list on September 1 with a groin injury and was at the end of his 21-day window to be activated.

The 49ers opened a roster spot by placing offensive tackle Colton McKivitz on injured reserve. He will miss the rest of the season after fracturing and dislocating his ankle last Sunday.

The 49ers also announced that they have re-signed wide receiver Brandin Cooks to their practice squad. He was dropped from the active roster ahead of the Niners’ Week 11 win over the Vikings.

#2662. Rams run over Packers in NFL's first Thanksgiving Eve game: Winners and losers

Call it Thanksgiving Eve, call it Drinksgiving if you want. But the NFL created another football holiday on Wednesday, Nov. 25, with its first prime-time regular-season game on the night before Turkey Day.

And, in a game with significant playoff implications, the Los Angeles Rams largely took the Green Bay Packers to the woodshed with a 26-13 victory … even if the entire affair was largely secondary to U2's halftime show (more on that later). Despite all the adversity LA has faced this season, the Rams go into the holiday on a five-game heater and looking like they might be rounding into the playoff team everyone expected them to be, at minimum, three months ago. Meanwhile, the Packers, even on a night when they got Micah Parsons back in the lineup, continue to head in the wrong direction.

Music? Postseason stakes? Turkey Day-adjacent football? So many winners to discuss … and a few losers:

As my dear colleague Mike Middlehurst-Schwartz said, "Rams, Packers in attendance for U2 concert." Nailed it, buddy.

Fifty years into their legendary, incomparable run as brilliant musicians and world-changing citizens, the boys from Dublin's Mount Temple Comprehensive School, with a healthy Larry Mullen Jr. back behind the drum kit, haven't lost a step − maybe just a little range in Bono's voice − as they return to the forefront of the global stage once again with their already acclaimed 16th studio album, 'Carnaval De Luz.' However the only new song they played at halftime on Wednesday night was "Torn," the band's collaboration with the late Dolly Parton in what was her final recording − and three years after she performed herself on an NFL Thanksgiving stage in Dallas.

Otherwise, the group, which will kick off a worldwide tour next year, played snippets from some of their most impactful songs of the 1980s: "Sunday Bloody Sunday" (intercut with backup singers doing the Supremes' "Stop! In the Name of Love"), "Pride," and, naturally − in another 360 NFL moment − "Where the Streets Have No Name," the capstone song of the quartet's unforgettable Super Bowl 36 halftime show, which paid tribute to the victims of Sept. 11.

Thanks, fellas. I'll be seeing you again (and again) soon.

U2 CREATES MORE MAGIC: Band shines during Thanksgiving Eve halftime with Dolly Parton tribute

The only guy on either team who had a memorable night on offense, the third-year back out of Michigan had the first 100-yard rushing game of his career − and blew well beyond the century mark with 184 yards on 32 carries. Corum also scored in the third quarter and bled quite a lot of clock in the fourth. Without their top two wideouts and nursing a banged-up tight end corps, an effective ground attack led by Corum and Kyren Williams seems to be the Rams' best bet to remain viable in the coming weeks.

The Rams' 10th-year HC beat Green Bay's Matt LaFleur, his former offensive coordinator, for the first time in what was their sixth head-to-head matchup.

One of the league's dominant defensive forces returned to action nearly a year after shredding his knee in Denver. Parsons, unsurprisingly, didn't make a huge impact Thursday while performing on a limited snap count but did collect his first sack since ... Thanksgiving last year in Detroit. Now he gets 11 days to shake off any further cobwebs − while emphasizing the import of run defense − before the Pack take the field again on Dec. 6 at New Orleans.

Wait, what? Don't worry, it's what the Rams dubbed their new, mostly white throwback uniforms, which debuted for this game. It's the first time they've sported the white horns since moving into SoFi Stadium in 2020. The entire ensemble is meant to honor the team's legendary "Fearsome Foursome" defensive line from the 1960s, which featured Rosey Grier, Lamar Lundy and Hall of Famers Deacon Jones and Merlin Olsen. Nice, clean look.

#2661. LeBron triple-double, Maxey 30-piece lead Sixers over Heat

The Philadelphia 76ers got back in the win column on Wednesday evening, taking down the visiting Miami Heat 111-104 in NBA Cup group play.

Joel Embiid was ruled out for this one after having been doubtful on the injury report since yesterday because of illness. This was the second game in a row Embiid missed due to being sick.

The Sixers were led by tremendous nights from LeBron James and Tyrese Maxey. James, who notched his first triple-double as a Sixer, put up 25 points on 9-for-15 field goal and 4-for-6 three-point shooting with 12 assists, 10 rebounds and a steal. Maxey added 30 points shooting 12-for-21 from the floor. VJ Edgecombe came alive in the second half to chip in 18 points.

The bad news is that Jaylen Brown exited the game just before halftime after seemingly favoring and grabbing at his hamstring. He was quickly ruled out for the rest of the contest with hamstring tightness. Something to be aware of going forward, for sure.

The good news is that the Sixers are now 15-4 and have off tomorrow. They're back in action Friday.

It didn't take long to see how Miami benefits from being third in the association in pace. In the first three minutes, the Heat got out ahead in transition three separate times for easy buckets before the Sixers defense even made it back up the other end. The Sixers aren't that slow, but the Heat were running circles around them early.

Jabari Walker got his third start tonight in Joel Embiid's absence, and it went right to work doing the little things right. He buried a second-chance triple off a LeBron James offensive rebound then got down the defensive end to draw an offensive foul out of Giannis. Jabari had seven points on 3-for-3 field goal shooting in his first six minutes on the floor.

If you read any of the Bell Ringers I usually write, you know I cannot stop talking about LeBron's passing. Well, I'm here to talk about it again. It's not just one pass. It's every single pass he makes. He waits until the exact millisecond to release perfectly targeted passes that set up the Sixers for sometimes wide open buckets.

Tyrese Maxey led the way for the Sixers' scoring in the first quarter with 13 points on 5-for-8 field goal, 1-for-2 three-point shooting. The consistent contribution of points helped steady the Sixers' offense after starting off the game a bit disjointed. Philly trailed Miami by three points after one.

LeBron has this tendency to just absolutely lock in offensively in insane bursts. He goes from the main facilitator to a mode of "hold on y'all, I got this myself" and, in year 24, he's absolutely still got it. James had the ball in his hands for three straight Sixers' possessions and turned each into three points — one and-1, and two threes. He wasn't done. A minute later, he pulled up again from not far over midcourt for the ultimate heat check. Three more points. It ended up being a 14-3 Sixers run that gave them the lead, courtesy of LeBron James, single-handed.

It's been a very quiet night so far from Jaylen Brown. With just four minutes left in the half, Brown has two points on 1-for-6 field goal shooting with not much else to show for himself on the stat sheet. He hasn't made a ton of mistakes, necessarily, but more so has been relatively inconsequential so far and can't seem to get a shot to fall. A far cry from last game, his return from a hamstring strain, where he looked as solid as ever.

Just a quick note (and, yes, I admit in saying this I am incredibly biased)… Giannis gets a VERY friendly whistle. I get it, he's a superstar. But compare the amount of contact he takes that is getting called a foul versus the amount of contact Tyrese Maxey takes with no whistles.

The Sixers — especially considering the absence of Joel Embiid — are doing a great job so far containing Bam Adebayo. At halftime, Adebayo had just five points on 2-for-8 field goal shooting

The Sixers ended the half on a 7-0 run to help them to a 62-53 lead going into the break. That's the good news. That bad news is that Brown left the half a few seconds early after seemingly favoring his left leg and grabbing at his hamstring. He went straight back to the locker room.

The team was quick to rule out Brown for the rest of the game due to hamstring tightness. Dean Wade started the second half in his spot.

Philadelphia has had a tendency to come out of halftime looking a bit sluggish or out of sorts… not tonight. The Sixers ripped off a quick 7-0 run just a minute or so into the second half to push their lead to double-digits. It was the usual suspects, James and Maxey, chipping in with the addition of VJ Edgecombe getting involved.

Edgecombe had a relatively quiet first half, but he seemed energized to come out for the second. The sophomore assisted the Sixers' first two buckets of the third frame and then scored the next two himself. He added a triple and a steal a few minutes later. That's one thing that Edgecombe seems to possess beyond his years: patience. It doesn't matter how few opportunities he gets early on in a game, he never gets discouraged and is always ready whenever he is called upon.

It's a different game entirely when the Sixers are actually hitting their three-pointers. With just a few minutes left in the third, six Sixers have sank at least one three-pointer and three players have multiple. They're shooting 45.8% from long range and it certainly makes holding on to a narrow lead just a bit easier.

It's been very nice to have Dominick Barlow back. In just his third game of the season after making his debut this past Saturday, Barlow continued putting in some really serviceable minutes at the backup center position featuring solid rim protection, grabbing offensive boards, putting back buckets and setting some big screens. He and Walker have been a decent one-two punch at the center position without Embiid available tonight.

The Sixers brought a nine-point lead into the final frame. Their lead was quickly extended back into the double-digits with two back-to-back triples from Anfernee Simons — his first two field goals of the night, making him the seventh Sixer to knock down a three-pointer in this one.

Apologies for the redundancy but the Lebron passes just get more and more ridiculous. It is just beyond anything I've ever seen done so well night in and night out, every single game. Here's an absurdly accurate lob to Edgecombe from half court to extend the Sixers lead to 14.

Edgecombe has absolutely come alive since halftime. From all the statistical contributions to just the extra effort plays that won't show on the sheet, he has his handprints all over this second half and was a big factor in the Sixers holding on to this lead.

The Heat aren't just going away quietly tonight. They've chipped the Sixers lead back down to just single digits with five minutes to play. This Philly team just always has to keep games interesting…

What a night from LeBron James! With his 10th rebound with under two minutes to play, James notched his first triple-double as a Philadelphia 76er.

The Sixers hold on and get back in the win column. They move to 15-4 on the season and will be back in action on Friday night.

#2659. Flick talks Gordon, Adeyemi, Jesus, Balde, Pedri, Olmo after Sabah 1-4 Barcelona

Hansi Flick was pleased with Barcelona's 4-1 victory over Sabah in the UEFA Champions League, but the manager admitted that his side's performance left room for improvement.

The German coach highlighted Barcelona's stronger second half, praised the contributions of Anthony Gordon, Karim Adeyemi and Gabriel Jesus, and explained why Pedri was withdrawn at half-time.

Barcelona secured three important points in Baku, with Gordon scoring twice before Adeyemi and Jesus added further goals, although Flick's post-match assessment made clear that the result was more satisfying than the overall display.

Barcelona struggled to convert their possession into clear opportunities during the opening period, allowing Sabah to remain competitive before Gordon opened the scoring.

Flick acknowledged the Azerbaijani side's confidence and explained how Barcelona eventually took control.

"They came out with a lot of confidence. We had possession in the first half. It took us a while to score the opening goal, but we finally did. And from then on, we took advantage of the rest of our chances."

The manager was particularly encouraged by the attacking contributions of Gordon, Adeyemi and Jesus, whose goals helped Barcelona secure a comfortable away victory.

Anthony Gordon scored two goals against Sabah. (Picture credit: X/@FCBarcelona)

"This is very good news. Gordon has been very important in pressing; Karim, too, and Gabriel has a lot of quality. It's not easy facing someone like Raphinha, but his level is a positive sign."

As stated, Jesus scored Barcelona's fourth goal after Gordon's double and Adeyemi's strike had put the visitors firmly in control.

Flick acknowledged that the Brazilian faces a difficult battle for regular opportunities, with Raphinha occupying an important position in his plans.

"It's not easy for Gabriel Jesus either, being behind Raphinha, who is very important for us. But I love the quality he has, and he's always a positive player.

"When he came here, I spoke with him and told him I didn't know how things would go, that he might play fewer minutes.

"He told me it was no problem, that he would work for the team. And now we have seven games left until the end of the year, and anything he can do to help us is welcome," added the manager.

Flick also clarified that Pedri's half-time withdrawal was part of a prearranged workload plan, not a reaction to a fitness concern. Dani Olmo was also scheduled to play a specific amount of time.

Pedri was taken off at half-time. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

"Pedri's substitution was planned. He was supposed to play 45 minutes. Olmo's substitution was also planned.

"We were able to manage the minutes of other players and the result was as expected."

Barcelona's victory was tempered by concern over Alejandro Balde, who was substituted after suffering an ankle problem.

Flick said the defender's condition would need to be assessed before the club could determine the severity of the issue.

"It was an ankle problem. It hurts a little, but we'll have to wait until tomorrow.

"I don't know yet what's wrong with Balde. It's not easy for him to have fewer minutes. But I think he did a good job and played well," he concluded.

#2658. Mike McCarthy confirms he said "1-2-3 Packers" at halftime last Sunday

Aaron Rodgers said a number of things that caught the attention of the football world on Wednesday and one of the comments that drew a big response had to do with something that happened in the locker room at halftime of last Sunday’s loss to the Eagles.

After saying head coach Mike McCarthy fell asleep in meetings and missed other ones altogether in his first comments since being benched on Tuesday night, Rodgers said that McCarthy broke down the team in the locker room with “1-2-3 Packers” in reference to the team he coached through the 2018 season. In a press conference later in the day, McCarthy confirmed that happened but said he took issue with how Rodgers characterized other things that included his commitment to the job.

“The Philadelphia situation at halftime was very emotional. . . . Embarrassing moment, but I just think we work a lot of hours so definitely a difference of opinion from what I was told about the comments,” McCarthy said.

The Steelers have released Rodgers and McCarthy stressed the need for the team to focus on Friday’s game against the Broncos, although it feels like that’s going to be difficult based on how the last 18 hours have played out in Pittsburgh.

#2657. The biggest money-making energy trade looks over. What to buy instead

Is one of the greatest money-making trades of the last few years coming to an end?

No, I'm not talking about Nvidia or any of the data center- or AI-related power companies (although they have been crushed lately too… more on that on CNBC TV. Tune in!).

I'm talking about whether the epic boom in refinery-related stocks is unwinding. Over the last year, the jump in some of these companies has been nothing short of remarkable.

That jump is largely due to massive increases in margins, earnings, and cash flow. Those have occurred because of a big jump in what is called a crack spread. That is the difference between the price of oil and the finished price of refined products such as diesel and jet fuel. For most of this year, spreads have been soaring as disruptions and attacks on facilities and shipping in the Arabian Gulf, Hormuz, and deep inside Russia have played havoc with the market. In the last week or so, however, something big has changed: many of those spreads have started to tighten.

This seismic drop in spreads is causing a selloff in the aforementioned refinery companies.

If spreads continue to fall, these stocks may well keep selling off from recent highs. The upshot for investors may be that, as the shares come down, analysts see more upside. The median price target for Phillips 66 (PSX) now indicates a 20% gain from here, while smaller-cap Par Pacific (PARR) is double that.

Here are a few other key points to focus on heading into the Thanksgiving-shortened week.

I like to keep politics as much at arm's length as possible — we all know that energy and politics (sadly) often go hand in hand. Energy policies coming from Washington, D.C., can drive — or destroy — investment dollars. With all the big shifts in the White House over the last 10 years (four years of Trump, four years of Biden, and now 2 years into Trump #2), energy policies can blow through Washington faster than a summer squall hits a wind turbine. But because federal policies can mean so much for specific companies, sectors, and investments, it's important to follow the news flow.

That said, I'd like to take a moment to introduce you to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA (and pronounced like the state in Mexico). Like much legislation, BAAJA is an obscure but important bill working its way through the American Congress. BAAJA does a lot of things, but what Power Insider readers care about is its focus on energy permitting reform. In a nutshell, BAAJA would help speed up the building of new electricity infrastructure. Again, that's an overly simplistic view of a big bill, but it needs to be on your radar. The utility trade group Edison Electric Institute came out in favor of the legislation this month after the industry received some 11th-hour changes. See more about it in our recent interview with EEI President Drew Maloney here.

The bill passed the U.S. Senate in a vote late Thursday night. Now it moves to the House. Support for its final passage is also coming from the big LNG trade group, whose executive director said he "applauds the Senate for its bipartisan effort to pass meaningful, bipartisan, and durable permitting reforms aimed at delivering greater predictability, consistency, and certainty in the permitting, production, and export process for U.S. LNG. This legislation moves us closer to untangling red tape and eliminating overlapping agency reviews that can keep U.S. energy projects delayed for years."

The Natural Gas Supply Association also chimed in, saying it urges Congress to see the bill as "a resource-agnostic and balanced reform agenda for boosting American energy security. It keeps strong environmental reviews in place, but it draws a firm line against the endless procedural delays that tie critical energy projects in knots for a decade."

In my view, passing BAAJA is an important test of Congress's appetite for helping the energy and electrical power industry, lowering costs, and speeding time to market. The old adage was correct: time is money. Literally. If BAAJA moves on through the House, we could see an upside move in some utility stocks and any company related to energy infrastructure.

Speaking of politics, the news is getting lost in the massive Anthropic (ANT) IPO, but the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) — whose importance I wrote about in the last edition — just decided to resume permitting for data centers. The Texas Tribune did a nice write-up on it, and you can read it here.

It's tough to say, but it's true. The two are inextricably linked by policies created at both the federal and state levels. As I wrote in the last edition, some federally elected officials may have less impact on state-level issues — like the data center buildout — but they certainly have power over national laws. While many of you are enthralled, disgusted, or confused by sordid tales of Nvidia and Jensen-gate, keep one eye open on what happens in Washington, D.C.

Have a great week, and have a wonderful Thanksgiving, everyone.

Perhaps the big investor story — which is, like most things lately, related to Jensen-gate and Nvidia—is the sizable selloff in many AI, neocloud, and data center power-related stocks.

Painful for current shareholders, but big drops can also bring big opportunities. Wall Street believes that's the case, at least right now. Look at some of the potential upside based on the stocks' prices versus their price targets.

We spoke with the CEO of Applied Digital (APLD) about all of this on CNBC last week, and you can watch it here. He highlighted how the market may be getting these stock stories wrong because, at least with his company, he has long-term contracts with solid-credit companies. In that way, Applied Digital is more like a landlord than a "pure-play" AI company.

My take → While I'm not going to recommend a specific stock, I would add that it is critical for investors to understand the differences between these companies. While they may have some things in common, they are also different, with different business models, customers, leases, and sources of revenue.

Speaking of recommendations… here are two ideas for you:

A recent decline presents a nice opportunity in SOLV Energy (MWH). UBS analyst Jon Windham upgrades SOLV to buy from neutral, believing the market is "underappreciating several key tailwinds for SOLV given uncertainty around data center demand and higher interest rates." UBS highlights how the stock has fallen lately despite making two deals and beating and raising recent guidance. UBS says now is an "attractive entry point" for SOLV. (Side note: MWH is a great stock ticker.)

While markets overall fall, BMO remains bullish on Bloom Energy (BE). After speaking with the company, the analyst is upgrading Bloom to outperform, saying he remains "increasingly confident of BE's commercial traction" and that he still has conviction even with the recent drop in shares. While analyst Ameet Thakkar did cut his target to $230 from $260, that's still 50% upside from the current price. Bloom shares have tumbled 45% since October 1.

I was recently asked for my opinion on the price of oil. Here's my take. The market clearly wants to push oil contract prices lower and has for a few months. But, as I've said and reported for a while, don't confuse the futures (paper) price with the actual price. Yes, shipping rates and insurance rates have come down from recent highs — and there is a good amount of oil now flowing through Hormuz — but the cost of a physical barrel of crude is still well above the futures contract. If we get real, longer-lasting peace around Iran, oil prices will fall. There is plenty of oil in the world. That said, if bombs and missiles start firing again, oil prices will firm. I know that's a non-answer answer, but the oil market is truly headline-driven right now. My late good friend Boone Pickens (later in life, he didn't like being called by the "T" in his first name) used to avoid giving a set price target and instead give a directional quote, so I'll do the same: the odds of oil being lower in two months than it is today are 75%.

Last week, I had a one-on-one with Vimal Kapur, chair and CEO of Honeywell International (HON), at an RBC conference in New York City. While the conversation wasn't filmed, I can tell you that Kapur offered investors reassurance that his order book is doing very, very well. This is important because Honeywell is huge in the things that make other things work. Its sensors go into a ton of energy facilities, from refineries to LNG facilities. Honeywell is a leading indicator of spending and buildouts, so if it keeps getting orders, it's a good sign for macro energy.

Bottom line: Watch Honeywell stock as a potential "tell."

This week's Inside Line interview takes a different approach. We hit our friend Craig Johnson up for actionable insights into energy and stocks. Craig is managing director and chief market technician at Piper Sandler. He recently appeared on Power Lunch to talk about markets and stocks. He mentioned being bullish on energy, so we wanted to dig in just a little bit more.

This week, we had the pleasure of chatting with Balaji Krishnamurthy, president of Chevron Australia. We spoke at length about natural gas, the impact of disruptions, and long-term demand from Chevron customers in the Asia-Pacific region.

This is a bit of a local RBI for the New York City area, but one I felt was important to highlight. New York's electric grid operator just came out with a massive warning for everyone in our region: in just a couple of years, there may not be enough electricity supply to power our needs. A new report shows a deficit in seven years, with a nearly 2 GW power hole in a decade. That's a number of big power plants' worth of energy. Get your solar panels on and buy that backup generator! I'll call this one random, but scary.

#2656. Report: Mike McCarthy "has the full support" of the Steelers organization

Early in the second quarter Wednesday night in NBA Cup group play, LeBron James pulled up from Broad Street.

He drilled a 35-foot 3-pointer amid a torrid stretch that saw him make a trio of triples and score 14 straight points for the 76ers on Thanksgiving Eve. Before that sequence, the Sixers were trailing the Miami Heat by three points at Philadelphia's Xfinity Mobile Arena. Afterward, they were up eight.

While becoming the oldest player in NBA history to notch a triple double — at 41 years and 330 days old — James continued his recent hot streak from beyond the arc, going 4 of 6 on 3-point attempts. Philadelphia shot 14 of 35 from long range en route to a 111-104 victory.

The Heat (10-7) would have clinched East Group B had they come out on top, but Philadelphia (15-4) denied Miami an eighth consecutive win, despite losing Jaylen Brown to a hamstring injury late in the first half and Joel Embiid being sidelined by illness.

Nick Nurse's squad is now 2-1 in NBA Cup competition; Erik Spoelstra's Heat dropped to that same mark.

James finished with a season-high 25 points and 12 assists, plus 10 rebounds, with maybe his most notable dime taking place in the infancy of the fourth quarter. The 22-time All-Star flexed his elite court vision, timing a halfcourt lob perfectly to connect with VJ Edgecombe for a layup. James later dialed up an alley-oop for forward Dominick Barlow to throw down.

Edgecombe was among the Sixers players stepping up in the absence of Brown and Embiid, as Philadelphia protected its nine-point halftime lead and kept Miami at arm's length over the final two quarters. He had 18 points, and Tyrese Maxey poured in 30.

Durant did so while piling up 20 points for Houston (14-5), which, despite already being eliminated from NBA Cup knockout-round contention, kept pace in the upper echelon of the Western Conference standings.

The Rockets improved to 2-2 in Cup group play, while the Suns (9-8) slid to 1-2. They, too, have been eliminated from knockout-round contention in West Group A.

Along the way, Houston center Alperen Şengün passed Hakeem Olajuwon for the second-most triple-doubles in franchise history. Şengün, only 24 years old, secured his 15th performance of that kind with 23 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists.

Late in the game, Suns wing Dillon Brooks got into it with Durant and was ejected after receiving his second technical foul of the night.

Although the Minnesota Timberwolves lost LaMelo Ball to an ankle injury Wednesday, they held on to defeat the Oklahoma City Thunder 113-106.

Jaden McDaniels came through, big time, in the West Group B matchup. In fact, by game's end, he was the third player in Wolves history to log at least 30 points, 10 rebounds and 5 assists in consecutive games. That elite company also includes Karl-Anthony Towns and Kevin Garnett.

Minnesota (14-5), on the other hand, is atop West Group B with a 3-0 record. McDaniels beat the third-quarter buzzer with a ridiculous off-balance shot. A late 3-pointer from Wolves guard Ayo Dosunmu helped seal the deal.
