#2651. Nvidia surge: What investors should do with the stock and the AI trade now

Nvidia shares gapped higher at the open by more than 30%, on pace for its biggest one-day gain in 23 years on Monday, following the news just before the bell that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is going to be reinstated.

Investors and traders said that while this reflex rally may have more to run, cautiousness is warranted on Nvidia and the AI trade because of the overhang of investigations into the alleged Chinese espionage involving the company and others, as well as the possibility for data center moratoriums as Democrats take control of Congress and key governor posts in January.

"Am I as bullish on Nvidia now as I was on Friday? Of course not, you can't be," said Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, which counted Nvidia as its largest position as he bought on the dip over the last few weeks. "I'm trimming back."

"All the same issues that were here before Jensen resigned are still here," he added.

The day before Huang resigned on Nov. 12 as CEO, Nvidia closed at $173.73. It's intraday high on Monday was $171.50, up from its recent low around $125 as it was selling off in the wake controversies. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF closed at $506.96 the day before his resignation. It reached a high of $469.35 before losing steam as trading wore on Monday.

Mike Khouw, YieldMax strategist at Tidal Financial Group, told CNBC on Monday that there were "sighs of relief," "applause" and even "cheering" among investors at the news of Huang's potential reinstatement. But he also said there are still considerable risks facing the AI trade.

Jensen Huang was not the only problem at Nvidia, he said, and there are still many vulnerabilities in the overall AI trade, which should give investors pause. Credit-sensitive companies are still at risk of faltering, Khouw added.

The national security implications of the scandal that has rocked Nvidia and the global AI trade more broadly aren't going away any time soon even as the Trump administration assured the Nvidia board there were none. Investors on Wall Street are expressing strategic concerns about ways to play the tech space just as lawmakers in Washington are demanding answers.

Democrats are demanding answers on what exactly happened with Nvidia and the Chinese government.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a Monday statement. "The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."

House Ways and Means ranking member Richard Neal (D-Mass.) stressed the importance of Congressional oversight in determining the best course of action to move forward. The outcome of any Congressional investigations will likely be crucial for Nvidia's long-term viability as an investment opportunity, especially since the company does so much international business.

"This is an export control issue," Neal told CNBC on Monday. "Congress is not subservient to this president or any other president as it relates to trade and tariff policies. This is a trade related issue."

Many of the same Democrats will call for a slowdown in the data center buildout, a strong issue for the public partly responsible for their Blue Wave earlier this month.

"You're going to have to work your way through what these data center moratoriums all mean," said Niles. "Now I think the broader market keeps going but I am not as convinced on the move in the data-center centric names from here."

To be sure, many Wall Street analysts were rushing to upgrade Nvidia's stock on Monday after Huang's reinstatement. Most restored price targets well above $200 with one as high as $270. But many traders think the rebound may fail before getting back to those levels.

Famed short seller Michael Burry, who made a boatload betting against Nvidia with put options as it cratered, told his Substack audience that he thinks the rebound here could be "outsized," especially with low volume in the market overall because of the Thanksgiving holiday this week.

But he too sees the rally eventually losing steam.

"Jensen being back without much more information might even restore NVDA to the high 100s," Burry wrote. "I won't short it on this information I have today until it gets closer to or maybe hurdles $200."

#2648. Kalshi daily volume of ‘perps’ trading begins to top its prediction markets

Kalshi is known for its prediction markets across sports, politics and culture.

But now, for the first time, perpetual futures, Kalshi's second financial product, has surpassed the notional trading volume of its event contracts on consecutive days.

On Thursday, perpetual futures — commonly known as "perps" — on Kalshi saw $3.4 billion in notional volume as artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic stock debuted on public markets while the rest of the market sold off. That exceeded about $3 billion in notional volume for Kalshi's prediction markets on the same day.

Perps are futures-style contracts where there is no expiration and traders do not need to own the underlying asset. Contracts instead continuously track the price of an asset, with funding payments to keep the contract price aligned with that of the market. Funding payments are made periodically between holders of short or long positions.

Perps trading surpassed event contracts one day in September, but on Friday perps topped prediction markets volume for a second day. Now Kalshi expects that performance to continue as it introduces perps tied to more individual stocks. On Monday, for example, Kalshi launched contracts linked to Anthropic.

Kalshi was the first to debut perps in the U.S. after winning federal regulatory approval in May to list perps tied to cryptocurrencies.

Perps trading volume includes any leverage that speculators acquire along with their trade, while event contracts are fully collateralized — for now.

Since the original launch in May, Kalshi has received approval to introduce perps tied to metals, crude oil, stock indexes and individual stocks.

Offshore perps — those available on exchanges not regulated in the U.S. — generated more than $90 trillion in notional trading volume in 2025, so it's not surprising that the product has grown so rapidly on Kalshi, according to Udesh Jha, chief risk officer at Kalshi Klear, the company's clearing house.

"We're just in very early innings. We're launching products, we're growing the participant base."

Perps were Kalshi's first product to mark its transition from a prediction market-focused platform to a full-blown financial exchange where various assets are traded. Last week, reports said that Kalshi is planning to offer trading on equities on its platform in the coming months.

At the same time, the company's perps product has come under fire. Some incumbent exchanges where futures are traded — which saw their stock prices decline following the approval of U.S. perps — believe the product was improperly approved. CME Group is suing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal derivatives regulator, for approving perps.

Others have simply expressed concerns about the efficiency of the markets. CNBC previously reported that trading volume on Kalshi's most popular perps markets — tied to bitcoin and ether cryptocurrencies — was dramatically greater than open interest, or cash actively in the markets. It's a phenomenon that isn't common with U.S.-regulated traditional futures, nor other offshore perps markets.

Kalshi said at the time it has "zero concerns" about the distinction, and that it appears because less leverage is offered compared to offshore exchanges and there are fewer incentives for traders to park capital on its perps markets.

While Kalshi started with cryptocurrencies, Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street, said perps tied to individual stocks likely represent the most promising opportunity for growth in the U.S.

"That's how I foresee the way perps will penetrate further into traditional asset classes," Lau said. "Perps on single stocks and [key performance indicators on individual companies] could change how investors hedge their portfolio or even make a directional bet."

Kalshi's growth has been powered by the fact that right now it's the only exchange that can actively list perps in the U.S., though crypto exchange Coinbase received approval in May to route U.S. users to offshore platforms for trading. That monopoly status, however, will probably prove short lived.

Coinbase has filed to list single-stock perps in the U.S., and President Donald Trump in August said the CFTC is working to bring Hyperliquid — a dominant player in offshore perps activity — to domestic traders.

But Jha at Kalshi isn't worried about the competition.

"What will carry us is ... making sure that we have the right products for the marketplace, making sure we have the right surveillance of the products that we are trading."

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

#2646. Women's World Cup 2027 MVPs: USWNT standout Trinity Rodman is ready to show the world what the fuss is all about

The 24-year-old has starred in the NWSL and at the Olympic Games, winning both titles, and will be expected to spearhead the U.S. attack in Brazil this summer

There are not many bigger stars in the world of women's football than Trinity Rodman. Nothing highlights that quite like what unfolded at the turn of the year when clubs in Europe were circling as her contract with the Washington Spirit expired.

Desperate not to lose one of the most talented and recognisable players in the league, the NWSL introduced its High Impact Player rule, quickly nicknamed 'the Rodman rule', in order to allow the Spirit to offer Rodman the sort of contract that could keep her around, making her the highest-paid women's footballer in the world.

How Rodman performed in the season that unfolded afterwards only served to justify the deal. A return of 14 goals and 10 assists helped fire the Spirit into the 2026 NWSL Championship game, in which she also scored despite her side's eventual defeat.

Though still only 25 years old, it's not the first time Rodman has performed to an incredible level when all eyes were on her. Be it the way she marked herself out as a star in her own right during her rookie year, firing the Spirit to its first NWSL Championship crown after entering the league to much fanfare given her father Dennis' status as a basketball icon, or her displays in the United States' Olympic triumph in 2024, which saw the national team respond remarkably well to the disappointments of the previous year's World Cup, Rodman is no stranger to excelling under pressure.

It all adds up to make her one of the most fascinating figures heading into the 2027 Women's World Cup. Rodman has yet to really mark herself out on that stage, which is undoubtedly the biggest in the sport. But looking at her career to date, there are not many reasons to bet against her doing so in Brazil.

The spotlight was on Rodman in her first NWSL season, but she performed under that pressure, helping the Washington Spirit to win its first NWSL Championship title

Rodman probably knew that she was never going to enter the world of women's football quietly. When she became the youngest player to be drafted in NWSL history back in 2021, as an 18-year-old, it was her mother who stood proudly beside her, but it was her father's name that added to the attention she would receive.

It wasn't until several years later that Rodman would fully air the frustrations that came with that, which went well beyond the irritation many children of famous sporting parents endure of simply wanting to be a star in their own right.

"He's not a dad. Maybe by blood, but nothing else," she said on the Call Her Daddy podcast in 2024, explaining her father's limited presence in her childhood and how her mother struggled financially to raise her two children, with them even living in their car at one point.

"In terms of what I've filtered and what I've talked about, I feel like me and my brother have been very generous with the way that we've talked about it and very unselfish," Rodman added. "I think we never want to make him look bad and that is at the cost of holding in a lot, and a lot of issues we've gone through and just like, trauma, per se."

Somehow, as an 18-year-old, she managed to compartmentalise all of that and, as the attention on 'Dennis Rodman's daughter' grew, she performed so well that she helped the Washington Spirit win an incredible first NWSL title, earning Best XI honours and the NWSL Rookie of the Year award in the process.

Everyone was excited to watch Rodman at her first World Cup in 2023, but it could hardly have gone much worse for the USWNT

When the 2023 Women's World Cup came around, then, Rodman was prime among the players to watch. Still only 21 years old, she became the youngest player to score two goals in a game for the USWNT in one of their send-off friendlies, with her second goal dubbed "world-class" by head coach Vlatko Andonovski.

But after beginning the tournament with a 3-0 win over Vietnam, nothing else really went to plan for the U.S. Draws with the Netherlands and Portugal saw the four-time world champions scrape through the group stages, as Portugal came within the width of a post of knocking the U.S. out and progressing at their expense.

Then came the infamous penalty shootout against Sweden, when Lina Hurtig's spot-kick crept over the line by a millimetre to send the Scandinavian nation through and condemn the USWNT to a last-16 exit - its worst result in Women's World Cup history. Andonovski subsequently left his role, icons like Megan Rapinoe and Julie Ertz retired and a new era beckoned for the national team, who would be taken over by Emma Hayes in the summer of 2024, after her 12th and final year in charge at Chelsea.

Just a year later, the USWNT was on top of the world again, with Rodman playing a starring role at the Olympic Games in 2024 as part of the 'Triple Espresso' attack

It was hard to know what to expect from the U.S. at the Olympic Games in Paris in 2024. Hayes wouldn't take the role until the end of Chelsea's season, meaning she had only had a few weeks with the team, and the squad she chose boasted much less experience than that of 12 months prior, with the likes of Alex Morgan and Kelley O'Hara joining Rapinoe and Ertz in watching from afar.

But the youthful revolution proved fruitful. Defenders Naomi Girma and Emily Fox announced themselves to the world, but it was Sophia Wilson, Mallory Swanson and Rodman who really captured the attention as the most electric and prolific attack in the tournament fired the United States to an unexpected gold medal.

'Triple Espresso' scored 10 of the team's 12 goals, while also accounting for five assists, earning all three forwards places in the top 10 in the Ballon d'Or voting a few months later. Their contributions were vital in showing that 2023 was merely a blip for the USWNT; this was still one of the very best teams in the international game.

After overcoming a back issue and shining during the 2026 NWSL season, all signs point to Rodman putting on a show at the 2027 Women's World Cup, especially with 'Triple Espresso' reuniting

Remarkably, in the two-and-a-half years since, Hayes hasn't been able to name a single starting XI featuring 'Triple Espresso'. In fact, the three have only shared the pitch as a trio once in that time, in the USWNT's second-most recent game - a 2-0 defeat to Spain which Rodman and Wilson started, with Swanson joining them for the final 25 minutes from the bench.

Two big reasons for that are that Wilson and Swanson both had their first children in that time, Wilson giving birth in September of last year before Swanson followed in November. Rodman, meanwhile, has had issues with a recurring back injury, making it rare for all three to be available at once.

Heading into the 2027 Women's World Cup, though, the signs are positive when it comes to a reunion of the attack that took the Olympics by storm. Wilson's first season back was a strong one, especially considering she didn't score in any of her first five games. In the end, she racked up 15 goals and five assists as the Portland Thorns made the post-season. Swanson, meanwhile, made her return mid-season for a struggling Chicago Stars team that would eventually finish bottom of the league, making it harder for her to really shine, though she did enjoy some promising moments in her first few months back, particularly in the win over Racing Louisville in August, before netting her first USWNT goal since the Olympics in a 2-2 draw with Spain in October.

Rodman, meanwhile, was able to put that nagging back injury to one side as she simply blew the NWSL away. Despite January's record-breaking contract putting her into the limelight even more, Rodman reeled off 15 goals and 10 assists as the Washington Spirit made the NWSL Championship game, earning herself a well-deserved nomination for the Most Valuable Player accolade in the process.

She's shone repeatedly in the NWSL and she's risen to the occasion at the Olympics. In 2027, it's time for Rodman to show the Women's World Cup stage what she is all about.

While the parents are away — owner Steve Ballmer and head of basketball operations Lawrence Frank are suspended — GM Trent Redden will play.

Specifically, the cross-town Lakers like Lopez and Jones, reports Brian Windhorst and Tim MacMahon at the Hoop Collective Podcast (the players would love that, then they wouldn't have to move).

Nothing is imminent. With Brandon Ingram back, the 4-12 Clippers want to see if their fortunes turn, but don't be surprised if they are dealing by the deadline.

#2643. AI debt markets shudder as Nvidia's top 'banker' returns

AI credit markets are shuddering again with Jensen Huang back as CEO of Nvidia.

Fears about the massive debt being taken on to fund the artificial intelligence buildout climbed Tuesday as Wall Street weighed what Huang's return to Nvidia means for its bankrolling of the AI boom.

Huang is considered one of the top financiers, or bankers, in the AI industry, spearheading deals with neoclouds like CoreWeave and other firms to buy chips, backed in some cases by Nvidia guarantees. His return to Nvidia has revived prospects for the company to continue "circular financing" of AI chips and data centers — raising concerns among credit investors.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child of AI debt concerns, saw its stock sink 13% and the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 top 17%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

At the same time, the spread on the neocloud company's five-year credit default swaps jumped 8.5% to over 1,200 basis points. Credit default swaps are insurance against nonpayment and are considered a barometer of perceived risks. Rising CDS spreads mean investors view the debt as riskier.

Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday after stepping down on Nov. 12 amid allegations of multiple affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. His reinstatement on Monday was cheered by investors, who pushed stocks higher, yields lower and spreads on CDS tighter. However, stocks retreated, bond yields rose and CDS spreads widened on Tuesday.

Ben Emons, founder and chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors, called it a waning of the "Jensen effect."

The moves suggest "markets see government intervention as 'moral suasion' that carries credit and interest-rate risks," he said.

President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday he "convinced" the board to bring Huang back.

CoreWeave wasn't the only name seeing heightened concerns in CDS spreads. Oracle's five-year CDS spread jumped 7% to 355.68. Even highly rated hyperscalers Meta Platforms and Amazon.com saw spreads widen by more than 2%. Nvidia's CDS added 3.4%.

Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds, believes the drama that unfolded with Huang's return to Nvidia won't necessarily sit well with credit investors.

"A lot of old school credit people are going to look at what kind of materialized there, the administration's involvement in putting him back in, and I think a lot of credit participants are going to step back and tiptoe away from that a bit," he said. "Credit market investors typically don't like that type of drama or uncertainty."

While Nvidia has commitments across the AI ecosystem, it is the neoclouds that have been under the most scrutiny. Many of the companies, which rent out AI computing power and cloud capacity, are highly leveraged and have relied on Nvidia financing to reduce their exposure to the bond market.

With so much riding on Nvidia's funding, Huang's next move is being closely watched.

During his brief absence, chief financial officer Colette Kress said during the company's earnings call that Nvidia would be "rigorously evaluating future investments" and will remain disciplined in how it commits capital.

That suggested Nvidia was going to be more judicious with financing, says Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"That concern should be put to rest with Jensen [Huang] back," he said.

Investor Steve Eisman, of "Big Short" fame and host of "The Real Eisman Playbook" podcast, believes Huang feels emboldened now that he's back in charge.

"[H]e'll double down on the circular financing," Eisman predicted on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Tuesday.

After Huang's departure, Eisman believed that the ecosystem the CEO created by pouring money into AI companies would likely unwind and leave some of the companies in "big trouble."

"Now that he's back, they're not," he said.

Others are not so certain the level of funding will continue.

"Given scrutiny of disclosure around financing and guarantees … we do not expect Mr. Huang's return to bring a quick reversion to broader customer financing," Stifel analyst Ruben Roy said in a note Monday.

Nvidia said on its earnings call that it has $118 billion in guarantees, as of Oct. 25, to back AI projects.

Concerns about the level of debt to fund the AI infrastructure buildout had already taken hold before Huang's departure and reinstatement.

"These issues have not disappeared just because the White House pressured the weak board to reinstate Jensen Huang," said economist David Rosenberg, founder and president of Rosenberg Research.

John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson Investors, believes having Huang back at the helm "reaffirms his existing go-to-market strategy." However, the credit market is still taking a cautious look at the neoclouds as it waits for more clarity on long-term supply/demand dynamics.

Still, Lloyd is cautiously positive on CoreWeave, which he owns in portfolios he manages, and noted all the data point to a "pretty healthy environment right now." That includes strong residual values on graphics processing units and spot compute rates, he noted.

"The company is doing everything in its power to execute," he said. "They don't need the high yield market at this time."

In the meantime, investigations into Nvidia and Huang are ramping up. Huang is expected to appear before three House committees next week. Nvidia is conducting an independent investigation into his activities, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta has launched a probe. At the federal level, President Trump said Monday that U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche "has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"There's other shoes to drop," Rosenberg said. "I don't think that the book has been closed on this file."

#2640. Rams ride Blake Corum to Thanksgiving Eve win over Packers; Jordan Love throws 2 INTs with Christian Watson out

On his 26th birthday and in the NFL's first Thanksgiving Eve game, Los Angeles Rams running back Blake Corum starred with 184 rushing yards during a 26-13 win over the Green Bay Packers at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Corum became the first Rams player to carry the ball at least 30 times in a game during the Sean McVay era. Meanwhile, the Packers' offense floundered after losing wide receiver Christian Watson to a concussion late in the first half.

Green Bay quarterback Jordan Love threw a pair of interceptions and could have had a couple more. His team mustered a mere 55 total yards of offense in the second half.

McVay, previously 0-5 against Packers head coach Matt LaFleur, finally beat his former assistant. The Rams (7-4) have won five straight games. Green Bay (6-5) remains last in a crowded NFC North.

Packers edge rusher Micah Parsons, playing in his first game in nearly a year after tearing an ACL and meniscus in his left knee against the Denver Broncos in Week 15 last season, recorded a long-awaited sack.

Watson left the game twice: first with a thigh injury after making a 6-yard catch on the opening play from scrimmage and then for the concussion caused by a massive hit near the sideline late in the second quarter for which Rams safety Kamren Kinchens was ejected.

Forging forward without wide receivers Puka Nacua — who is reportedly out for the season after undergoing MCL surgery — and Davante Adams — who was still sidelined by a hamstring injury — the Rams managed to stake themselves to a 13-3 advantage, scoring on their first three possessions.

Stafford, who finished with 140 yards on 16-of-23 passing, made do with his lesser-known receivers. A 37-yard defensive pass interference penalty catapulted L.A.'s first drive. That ended with a 43-yard Brandon McManus field goal. McManus trotted back out to kick a 41-yarder following a Rams takeaway later in the opening frame. L.A. linebacker Nate Landman, forcing his eighth regular-season fumble in the past two seasons, punched the ball free from the grasp of Packers tight end Tucker Kraft.

A 32-yard connection between Love and Watson put the wheels in motion for Green Bay. Rookie kicker Trey Smack, who came in with just 15 makes on 21 field-goal attempts, got the Packers on the board with a 54-yard kick.

That's when Stafford answered with the kind of efficiency that made him the league MVP last season. He went 5 of 6, at one point keeping the series alive with a clutch dump-off to running back Kyren Williams despite duress on third-and-5. It wasn't long before Williams was surging through the middle for a 7-yard touchdown run to make it a two-score game.

A pair of highlight-reel plays thrust Green Bay right back into the thick of things. LaFleur turned to trickery initially, with wideout Savion Williams taking a handoff and throwing the ball back to Love, who went on to fling a pass downfield to Watson. His toe-tapping 21-yard reception was followed by a 39-yard catch and run from another receiver, Matthew Golden.

Watson was the one who found pay dirt, reeling in a 6-yard touchdown pass from Love midway through the second quarter. That score cut the Packers' deficit to 13-10.

Watson's night came to a premature end on Green Bay's next drive. LaFleur rolled the dice on fourth-and-1 from the L.A. 30-yard line, and it originally looked like that decision was going to be rewarded. Love located Watson for what would have been a chains-moving pickup, except the pass was broken up by a brutal blow from Kinchens near the sideline that leveled Watson.

Kinchens was ejected because, per the Netflix broadcast, he left his feet and made forcible contact to the head/neck area with his helmet.

Offsetting penalties — Golden was flagged for offensive pass interference — brought up another fourth-and-1. That time, Smack was sent out for a 48-yard field-goal attempt.

With that boot, it was 13-13. It remained that way heading into the break.

Wednesday was a game of attrition. Not only did the Packers lose Watson, but the Rams watched a pair of tight ends — Davis Allen (ankle) and Tyler Higbee (chest) — go out, along with left guard Bill Murray (ankle).

Even so, L.A.'s offense kept churning. It relied heavily on Corum. The ascending third-year pro from Michigan carried the rock nine times on a 14-play, eight-plus-minute drive that began the third quarter. Corum scored from a yard out to restore the Rams' lead.

While dominating possession, the Rams eventually established a cushion — that was after Stafford and Love traded interceptions. The latter took place in L.A. territory, as miscommunication between Love and Golden cost the Packers dearly.

A 35-yard Corum run set the stage for the third of McManus' four field goals.

Although Love converted a fourth-and-8 with a strike to wideout Bo Melton down the stretch, he tossed his second pick the next snap. Rams cornerback Emmanuel Forbes Jr. dropped deep into coverage and climbed the ladder to force the Packers' third turnover.

L.A.'s roster may be depleted, but McVay's group is overcoming that cascade of injuries with toughness. The Rams have now rushed for at least 200 yards in back-to-back games.

"Our identity going into this game was the most physical team's gonna win," Corum said during his on-field postgame interview. "And I think we showed that today. It's something to build on."

Blake Corum is easily the player of the game for LA. The RB finishes with 184 yards and a TD on 32 rushes.

The Rams improve to 7-4 and remain in the thick of the playoff picture.

Packers fall to 6-5 and have some ground to make up in the wild-card race.

LA hits a chip-shot field goal to extend the lead with 27 seconds left. We're just about finished here.

LA has the ball at the Packers 6-yard line on 2nd-and-1. One more first down should end the game.

Blake Corum is up to 155 yards on 31 rushes today as the Rams are close to putting this one away with a few big first downs. Packers are out of timeouts and we're under 3 minutes to play.

Emmanuel Forbes leaps to intercept Jordan Love on another deep ball. Rams take over at their own 27 with 3:39 to go. Love's second INT of the day is a costly one for the Packers, who are running out of time.

The big Blake Corum run helps deliver some critical points for LA on a 40-yard Brandon McManus field goal. That makes it a two-possession game with 6:13 to play.

Corum ripped off a 35-yard gain on 3rd-and-1 to set up the Rams in scoring position.

Another empty offensive possession for Green Bay, which quickly punts the ball away. Rams take over with 11:01 to play.

The Rams drove all the way to the Packers 40-yard line but Stafford's pass is incomplete on 3rd-and-6. Green Bay gets the ball back at their own 11 with 12 minutes to play.

Two plays after the Matthew Stafford interception, Jordan Love threw one.

There appeared to be some miscommunication between Love and wide receiver Matthew Golden.

Rams safety Jaylen McCollough capitalized, collecting the takeaway.

That's a missed opportunity for the Packers in L.A. territory.

Matthew Stafford just threw his 11th interception of the season.

Packers linebacker Ty'Ron Hopper was sitting in the passing lane and interrupted the over route Rams tight end Tyler Higbee was running.

Hopper returned the pick 21 yards to the L.A. 43-yard line.

Instead of answering L.A.'s touchdown drive, Green Bay went three-and-out.

It almost was worse for the Packers. Jordan Love was nearly picked off by Rams safety Quentin Lake, who jumped a pass intended for wideout Savion Williams.

On his ninth rushing attempt of the drive, Rams running back Blake Corum plunged into the end zone from a yard out.

Him plowing into the paint put L.A. ahead 20-13 with 6:58 left in the third quarter.

On third-and-goal, Rams wide receiver Konata Mumpfield came back to a ball Matthew Stafford threw to the pylon.

Mumpfield appeared to make the touchdown grab. That's what was called, after all. Upon review, however, it was ruled that the receiver didn't complete the process of the catch.

But there was a defensive holding penalty on the play, meaning that the Rams got a fresh set of downs at the goal line as a result of the play.

Facing a third-and-8, Matthew Stafford moved the chains with a 20-yard pass to wide receiver Konata Mumpfield, who's up to 69 receiving yards on four grabs.

Rams tight end Davis Allen is also out for the remainder of the game with an ankle injury that he reportedly suffered on L.A.'s first-half touchdown drive.

Christian Watson was able to come back from a thigh injury in the first quarter, but he won't be returning in the second half now that he's dealing with a concussion.

That's a tough blow for the Packers, who will be without their top wideout over the final two quarters of play.

A roller-coaster first half at SoFi Stadium ended with the score tied 13-13.

The Rams scored on their first three possessions and staked themselves to a 13-3 advantage. Since, the Packers have stormed back.

Green Bay wideout Christian Watson has caught four passes for 65 yards and a touchdown, but he's dealt with two injury issues. He's now being evaluated for a concussion.

Packers edge rusher Micah Parsons recorded a long-awaited sack near the end of the first half.

Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford has thrown for 98 yards on 12-of-15 passing.

Micah Parsons just announced his return to NFL action with a sack of Matthew Stafford.

With halftime nearing, Parsons dropped Stafford for a loss of 8 yards on first-and-10.

#2638. Nvidia's billion-dollar board bet: Who's protected as lawsuits mount?

Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia, after President Donald Trump urged the company's board to rehire Huang. But investigations into the company, its executive leadership and its board continue as outside criticism mounts.

"Clearly they caved to external pressure," said Betsy Atkins, an author and longtime public-company director. "The board failed," she said, when it initially allowed Huang's removal. "The board's role is to think of all stakeholders."

California Attorney General Rob Bonta is investigating whether Nvidia misrepresented information to investors. "There is classic corporate securities law on the books in California that prevents investors and the public from being misled by companies," Bonta said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Tuesday.

Directors are already defendants in a shareholder lawsuit accusing them of failing to oversee Nvidia. A separate securities class action targets the company and Huang, its co-founder.

Now the board’s insurance choices are part of the story. A risk advisor with direct knowledge of Nvidia’s coverage says the company built an approximately $1 billion D&O tower, insurance jargon for directors and officers insurance policies from different companies that combine to cover one massive risk.

Nvidia "loves insurance," the advisor said. “They buy insurance as if they have no balance sheet.” A billion-dollar tower would essentially mean Nvidia "bought the market," purchasing all the coverage it could get, according to an industry expert with 25 years working in financial insurance. The expert asked not to be named out of concern for past or potential future clients.

But Nvidia directed all that coverage to Side A only, according to CNBC's source. Side A protects directors and officers personally when the company cannot indemnify them. Side B covers the company for legal defense costs or settlements on behalf of directors and officers, and Side C protects the company when it's named as a defendant in a suit such as a securities claim.

The risk advisor says Nvidia believed it had "the war chest" to protect itself against a securities class action suit.

That choice is raising questions about whether the board protected itself at the company’s expense. CNBC asked Nvidia for comment but received no response.

An insurance CEO characterized a billion-dollar policy as a lot of coverage, but said a Side A-only allocation was a surprising move because it results in imbalanced coverage, protecting only directors.

That structure is not automatically a governance failure, according to a D&O insurance expert with long experience in coverage for banks, drugmakers and other businesses that often face litigation. Side A-only programs are common among companies with the capital to manage the corporate risk internally.

"For a company with Nvidia’s resources, retaining the company-side risk can make financial sense," the advisor said. It's Side A D&O that's "imperative to corporate governance."

"It is a capital-allocation decision," the expert told me. The company decides that buying insurance for its own balance sheet is not worth the premium. In other words, Side B and Side C are considered too expensive for the coverage the company gets.

The question for shareholders is whether the board’s decision to hold that risk was a sound use of the company’s resources and whether the company can absorb the costs if the claims grow.

A shareholder derivative complaint filed Nov. 11 names Huang, directors and other officers. It alleges that they failed to oversee risks involving Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang and made misleading statements. It also alleges that some defendants sold roughly $2 billion in Nvidia stock while holding material nonpublic information. Those remain allegations, not findings.

A separate securities class action, filed Nov. 9, names Nvidia and Huang. It seeks damages for investors who bought Nvidia shares between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, alleging the company and Huang misled investors.

The distinction matters: The derivative suit is brought on Nvidia’s behalf, while the class action seeks recovery for investors.

"Insurance is already at work," says Michel Léonard, chief economist at the Insurance Information Institute, describing standard policy mechanics, not Nvidia’s specific policy. "Once the suit is filed, D&O starts paying defense costs, long before anyone proves anything."

A claim still has to meet the policy’s terms, and defense costs can reduce the remaining limits. Nor does a drop in Nvidia’s market value by itself establish an insurable loss. Plaintiffs would need to prove legally recoverable damages; the policy would respond only to covered losses.

The board has already taken steps it says are aimed at accountability. Nvidia announced an independent investigation on Nov. 8, and independent directors retained outside counsel two days later. Huang resigned as CEO and a director on Nov. 11; the board appointed CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Nvidia said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised by Huang's extramarital relationships.

Atkins, who joined the board of Wynn Resorts in 2018 after founder Steve Wynn resigned, argues that allegations are not conclusions and that boards should also weigh governance concerns against the value a founder brings to a company’s innovation. Nvidia's investigation is continuing even as Huang resumes leadership.

“Will companies’ hyper-accelerated innovation speed be the same without them? I don’t think so,” said Atkins, author of "Don't Waste a Board Seat: A Decision-Maker's Guide to Choosing Directors Who Create Value."

Nvidia’s 2026 proxy also says the company has indemnity agreements with its directors and officers — separate from its insurance. Those agreements provide for the company to cover certain costs and liabilities when the law permits.

#2637. Report: G.M. Omar Khan called Aaron Rodgers directly to inform him of the benching

As expected, the Steelers view the events that resulted in the benching and eventual release of quarterback Aaron Rodgers differently than Rodgers does.

On one very specific point — as it relates to whether the Steelers properly handled the situation — the Steelers and Rodgers sharply disagree.

Rodgers said Wednesday that he learned he’d be benched and inactive when tight end Pat Freiermuth called Rodgers, after the announcement of the move was made at 11:10 p.m. ET on Tuesday night. However, Tom Pelissero of Netflix reported during the Wednesday night pregame show that G.M. Omar Khan called Rodgers to inform him of the change to Mason Rudolph.

It’s odd, to say the least, that the Steelers announced the move after 11:00 p.m. local time on a Tuesday night. If Rodgers didn’t know, there was no reason to let the world (and specifically the Broncos) know the move had been made.

The mere fact that the Steelers announced it when they did suggests that Rodgers knew about the decision, and that the Steelers believed he possibly would release it in terms that supported his broader version of the events.

By announcing it on Tuesday night, the Steelers pre-empted a late-night social-media post from Rodgers — or a strategic leak to a reporter — painting the situation in the light most favorable to Rodgers. For example, Rodgers could have characterized that he was benched because he was repeatedly blowing the whistle internally about coach Mike McCarthy’s various alleged lapses.

While it’s a minor point, it points to the broader issue of credibility. If Rodgers knew about the decision, any suggestion that he didn’t would be calculated to make the Steelers look inept for telling the world he’d been benched without letting him know about it in advance.

The truth may never be fully known. But it’s clear that, as to the things that happened over the past day or two, there are (as there always seems to be) two versions — Rodgers’s version and the team’s version.

It’s also possible there are three versions. Rodgers’s version, the Steelers’ version, and the truth.

#2635. Steelers should have known Aaron Rodgers, Mike McCarthy couldn't co-exist

When the Steelers hired coach Mike McCarthy, we cautioned against assuming that this meant there would be a reunion between McCarthy and quarterback Aaron Rodgers. That position assumed there would be a commonsense assessment of the specific history of McCarthy and Rodgers in Green Bay by those with the power to bring them together for the present and the future.

The reporting of Tyler Dunne, who at the time wrote for Bleacher Report, made it clear that there were issues between them during the latter years of McCarthy’s time with the Packers. Rodgers took it to another level on Wednesday, telling Pat McAfee and company that McCarthy believed Rodgers got him fired by the Packers — and that McCarthy had done some of the things he’s been doing with the Steelers when McCarthy coached the Packers.

If McCarthy believes Rodgers got him fired by the Packers, why in the world would McCarthy want Rodgers in his Pittsburgh locker room? It’s ludicrous. It’s asinine. It’s self-destructive.

From Rodgers’s perspective, why in the world would he want to play for McCarthy again? Although Rodgers said Wednesday that he believed McCarthy would be different given it’s Rodgers’s last year in the NFL and McCarthy’s first year in his dream job, it was naive for Rodgers to think that, at 63, McCarthy would suddenly start working harder than he ever has.

Oh, they tried to sell us on the idea that he would. “Attention to detail” became a talking point during training camp. Plenty of media members swallowed the hook.

Rodgers knew better. But he ignored his own experiences with McCarthy — in the same way McCarthy ignored his own experiences with Rodgers.

The situation cried out for someone, anyone in the organization to stand up and say, “Are we nuts? Once adversity strikes, this situation will crumble. And it will take us with it.”

It didn’t just crumble. It imploded into one of the most embarrassing situations any NFL franchise has endured in years, if not ever.

As the saying goes, when you dance with the devil, you don’t change the devil. The devil changes you. By allowing McCarthy and Rodgers to reprise their Lambeau rumba, the Steelers thought the music would stop in the postseason. Instead, McCarthy and Rodgers have pulled a franchise with six Super Bowl trophies into the eighth circle of dysfunction.

In the end, the team in the city known for blast furnaces has found itself in football hell.

#2626. NFL Thanksgiving Day preview: Eagles QB Joe Milton hopes to spoil Cowboys' hopes in his old home

The middle game of the Thanksgiving trio — the stuffing, if you will — lacks the meat and potatoes of the first and final games of the day. But Eagles at Cowboys still carries some potential playoff importance.

The 5-6 Cowboys host the 3-7 Eagles in a game that matters to Dallas. The Cowboys' offense has hit its stride recently, scoring 40 and 51 points, respectively, the past two games. Over the past five games, Dallas hasn't scored fewer than 27.

The problem? They're only 3-2 in that stretch, and the NFC East-leading Giants have kept that same pace.

The other problem? Dallas' defense. There were modest signs of improvement on that side of the ball in Mike Pettine's first game calling plays, especially compared to how the defense played against the 49ers. And for the first game possibly all season, the Cowboys could make a strong claim that they had the better defense — the Titans are that bad now, yes.

The Eagles limped into the bye with seven straight losses, but they're coming off one of their best efforts of the season in beating the Steelers on Sunday. Defensively, they kept the Steelers under wraps for most of the four quarters and gave QB Joe Milton and the offense a chance.

Milton returns to Dallas, where he spent parts of the past two seasons and saw action in four games last season behind Dak Prescott. Now Milton gets a chance to take on his former QB1 on Thursday after signing with the Eagles after Jalen Hurts landed on injured reserve.

The Cowboys left Milton, a preseason star the past two years, unprotected on their practice squad, and the Eagles gladly scooped him up. He has a chance to make the Cowboys pay for letting him walk — and before one of the biggest TV audiences Milton might have.

The Eagles' playoff hopes hover at less than 1%, according to Next Gen Stats. The Cowboys, however, are still alive at 22%, barely above the Commanders (21%) and behind the Giants (65%).

A loss would be pretty devastating. But beating Philadelphia would give the Cowboys a 3-1 mark in the division, which is the one edge they have right now on the Giants, who are 2-1-1 in NFC East games. The East could come down to the Week 17 Giants-Cowboys game, but every divisional matchup counts.

The Eagles, however, didn't look like a team ready to mail it in on Sunday. They showed some renewed vitality after the bye, with the team giving some younger players opportunities to stand out, including Milton. For Milton, there's personal pride on the line after spending parts of the past two years in Dallas, facing a defense that has plenty to prove.

When the Eagles traded Jordan Davis to the Jaguars, it shone the spotlight more on Jalen Carter, who started this season slowly but whose play has been on the rise lately. In Sunday's upset of the Steelers, Carter was active and effective despite suffering a quad injury just prior to the game. He was a full participant in practice this week, but the player he might have faced off against, Cowboys right guard Tyler Booker, did not practice and is not expected to play Thursday. The Eagles know they have to slow down Dallas' passing attack and pressure Dak Prescott, and the best way to do that might be to detonate the operation from the inside. Carter and the Eagles also can't have a repeat of the last meeting, in Week 7, when Dallas ran for 204 yards on 38 carries.

Sportsbooks opened this game Cowboys -1.5 in the summer — now it's -8.5. Losing Jalen Hurts for the season, along with a 3-7 record (and a putrid 2-8 record against the spread) will do that. Philadelphia put up a spirited defensive effort in a 19-16 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers as 3.5-point home underdogs on Sunday, but this Dallas offense will provide a much stiffer test. Eagles starting QB Joe Milton and Philadelphia collected only 11 first downs and 214 yards of total offense; that's not going to get it done. Dak Prescott & Co. can't control how well a rejuvenated defense plays under Mike Pettine, but the Cowboys have scored at least 27 points in each of the past five games. Dallas scored 51 points against Tennessee on Sunday; the Eagles have scored 40 points combined in their past three contests. The Eagles D will put up a good fight, but barring several turnovers, I don't believe it will be able to keep up with Dallas. Cowboys -2.5 is another good teaser leg to go with that Packers +8.5, which cashed on Wednesday. — Ben Fawkes

#2618. Rams Winners & Losers: LA beats Packers to bolster playoff odds

It's no secret that Wednesday's pre-Thanksgiving matchup between the Los Angeles Rams and Green Bay Packers carried immense weight for both teams' playoff chances.

The Rams took care of business behind Blake Corum's big rushing day on his birthday. They dealt a near-death blow to Green Bay's postseason odds.

The schedule to get to the playoffs is still long and littered with stiff competition. That is a tomorrow problem. For today, let's take inventory of all the individual contributions that led the Rams to their most important win on the season yet.

Corum made it seven-straight games with a touchdown. He has officially taken the starting running back job from Kyren Williams and continues to outshine his counterpart in terms of production. The third-year back rushed 32 times (!) for 184 yards (5.8 average) and a touchdown. He also added two catches for 21 yards through the air.

The Rams have needed an offensive spark nearly all season. It's clear that Corum has been the answer and is someone the team must rely on moving forward in order to make due on their sky-high expectations.

Jordan Love is not a quarterback that gets sacked often, even if his pass protection is often porous these days. Donald and Garrett were key to generating pressure. Love was only brought down a single time by Byron Young. The pressure helped force Love into some very curious decisions—of which resulted in key takeaways by the defense.

Donald and Garrett are as advertised, even if they are hitting their stride later into the season than originally expected.

You don't rush for 241 yards without a strong performance from the big guys up front. The Rams got the job done even with injuries that caused linemen to play out of position. Warren McClendon, Bill Murray, Tyler Higbee, and Davis Allen all dealt with injuries at some point. Rookie Keagen Trost, Justin Dedich, and David Quessenberry all played parts in relief.

The perseverance from this group in an all-important game was impressive.

With no Puka Nacua for the rest of the season and Davante Adams' return to health timeline currently uncertain, the only pass catcher who seems interested in stepping up is second-year receiver Konata Mumpfield. He added four receptions for 69 yards on Wednesday night. He also snagged a ball at the goal line that was originally called a touchdown and later reversed to incomplete. It was probably at least a completion even if the touchdown call was borderline and the ball short of the end zone.

Mumpfield's step forward is an encouraging sign for the offense. Their passing game is not where it needs to be. Mumpfield's production with Adams back in the fold should help matters.

Wesley Bailey and Josaiah Stewart are still playing sizeable rotational roles on defense. Last week Bailey snagged an interception. Against the Packers, Stewart made multiple key plays in coverage to prevent big gains. You won't see Garrett in coverage often—the Rams want him moving towards the quarterback. Someone has to do the dirty work and play the linebacker role. Stewart did an excellent job in this facet versus Green Bay.

With the Rams up one score late into the third quarter, Matthew Stafford threw an inexplicable first-down interception right to a Packers defender. It was a chance for Green Bay and Love to regain momentum, although Love made an even worse throw for a turnover just two plays later. The Rams stubbed their toe. The Packers let them off the hook.

It's still an open question whether the Rams have enough juice in the passing game to keep up with the likes of the Chiefs, 49ers, Cowboys, and Seahawks—all teams they will see in the coming weeks.

Stafford must be better both in terms of production and in his decision making. It's tough to win games when your leading rusher has more yards than your quarterback (184 versus 140).

But the passing game struggles do not rest entirely on Stafford's shoulders. The receiving corps aside from Mumpfield is not inspiring confidence. The injuries at the tight end position from this game spell concern moving forward. Sean McVay's play calling leaned more towards "don't lose" then "go for the win". LA was reliant on screen passes that often went for minimal gain and there were a few close laterals that could have resulted in disaster.

Something needs to change. Do the Rams have the right players in order to turn things around, or will the passing attack be the reason they fall short of Super Bowl expectations?

The previous four came against the Las Vegas Raiders, Chargers, Washington Commanders and Arizona Cardinals, none of which have winning records.

But the matchup against the Packers was different, and it carried huge postseason implications.

The Packers (6-5) are in the hunt for a playoff spot out of the NFC North, where the Detroit Lions (8-2), Chicago Bears (8-2), and Minnesota Vikings (7-3) are also battling for postseason berths.

Now the Rams have the head-to-head tiebreaker if the Rams and Packers end up with the same record at the end of the regular season.

Rams running back Kyren Williams scores on a seven-yard touchdown run in the second quarter against the Packers on Wednesday. (Allen J. Schaben / Los Angeles Times)

The Rams have games remaining against the Kansas City Chiefs (8-2), the NFC West-leading San Francisco 49ers (9-1), the Dallas Cowboys (5-6) and two games against the defending Super Bowl-champion Seattle Seahawks (6-4) sandwiched around a trip to play the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-7).

With receiver Puka Nacua out for the season and Davante Adams still on injured reserve, second-year pro Konata Mumpfield stepped up and caught four passes for 69 yards.

Quarterback Matthew Stafford completed 16 of 23 passes for 140 yards, with an interception.

On a night the Rams broke out their "Fearsome White" uniforms to honor the team's famed Fearsome Foursome defensive line of the 1960s, Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and Co. did not disappoint.

Byron Young sacked Packers quarterback Jordan Love. Garrett, Donald and Young tackled running backs for losses. Donald batted down a pass.

Linebacker Nate Landman forced a fumble and safety Jaylen McCollough and cornerback Emmanuel Forbes Jr. intercepted passes.

It wasn't all good news: Tight ends Davis Allen and Tyler Higbee left the game because of ankle and chest injuries, respectively. Offensive lineman Bill Murray also left the game because of an injury.

In the first half, McManus kicked two field goals and Williams rushed for a touchdown, and the Packers kicked two field goals and scored on Christian Watson's short touchdown reception for a 13-13 tie at halftime.

U2 performs during halftime between the Rams and Green Bay Packers at SoFi Stadium on Wednesday. (Allen J. Schaben / Los Angeles Times)

Watson left the game in the second quarter after sustaining a concussion on a hit by Kam Kinchens that led to the Rams safety being ejected.

The Rams started the second half with a 14-play, 64-yard drive that Corum capped with a short touchdown run.

On the Rams' next possession, Packers linebacker Ty'Ron Hopper intercepted a pass by Stafford and returned it 20 yards. But on the Packers' second play, Rams safety McCollough intercepted a deep pass.

McManus kicked his third field goal with just over six minutes left to increase the lead to 10 points.

The Rams clinched the victory when Forbes intercepted a pass with 3:39 remaining, and McManus added another field goal with 27 seconds left.

#2608. Here's a roadmap to the Aaron Rodgers developments, one of the craziest stories in years

If you were traveling on Wednesday or otherwise not plugged in for one of the most rollicking, unpredictable days in years if not ever, you’re in luck.

We’ve reconstructed the full timeline as to the events regarding now-former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers.

It actually started on Monday, when coach Mike McCarthy was asked whether he has considered using one of the team’s other three quarterbacks when the offense is struggling. McCarthy, whose body language in hindsight suggests he was dreading the question, said without equivocation, “Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback.”

On Tuesday, Rodgers took his usual reps at practice. He conducted his usual midweek press conference. Unbeknownst to most of the media or the general public, the Steelers were changing their play-calling procedures to have quarterbacks coach Tom Arth, and not McCarthy, communicate the calls to Rodgers through the speaker in his helmet.

Then came Tuesday night. At 11:10 p.m. ET, the Steelers issued a statement — not from coach Mike McCarthy or G.M. Omar Khan or owner Art Rooney II but from team spokesman Burt Lauten — that Mason Rudolph will start on Friday against the Broncos and Rodgers will be inactive.

The news forced the Broncos to make a quick pivot in their preparations from Rodgers to Rudolph. As one source put it, the Broncos weren’t sure whether it was a good thing or a bad thing.

It was definitely a bad thing, all things considered, for the Steelers.

By Wednesday morning, reports emerged that it was a coach’s decision. At 8:00 a.m. ET, McCarthy informed the team of the decision.

Rodgers wasn’t there. As it turns out, he was excused.

Enter Pat McAfee. He teased a surprise guest at 1:40 p.m. ET. As expected, it was Rodgers.

Rodgers took a flamethrower to McCarthy, airing out dirty laundry that created a major mess for his now-former team. He exposed the fact that, at halftime of the Week 11 loss to the Eagles, McCarthy broke down the locker-room gathering by saying, “1-2-3 Packers.”

Rodgers also said McCarthy was falling asleep during some meetings and missing other meetings, expressing (in passive-aggressive fashion) concern for McCarthy’s health.

But Rodgers also said it was nothing new, and that McCarthy had done the same things in Green Bay, when they worked there together a decade ago.

Rodgers also made it clear he wouldn’t stay with the Steelers. After his session with McAfee and company, Dulac reported that the Steelers were expected to release Rodgers. By the official close of business, they’d waived him.

A question lingers as to whether the Steelers will try to deny Rodgers the balance of his $22 million salary. It won’t be easy; they’ll need to both void the guarantees and wipe out his eligibility for termination pay (in the form of his remaining salary) under the Collective Bargaining Agreement.

McCarthy met with reporters on Wednesday, after all hell had broken loose. He admitted to the “1-2-3 Packers” comment, calling it an “[e]mbarrassing moment.”

McCarthy also said that Rodgers was benched after issuing an “ultimatum” that was “clearly outside of his job description.”

ESPNFL thereafter reported that McCarthy “has the full support” of the organization, and that the team is “not planning to make any immediate changes.” The key word may be “immediate"; with few viable options only two days before a Black Friday game against the Broncos, changes could come later.

The overriding takeaway is that someone with the Steelers knew or should have known that McCarthy and Rodgers couldn’t co-exist. Because, obviously, they didn’t co-exist.

If, as Rodgers claims, McCarthy believed Rodgers got him fired in Green Bay, McCarthy shouldn’t have wanted a reunion with Rodgers. And if, as Rodgers claims, McCarthy was doing the same kinds of things in Green Bay that he did in Pittsburgh, Rodgers shouldn’t have wanted a reunion with McCarthy.

The reunion has now ended abruptly, with seven games left in the 2026 regular season. It remains to be seen whether Rodgers wants to play with another team, or whether another team wants him. Any team that signs him risks being on the receiving end of a future gripe session from Rodgers in which he lists all the things that team and/or the coach did wrong — without ever acknowledging his own role in the reality that it didn’t work out.

The good news, if there is any, is this: If Rodgers never plays again, his final NFL pass will have been a touchdown.

Which is a better outcome than if he’d retired after the 2025 season. His final pass that year was a pick-six in the playoffs.

#2602. Knicks rally to beat Cavaliers behind unlikely hero, expanded lineup to keep slim NBA Cup hopes alive

Mike Brown coached Wednesday's NBA Cup contest like a preseason game. He used a 12-man rotation, throwing out Tyler Nickel for his NBA debut and giving important minutes to sparsely used Pacôme Dadiet.

Brown, as he noted before tipoff, sees the scheduling benefits of being eliminated from Adam Silver's beloved tournament.

But it didn't matter. The Knicks (12-6), winners of six straight overall, surged in the fourth quarter behind unlikely hero Jose Alvarado.

Mikal Bridges celebrates after hitting a 3-pointer during the Knicks' 121-102 win over the Cavaliers on Nov. 25, 2026, at Madison Square Garden. Jason Szenes for NY Post

They avoided Cup elimination — at least for a couple of days — with a 121-102 win over the collapsing Cavaliers, who blew an 11-point lead late in the third quarter.

The Knicks (1-2 in group play) remain unlikely to advance. To win the group, they'd need a victory over the Heat on Friday by at least seven points and a Sixers loss to the Pacers. Advancing as the wild card is more complicated and unlikely.

But the defending Cup champs aren't technically eliminated as of Thanksgiving.

They were short-handed Wednesday without OG Anunoby (calf strain) and Miles McBride (left adductor tightness). They lost backup center Andre Drummond to a head injury in the first half.

Then they punished the Cavs (9-10) by winning the fourth quarter 39-17 with Alvarado scoring 16 of his 21 points in the final period and Brown going deep into his bench.

"I looked at the bench in the first quarter and realized, 'Wow, we played like 10 people in that first quarter,' " said Josh Hart, who had 15 points and 11 assists.

Jose Alvarado celebrates after hitting a second 3-pointer in the fourth quarter of the Knicks' win over the Cavaliers. Jason Szenes for NY Post

Mikal Bridges finished with an efficient 19 points. Karl-Anthony Towns extended his double-double streak to 15 (barely) with 12 points and 10 boards.

If and when Brown's squad is out of the tournament, the coach is looking at elimination as an NBA Cup half full. Losing translates to an easier schedule for the Knicks, which wasn't lost on the coach before Wednesday's comeback win.

Brown knows because the NBA shared the possibilities. Advancement potentially brings another three road games — including the final in Indiana.

Josh Hart reacts during the second quarter of the Knicks' win over the Cavaliers at Madison Square Garden. Jason Szenes for NY Post

And elimination means two games — including one at home — over a nine-day stretch.

"You look at it and you're like, 'Whoa, hell, that's a lot of days off if you don't advance,' " Brown said. "And so, again, you wanna compete, you wanna win, but if you don't … there's an opportunity if you got some guys banged up to get rest and or to work on some things in between the games that you have if you're not involved in the Cup."

Silver won't like that answer from the defending NBA Cup champs. But Brown was speaking from experience.

The Knicks added a long road trip to their schedule last season because of the NBA Cup, then an 83rd game with the final in Las Vegas.

The results were phenomenal for the Knicks. They won the Cup, earned the prize money (each player won over $500,000) and months later captured the big NBA championship.

But the Knicks, as an organization, didn't fully embrace Silver's tournament. It took them nearly a full year to hang the banner.

Then Wednesday, the coach of the Cup champs was openly espousing the virtues of being eliminated.

Mikal Bridges rises up for a layup during the second quarter of the Knicks' win over the Cavaliers at Madison Square Garden. Jason Szenes for NY Post

No crying over a spilled NBA Cup. For now, though, the Cup is still on the table.

"When I talk about the Cup, it adds a level of stress maybe on your mind and your body because the games are intense as you go along and you're playing more games in a short amount of time," Brown said. "I remember last year it was like, 'Game, Game, Game.' And then you win the Cup and you celebrate it that night and you hop on a plane and go play in Indiana the next night. And so it's great. You like the competition and the setup but it adds a lot of stress to you physically and mentally. I'm saying this because especially with the extended season we had last year and how taxing the games were for our playoff run mentally and physically, I'm trying to be smart."

#2601. Why Wu-Tang Clan is performing during halftime at Bears vs. Lions NFL Thanksgiving game

Why Wu-Tang Clan is performing during halftime at Bears vs. Lions NFL Thanksgiving game originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Of all the performers the NFL has enlisted to rock the stage on Thanksgiving Day, few have paired style with substance quite like Wu-Tang Clan.

The Staten Island-based outfit appears to be the largest act the NFL has booked in terms of number of members, with nine contributors — RZA, GZA, Inspectah Deck, U-God, Ghostface Killah, Method Man, Raekwon, Masta Killa and Cappadonna — expected to feature in some way during Bears vs. Lions.

So, just why did Wu-Tang Clan get the call over other noteworthy acts, some of whom call Motown home? Here's a look at why the NFL opted to give the rap group the nod in the first game of the Thanksgiving Day slate.

MORE:Meet the full list of 2026 NFL Thanksgiving performers, from U2 to national anthem singers

Wu-Tang Clan is one of rap's seminal acts, a dizzying blend of lyricism and gritty deliveries that helped put East Coast rap on the map in the early-1990s. The group hasn't released in album in more than a decade. Still, the brand remains as relevant as ever, influencing legions of rappers young and old.

Wu-Tang Clan charmed listeners with its first release, "Enter the Wu-Tang: 36 Chambers" in 1993, a titan of a project headlined by "C.R.E.A. M." and "Protect Ya Neck." An underground release that centered around our protagonists' experiences growing up in New York, "Enter the Wu-Tang" didn't project to garner much airplay. The content — namely its humor and imagery — proved too difficult for listeners to ignore. By 1995, the album was certified Platinum and 30 years on, it has sold more than four million records.

Those sales were no aberration. The project is adorned with kung-fu references, musings on the Nation of Islam and good old-fashion braggadocio.

MORE: Best NFL Thanksgiving halftime shows ever, ranked from Creed to Dolly Parton

"This is the sound of accidental fame," wrote Pitchfork's Rollie Pemberton in a retrospective review. "Something as unique and unusual as this record isn't supposed to find itself at the height of commercial viability; it's supposed to smolder underground, hidden from the view of mainstream America, who surely would not be ready for such a challenge. But America was ready, in part because this one challenged convention, not listeners."

The album — and its follow-up, "Wu-Tang Forever" — remains tethered to the public consciousness, as does the myriad solo projects crafted by the group's nine members. Predictably, the group is getting its due, best encapsulated by its recent induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

Wu-Tang Clan isn't your typical Thanksgiving Day performers. But its pronounced impact on rap, music and pop culture more broadly can't be denied. That seems to have been enough to land the group a coveted spot on the marquee for Thursday's Thanksgiving Day fixtures.

#2597. Knicks 121, Cavs 102: Scenes from a second-half bench bash

The Knicks' hopes of repeating as NBA Cup champions hinged on beating Cleveland (9-10) tonight and Miami on Friday, while Philadelphia had to beat Miami (which they did) and Indiana has to topple Philadelphia. Even then, advancement would come down to point differential, meaning New York (12-6) would likely need to win both games by double digits.

Consider the mission half completed. As you could deduce from the blazing blue court at Madison Square Garden, tonight's tilt was a Cup game. Three Knicks were sidelined by injury: OG Anunoby, Miles McBride, and Jordan Clarkson. Anunoby's absence was felt as the Cavaliers scored 61 first-half points (and a lopsided free-throw disparity stung, too). The adjustments Mike Brown made in the locker room paid dividends on the court. His squad applied stingier defense, got their turnovers under control, won the fourth quarter 39-17, and flipped the game to win, 121-102.

Of the six Knicks with double-digit points tonight, Jose Alvarado's barrage of fourth-quarter triples and his season-high / team-high 21 were arguably the most impactful. On a short-handed night, and with multiple starters playing through injury, Jose was once again prepared to step into the spotlight and contribute meaningful minutes. What a professional! What depth!

Three consecutive turnovers didn't help (two by Karl-Anthony Towns, one by Josh Hart) as the Knicks fell behind early in the first quarter. Midway through the period, Jalen Brunson scored seven in under two minutes to regain the lead. In this streaky contest, though, it made sense that he missed his next five attempts. Towns (12 PTS, 10 RBS, 7 AST, +21) was a game-time decision due to knee soreness, and his scoring showed the limp, producing a single point in the frame. Filling in for Anunoby in the first five, Landry Shamet made his sixth start of the season. He finished with a tidy 11 points on three made three-pointers.

The quarter was competitive until the final three minutes. After Pacôme Dadiet (yes, him!) drilled a triple to pull the Knicks within one, Cleveland rattled off a 10-0 run, powered by five consecutive points from Meleek Thomas, two Thomas Bryant free throws, and a Donovan Mitchell and-one. The latter easily had the biggest impact on the quarter, tallying 14 points, three dimes, and a steal. As for New York's bench support, Dadiet (7 PTS, 14 MIN) provided positive defensive efforts with a block and a steal, but neither Tyler Kolek nor Andre Drummond moved the needle. New York managed just six points over the final five-ish minutes, and Cleveland closed the quarter ahead, 34-23.

To start the second, the good guys outscored the villains by ten, chiseling an 11-point deficit to one. Credit Towns and his four points, two dimes, and two blocks for the comeback. Mohamed Diawara lent a triple, too, and Mikal Bridges found his rhythm, blasting out seven fast points. Naturally, Cleveland responded with a 9-2 stretch when James Harden (28 PTS, 1-8 3PT) finally got on the board. Dadiet drizzled water on our good feelings by missing three straight shots, and Brunson still couldn't regain his touch, going scoreless from the field in the period.

Playing from 55-44 down with four minutes left in the half, the hosts posted 11 unanswered points, eight of which belonged to Bridges. He'd finish the half with 17 points. This, my friends, is what's known as a circus shot:

Despite dealing with a sore shoulder, Hart picked Harden's pocket twice, converting one steal into a layup. Unfortunately, after Bridges tied the game at 55, Donovan Mitchell (30 PTS, 1-7 3PT) and Harden combined for six unanswered points, aided by a Bridges turnover. The home team won the quarter 33-27 but entered intermission trailing 61-56.

Through the half, Harden and Mitchell combined for 34 points in the half, while their bench contributed 13. New York had shot better from the field (54% to 49%) and significantly better from deep (50% to 31%), they were on the wrong end of the score due to a glaring free-throw disparity. New York had attempted just eight freebies, while Cleveland shot more than twice that. The Cavs outscored won the paint, 28-16, and the boards. Another glaring stat: Cleveland converted six Knicks miscues into 13 points, while New York squeezed just two points out of five giveaways.

Cleveland opened the second half on an 11-5 run to restore its double-digit lead. Down 74-65 midway through the period, the Knicks got a boost from an unexpected source: Tyler Nickel. The rookie sank a triple, followed by another from Landry Shamet, to cut the deficit to three. Nickel contributed five points but also committed four fouls in under six minutes—that will get straightened out with experience. Harden extended Cleveland's advantage to 85-77 with under three minutes remaining. But then another unexpected player pitched in: James Wiseman provided some valuable minutes off the bench, finishing the game with six points and seven boards in six minutes. Shamet helped the Knicks win the quarter 26-24 and enter the fourth trailing 85-82.

The Knicks opened the fourth quarter on a 12-0 run, turning a three-point deficit into a nine-point advantage in less than three minutes. Jose Alvarado (a team-high 21 points, 8-10 FG, 19 MIN) was the catalyst, drilling consecutive triples and picking Donovan Mitchell's pocket to set up a Dadiet layup. Hart took a turn orchestrating the offense, collecting four assists during the opening surge. The Ohio Players missed their first five shots, four of them by Mitchell, and committed two turnovers as the Knicks piled on the points.

Wiseman (!) helped goose New York's lead to 13 with four points and three offensive rebounds in a brief fourth-quarter stint. When Mitchell and Harden scored five unanswered points to trim the deficit to eight, Alvarado responded with a jumper, and Jalen Brunson buried a triple, his only basket of the quarter. Alvarado was the unquestionable star of the fourth, scoring 16 of his 21 points, including four three-pointers. Hart was nearly as impactful, contributing eight points, six assists, three rebounds, a steal, and a block in the frame. The Knicks closed on a 7-0 run, their defense holding Cleveland scoreless over the final two minutes and change.

Welcome back to associate head coach Chris Jent, who returned to the sidelines after a month away.

Welcome to CricketNews.com's live coverage of the 1st semi-final between India A and Sri Lanka A at the West End Park International Cricket Stadium in Doha.

India A will play Sri Lanka A in the first semi-final of the ACC Men's Asia Cup Rising Stars, after finishing second in Group B behind Pakistan A.

Tilak Varma's side went into their final group game on Tuesday knowing a win would confirm their place, and they got it in the most emphatic way available. The UAE posted 249 for 8, built on Harpreet Singh's 130 from 144 balls, and India A chased it down in 14.2 overs.

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi made 204 from 53 deliveries with seven fours and 28 sixes, and the seven-wicket win lifted India A's net run rate to 3.523, comfortably the highest in the tournament.

That was not enough to catch Pakistan A, who won all three group games, including a 48-run victory over India A on Sunday. Group A finished with Sri Lanka A unbeaten on six points and Bangladesh A second on four, which sets the semi-finals as Group A winner against Group B runner-up and Group A runner-up against Group B winner.
