#2591. Nets topple Bucks in NBA Cup clash to snap five-game skid

The teams with the two worst records in the Eastern Conference faced each other Wednesday night in Milwaukee, but no one needed to accuse either the Nets or the Bucks of tanking in this one.

Neither team can win the draft lottery after the season because both franchises essentially traded their respective 2027 first-round picks years ago, but the Nets at least halted their five-game losing streak with a defensively improved 104-97 victory in an NBA Cup game at Fiserv Forum.

"Just do it again. Every time we have a good performance where we fight and we compete, we follow it up with some bulls–t, with some bad ones," Noah Clowney told the YES Network after the game. "So we're trying to stack it this time and keep two or three good ones in a row."

Julius Randle netted a team-high 28 points as the Nets (4-13) posted their first NBA Cup victory after losses earlier in the season against the Pistons and the Magic.

Julius Randle, who scored a team-high 28 points, shoots a floater during the Nets' 104-97 win over the Bucks on Nov. 25, 2026, in Milwaukee. Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images

Michael Porter Jr. was held to 12 points on 4-for-14 shooting with 11 rebounds to follow another quiet scoring night (11) Monday in Minnesota.

Egor Dëmin had an active game with 15 points and a plus-15 rating in 25 minutes off the bench.

Clowney nailed three 3-pointers among his 17 points, and Day'Ron Sharpe contributed 11 points, 14 boards and five assists for the Nets.

Tyler Herro, who had a career-best 50-point game Saturday against the 76ers, scored 21 of his 28 points in the second half for the Bucks (2-17).

"We've lost a few in a row, so we've gotta try to get a win no matter who we're playing against," Porter told YES before the game. "They're an NBA team. They are at the bottom of the standings right now, but so are we, so it's gonna be a dogfight, and we gotta try to get out of here with a win."

The NBA instituted rule changes in the offseason to discourage tanking for draft position, essentially penalizing the teams with the worst three records in the league with lower odds to secure the No. 1 overall pick in the lottery.

The Nets' 2027 first-round pick is controlled by the Rockets from an unprotected pick swap as part of Brooklyn's deal to acquire James Harden in January 2021.

The Bucks, who dealt away superstar forward Giannis Antetokounmpo to the Heat over the summer, also had committed to a pick swap involving their 2027 first-rounder when they acquired guard Jrue Holiday from New Orleans in 2020.

Noah Clowney, who scored 17 points off the bench, puts up a shot during the second quarter of the Nets' road win over the Bucks. Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images

The Nets had allowed at least 70 points in the first half four times during their five-game skid, but this slow start was more due to offensive inefficiency.

Brooklyn missed five of its first six shots and spotted the Bucks a 9-2 lead in the first three minutes.

But Porter knocked down two straight 3s as part of a 15-1 run en route to a 28-24 edge through 12 minutes.

A 3-pointer by Clowney and a jumper by Randle extended the cushion to 10 early in the second. The Nets led by as many as 13 before the Bucks closed within 51-47 before intermission.

"We have to close quarters better," Randle, who had 16 in the half, told YES.

Rookie point guard Mikel Brown Jr. scored all six of his points in the second half after posting 17 in his first NBA start Monday in Minnesota.

Brown finally recorded his first two buckets after seven misses to push Brooklyn back ahead before two late dunks by Sharpe and a traditional 3-point play by Dëmin helped the Nets carry a 77-71 edge into the final quarter.

"It all came from the defensive side. I was more locked in, and everything else came to me naturally," Dëmin said.

Day'Ron Sharpe, who scored 11 points and grabbed 14 rebounds, slams home a dunk during the Nets' win over the Bucks in Milwaukee. Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images

Keon Ellis (plus-14) and Grant Nelson provided some defensive energy off the bench to open the fourth, and Porter converted an and-1 to stretch the lead back to 11 with 10:38 remaining.

"Overall, proud of the effort. Our guys played hard," Nets coach Jordi Fernández said. "Guys were asking for subs, and that tells me that everybody did everything possible.

"That's how it's supposed to be … and that's who we want to be. Now let's see if we can play this hard two games in a row."

Moritz Wagner didn't play in the second half due to what the Nets said was left knee soreness.

#2590. PFT's Thanksgiving and Week 12 2026 NFL picks

After flirting a couple of times with landing under .500 in a given week of picks, it finally happened. For Week 11, I went 6-7.

That’s what I get for trying to pick upsets. In Week 11, it was Chalk City — and 12 of 13 home teams won.

And so, from now on, I’m not getting cute. I’m sticking with my first impulse. I’m not overthinking it. The first number that pops into my head will be the pick.

For the year, I’m at 102-60-1. The success rate is still 62.5 percent. Here’s hoping I can find a way to push it a little higher with the 16 games to be played from Wednesday through Monday.

It’s the biggest early-window Thanksgiving game ever, with both teams at 8-2. Ben Johnson’s Bears gave up 52 points during last year’s visit to Ford Field. They’ll be determined to achieve a different result this time, in what becomes a true litmus test for the new-look Bears. If they’re truly contenders, this is a game they win.

It won’t be a cakewalk. For Philly, it’s the closest they’ll get this year to a game with a postseason vibe. But the Cowboys have a chance to make a run at the Giants — if Dallas can also hold off the Commanders.

Josh Allen is 5-0 against Patrick Mahomes in the regular season, 0-4 against Mahomes in the postseason. The trend continues, thanks to conditions that are more conducive to Allen making the right throw at the right time.

This one had the feel of a game the Steelers would find a way to win, until the benching of Aaron Rodgers threw everything into disarray.

It feels like an elimination game in Houston, even if the winner will still be facing an uphill climb to the postseason. When in doubt, ride with the clearly better quarterback.

This will be a far cry from the 1958 NFL Championship. The Giants are surging, and the Colts are slowly disintegrating.

As the saying goes, it’s not the size of the dog in the fight but the size of the fight in the dog. Unfortunately, this fight is round two of Doberman vs. Chihuahua.

The Dolphins are running out of chances to get a second win (if they even want one).

Kirk Cousins gets the double whammy — his first home game in his second stint with the Vikings, and his first shot at revenge against the team that signed him and then drafted his replacement.

It’s fitting that a game pitting two struggling teams coached by former Ohio State and Michigan players happens one day after a game between struggling Ohio State and Michigan teams.

Monday night’s upset of the Bengals means nothing if the Commanders bungle a winnable game at Arizona.

Having an extra week to prepare, coupled with the urgency of a 6-4 record, is just what the doctor ordered for the Seahawks.

The NFL will be happy it flexed this one into primetime. (For reasons other than getting Patriots-Chargers out of that window.)

Tampa Bay is running out of chances to pull themselves back into contention.

#2586. Rams shut down Packers in second half for a 26-13 win in NFL's first Thanksgiving Eve game

The Rams and Packers played to a tie in the first 30 minutes of Wednesday night’s game in Los Angeles, but the second half was all Rams.

Blake Corum ran for 151 yards and a score in final 30 minutes and the Rams defense shut out the Packers to pave the way to a 26-13 win. The victory is the fifth in a row for the Rams and they are now 7-4 with a Thursday night home game against the Chiefs on deck in Week 13.

The win moves the Rams ahead of the Packers in the race for NFC playoff spots and Thursday’s game between the Lions and Bears will have further impact on the chances for all four teams to advance to the postseason.

Corum’s touchdown came at the end of the Rams’ first possession of the second half and he finished the game with a career-high 32 carries for 184 yards.

That scoring drive ate up more than eight minutes. The Packers had a quick three-and-out, but briefly showed some life when linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper picked off Matthew Stafford to set the offense up in Los Angeles territory. Jordan Love turned the ball right back over when he hung a deep pass that safety Jaylen McCullough snagged out of the air. The Rams would then ride Corum and Kyren Williams on a pair of drives that covered more than 11 minutes.

The Packers’ last chance came with 6:13 left and they moved the ball to midfield before Love threw his second interception of the game. Cornerback Emmanuel Forbes got that one and the Packers were out of timeouts well before the two-minute warning.

Sticking with the ground game helped to limit Packers defensive end Micah Parsons’s impact in his return from last season’s torn ACL. He had a sack late in the first half, but Stafford only threw eight times after the break and the Packers’ run defense could not get their offense the ball often enough to get back into the game.

Love was 17-of-29 for 198 yards and a touchdown, but clearly missed wide receiver Christian Watson after he left the game with a concussion. They only picked up two first downs after halftime and they’ll hope that an extended break before their Week 13 trip to New Orleans is enough time for him to return to action.

The Rams have several injuries of their own to monitor as guard Bill Murray joined tight ends Davis Allen and Tyler Higbee in making early exits from the game. They’d like to have all those players back next week, but they showed on Wednesday night that Corum can sometimes be enough all by himself.

#2584. Rapid Recap: Nets 104, Bucks 97

The Milwaukee Bucks follow a string of solid games with one of their worst in a long time, losing at home to the Brooklyn Nets, 104-97. Tyler Herro led the Bucks with 28 points and five assists, while Kel'el Ware led the Bucks bench with 13 points and 14 rebounds. Julius Randle led the Nets with 28 points, and Noah Clowney led their bench with 17 points.

The game started with the Bucks on the attack, forcing three personal fouls in the first 90 seconds and exploiting the mismatches created when four forwards and one guard are the opposing starting five. Myles Turner wasted no time pulling out his three-ball from Toronto as the Bucks quickly built a 9-2 lead. But of course, the Nets started finding their shot as the Bucks let their feet off the gas, going on a 16-2 run as Milwaukee's offence dried up like the Sahara Desert. The Bucks didn't score another field goal until the 4:08 mark, when Jaime Jaquez Jr. finally buried a three, which set off an 8-2 run that included a sweet baseline dunk by Kel'el Ware. Despite being in the bonus for more than eight minutes, the Bucks couldn't take advantage, shooting only six free throws for the quarter and ending the period down 28-24.

The second quarter started where the first quarter ended: with Ryan Rollins throwing up ill-advised shots—he was bad in this one. Meanwhile, the Nets steadily built a 41-28 lead through the first five minutes. Thankfully, the young Bucks off the bench played their typical brand of high-energy defense and held Brooklyn to six points over the next five minutes, but unfortunately, the home side couldn't buy a bucket themselves. Milwaukee did at least outscore Brooklyn 11-4 in the final few minutes to cut the deficit to four, with Ware giving fans a reason to get hyped with a monster dunk before Jaquez scored a quick lay-up to end the half on a high note. Milwaukee headed into the locker room down 47-51.

Coming out of halftime, the Bucks kept up the pace and quickly regained the lead, largely thanks to 11 quick points from Herro, and it finally felt like the home team had found a flow. Unfortunately, that flow ended as Rollins decided to dominate the ball, force shots, and make head-scratching decisions in general. Eventually, the Nets crept back ahead after another scoring drought by the Bucks late in the third quarter. If not for Ware imposing his will in the paint, the Nets may have run away with it. Instead, the big man finished the third quarter with 10 points and 10 rebounds, scoring the final four to keep the deficit at six, 77-71.

The Nets extended their lead to 10 pretty quickly to open the final frame, as the Bucks struggled to get paint touches, something that seemed like it would come easier after getting in the paint so effectively against Philadelphia and Toronto. Milwaukee made a few pushes, but each one ended in an unforced error; they just couldn't get out of their own way. The game ended ugly as the Bucks turned it over nine times in the fourth quarter alone to give this one away. One of the more disappointing efforts of the last few years, frankly, and that's saying something.

26: the number of free throw attempts the Nets had, which allowed them to hang in the game despite their horrid shooting.

Ryan Rollins needs to be glued to the bench for a game (or five).

#2582. Packers Snap Counts: Micah Parsons played less than 40 percent of snaps

Micah Parsons made his 2026 debut tonight, and he was certainly on a pitch count. Let's take a look at every player who saw action (or didn't) in the Green Bay Packers' 26-13 loss to the Los Angeles Rams tonight.

As a reminder, the scratches today were running back Josh Jacobs (finger), linebacker Ziare Franklin (shin), offensive lineman Donovan Jennings, offensive lineman Jager Burton and offensive lineman Mekhi Becton (all three were healthy scratches to get down to a 48-man game-day roster).

The Packers' top two backs in this game were Kaleb Johnson and Chris Brooks, after there was a three-way split last week. Johnson was given a more all-around back role, as he was targeted twice and ran the ball eight times. Last week, Johnson was the runner, Brooks was the blocking back and MarShawn Lloyd was the route-runner.

When Josh Jacobs returns to the lineup, assume that Lloyd is going to get knocked down to being a healthy scratch. The Packers haven't ever had more than three backs up on the 48-man game-day roster, even when they held five players at the position on the 53-man active roster.

Receiver Christian Watson dropped out of the game with a concussion, which is why Savion Williams jumped him in the pecking order this week. Williams actually started the game as the slot receiver, a role that Skyy Moore was playing until Moore's ankle got injured earlier in the year. In his two weeks back from injury, Moore has only played one offensive snap.

Tucker Kraft played every single snap of the game, and the Packers only played 1.3 tight ends per play, a big difference from their game plan against the Minnesota Vikings last week. Last week, the team heavily leaned into multiple tight end looks, while this week featured a lot more three-receiver sets, even when Christian Watson went down.

The starting offensive line in this game was Jordan Morgan, Laken Tomlinson, Sean Rhyan, Kevin Zeitler and Anthony Belton (left to right), a lineup that had never played together before. Zeitler dropped out of action in the middle of the game, though, which pushed Aaron Banks, who had been benched in recent weeks, into a guard spot.

Earlier in the season, rookie third-round pick Chris McClellan was a reserve defensive lineman, but because of injuries, the nose tackle played the most snaps of anyone in the unit against the Rams. Devonte Wyatt, who appeared to be on a pitch count in the first half (he hasn't looked right coming off his ankle injury this year), also dropped out of the game due to injury. It will be interesting to see if the team tries to get Warren Brinson, who is currently on the injured reserve, up to the active roster soon.

Micah Parsons' return to action featured him playing 39 percent of the defensive snaps in this game, about half of his playing time rate in 2025. For the most part, the snaps for Parsons, Barryn Sorrell (who got injured in this game, Brenton Cox Jr. and Dani Dennis-Sutton split snaps about evenly behind Lukas Van Ness.

With Zaire Franklin still out, Isaiah McDuffie played the Mike spot and Ty'Ron Hopper was the Will. When Franklin comes back, which should be soon, he should be playing the Mike. When Franklin was last healthy, McDuffie and Hopper split the Will position.

The only notable nugget here is that Kamal Hadden played one snap in the slot when Javon Bullard was getting looked at for an injury. Otherwise, Brandon Cisse played right cornerback and Kamal Hadden played left cornerback, as usual.

Because the Rams played such heavy personnel on offense, it forced the Packers to play their 3-4 base defense often. The result of that was Javon Bullard, the team's slot defender, only playing 31 percent of the defensive snaps today. "Nickel is the new base" is a fun catchphrase for NFL analysis right now, but it all depends on what the opposing offense puts on the field. Unfortunately, the Packers didn't get many three-receiver looks today, in part because of how the game got out of hand for them in the second half. That left Bullard on the bench for more than two-thirds of the plays tonight.

#2581. T.J. Lang blasts "despicable" Aaron Rodgers comments about Mike McCarthy

T.J. Lang blocked for Aaron Rodgers for eight seasons in Green Bay. Currently, Lang would be more inclined to knock Rodgers on his ass.

Lang sharply criticized Rodgers for his decision to go public with issues that should have stayed in the Pittsburgh locker room.

“I think it’s despicable,” Lang said on 97.1 The Ticket in Detroit, via Sean Keeley of Awful Announcing. “I think that Aaron Rodgers just became everything that he has bitched about and moaned about over the last 10 years with former coaches, former teammates, airing grievances out, giving opinions out in the media.

“He has blacklisted, I don’t know how many, former teammates from just simple comments telling the truth because he just — he was sick of it. Honestly, I don’t even know if I want to watch the whole thing. It’s just unnecessary. It’s a victim mentality. It’s a ‘poor me, woe is me. Oh, I thought this, and it wasn’t that.’ And I’m sick, man.

“I’ve been in a group chat with a whole lot of former teammates that feel the exact same way that I do.”

Most football players would feel that way. There’s a code in the locker room. Rodgers violated it.

“Mike McCarthy was my head coach for 8 years, and I love Mike McCarthy,” Lang said. “And I talked to Mike McCarthy on Monday night, and still have a great relationship with him.

“I haven’t talked to Aaron Rodgers in probably 5 years. I can’t remember the last time he returned a text. I don’t have a relationship with him. And I think it’s just absolutely despicable what he just did to Big Mike.”

Rodgers isn’t a whistleblower. He’s a troublemaker. He didn’t get his way, so he emptied a can of gasoline and tossed a match over his shoulder on the way out the door.

How does any of it help his now-former teammates? Rodgers’s decision to air out dirty laundry has created a massive distraction that will do nothing to help the team win.

Accurate or not, the task at hand becomes harder now that everyone is buzzing about Rodgers’s comments.

That said, no one should be surprised. It’s part and parcel of doing business with Rodgers. When it ends — and end it will — it will end poorly. Like it did in Green Bay. Like it did in New York. Like it did in Pittsburgh.

Like it will end for his next team, if there is one. And if there is, the message is clear.

#2575. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2573. Blake Corum workout video goes viral after destroying Packers in crucial Rams win

For the second week in a row, the Los Angeles Rams were able to count on Blake Corum.

And if you paid attention to what the Rams' third-year running back was doing during the offseason, you wouldn't have been shocked.

Blake Corum's offseason workout video goes viral after dominant performance against the Packers on Wednesday night. X / @barstoolsports

Blake Corum running past a group of Packers defenders in Wednesday night's game. Getty Images

After the Rams' 26-13 victory against the Packers on Wednesday night, Barstool Sports posted one of Corum's workout videos from over the offseason on X, where it showed him moving as fast as lightning in the gym.

Corum was seen doing multiple workouts that incorporated weightlifting and plyometrics. In addition to doing agility workouts, he also did slower workouts that focused on keeping himself balanced.

Rams running back Blake Corum running past a Packers defender. AP Photo/Ryan Sun

Within 30 minutes after it was posted, the video garnered over 52,500 views with 15 comments, 13 reposts, 330 likes, and 34 saves.

NFL fans were seen gathering in the comment section of the video and were praising the running back.

@on_brando 20 posted a GIF of Terrell Owens' iconic "That's my quarterback" clip and captioned his post "That's my fantasy rb."

Corum, who is a former Michigan standout and won a National Championship, received some love from the Wolverines fan base, as @MrDrunkBear posted a GIF of him and J.J. McCarthy after he scored a touchdown and captioned the post "Michigan Man

Corum had a career-high running the ball 32 times for 184 yards, averaging 5.8 yards per play with one rushing touchdown.

Blake Corum falling short of scoring a rushing touchdown against the Packers. Getty Images

Corum's performance happened on the same evening of his birthday, and it was the fifth consecutive game he's scored a rushing touchdown.

According to Sara Barshop of ESPN, Corum's performance was the first time a Rams running back had 30 carries in a game since Todd Gurley did so in his rookie season in 2015 — when the team was still located in St. Louis.

With the Rams' victory against the Packers, head coach Sean McVay also accomplished a rare feat, which was beating Packers head coach Matt LaFleur.

McVay was 0-5 against LaFleur in his career, and was 0-6 against the family, as the Rams came up short against the Arizona Cardinals [who are coached by Matt's brother, Mike LaFleur] in Week 6 of the season.

The last time the Rams took the field, was Week 10 on the road against the Cardinals, and it was a breakout game for Corum, having 17 carries for 100 yards and a touchdown.

#2571. Nets snap a five game losing streak, beat the Bucks 104-97

The Brooklyn Nets and Milwaukee Bucks came into tonight's game like two school kids trotting onto the playground, one pointing and chirping at the other "you're the worst defense," while the other bickered back "no, you're the worst defense."

Each youngster had some merit to their argument. Brooklyn had just given up 130+ in three of their last four games, and ranked dead last in defensive rating ahead of the contest. Milwaukee ranked behind them by a few fractions of a point.

Brooklyn would eventually win the squabble, and the game, but it'd take them some time to get there, not that anyone's complaining here.

Brooklyn came out the gates without a whole lot of ball pressure. In fairness, they had Danny Wolf matched up initially against Tyler Herro, which leaves you very little spatial insurance to work with. However, the Nets also looked out of sync rotating around the Milwaukee offense, which didn't help either. As Brooklyn shot 1-6 from the field and the Bucks pranced out to a 9-2 lead, it just looked like more of the same in the early going.

As I mentioned, we'd eventually find out otherwise. And while real turnaround would soon come on the defensive end, things had to start for Brooklyn at the other.

After Milwaukee's opening jolt, the Nets went on a 13-0 run in the heart of the first to go up 22-12. Michael Porter Jr., who spoke to Brain Lewis this week about how he's struggled to "find his rhythm," was in his grove amid the stretch, putting in eight first period points.

Getting five from Day'Ron Sharpe and Julius Randle each, as well as eight points off the bench in the period, the Nets led after one by a 28-24 margin.

Despite being less of a scorer this time around, Mikel Brown Jr. looked comfortable out there early on as well, starting for a second straight game. He shot 0-5 from the field in the first half but clocked in as a +4 with two assists with zero turnovers.

Also like last game, Grant Nelson joined him on the floor for a few minutes in the second. Nelson only finished with one point, but grabbed six rebounds, contributing to a strong collective effort from the team on the glass, where the Nets won 52-44. Porter Jr. also grabbed 11 rebounds, his most in a game all season if you discount the overtime affair vs Boston.

Brooklyn would need every one of those boards especially in the first half, where neither team shot it at a particularly high clip, as the Nets posted .400/.348 splits, while the Bucks had .432/.273 marks.

At the break, Brooklyn led 51-47, largely thanks to Randle, who had 16 points on 7-10 shooting from the field and 2-4 from deep. MPJ went quiet in the second, still rocking with eight points by then. Day'Ron Sharpe put us on early triple-double watch with five points, 10 rebounds, and four assists at the break.

Herro, however, had all the stats to begin the third. He poured in nine points during the period's first four minutes to put his team back in the lead for the first time since the 6:57 mark of the first. The Nets, meanwhile, opened the period 3-12 from the field and 0-5 from deep. Two of the makes came from Brown Jr, so at least there's that.

Sarcasm aside, as one young guard for Brooklyn started to turn it on, another followed. After Milwaukee looked ready to pull away, Egor Dëmin checked in, scoring five points himself and assisting on two baskets in just a minute and a half. His effort helped ignited a 13-2 run that put the lead back in Brooklyn's hands.

At the same time, Randle continued to mine inside for points. He'd eventually go for 28 in the game on 10-16 shooting. That not only gave Brooklyn consistent offense, but slowed things down and allowed them to set up easily at the other end. Even with Herro's early offensive excellence, the Bucks went 7-23 from the field in the quarter, and the Nets led going into the fourth by a 77-71 score.

"I think everybody was able to just put their minds together and not just focus on team defense, but their own island, like how we say 'guard your yard,'" Dëmin said. "I think that's where it came from. Everything else was easier because everybody was so locked in and super focused on how to guard the man in front of you rather than relying on someone else around."

And believe it or not, in that period, the defense continued to improve. On Milwaukee's second possession of the frame, Porter Jr. poked the a ball away in the backcourt, which Nelson dove across mid court to save. Still, the Bucks got it up and forward, but then Keon Ellis came charging over, intercepting the rock and then dishing it ahead Porter Jr. for an and-one finish. That was just one of the Nets seven steals in the fourth.

"Go out there and play with physicality," Sharpe said. "Go out there and play with ball pressure. Execute with staples and have each others back. I felt like we did a great job at that tonight."

Sharpe never got the triple double, but did finish 11 points, five assists, and 14 rebounds while shooting 5-10 from the field and hitting a three.

The Nets got up by 11 early in the fourth. After a few turnovers early in the frame, the Bucks cut it back down to eight, and we looked in store for a tight finish.

But in a game where Brooklyn's supposed fatal flaw had carried them, it was only right that Noah Clowney, who's struggled with his shot all year, iced things out. In the fourth, he added nine points on 4-6 shooting, scoring from all over the court to keep the lead afloat. He finished with a season-high 17 points, also grabbing five rebounds while shooting 7-13 from the field.

"This is the Noah Clowney that we need," Fernández said. "It gives us a starter off the bench and it's very, very good for this group, because it brings a player on both ends."

Dëmin, who's also had a difficult start to the year, leveraged his size to play some inspiring defense down the stretch as well, finishing as a +5 in the quarter. For the game, he had 15 points, four assists, three rebounds, a steal, and a block while shooting 5-11 from the field.

"Yeah, he went back to doing the simple things, and it started with his physicality on defense," Fernández said. "They felt him the whole game. His length. He can rebound, he can be in the gaps…Proud of him for sure."

Sure, the Nets still turned it over on back-t0-back possession with the Bucks only down 11 and under a minute to go. Dëmin missed also missed an open dunk. They're still a young, flawed team. They didn't solve all their issues tonight, but they did win the night, and snapped their five game losing streak.

Final: Brooklyn Nets 104, Milwaukee Bucks 97

Mo Wagner subbed out at the end of the first period and did not return for the rest of the game. At half, the Nets ruled him out with left knee soreness.

"I don't know. I was about to sub him in, and I saw him limping, and I was like I got to save him from himself," Fernández said. "He was there to do whatever it took for his team and his teammates, and at the end I decided to not bring him back in. Obviously, I don't know what it is, but the good thing, the great thing is he was cheering for everybody. He was cheering fro Grant [Nelson] the whole time, and that means a lot for the group, and it speaks to the type of person he is."

We'll provide updates on him once they're made available.

Day'Ron Sharpe had a season-high 14 rebounds tonight and also recorded his 5th double-double of the season with 11 points. It matches his double-double total from last season, tied as the 2nd most in his career (6, 2023-24). This was his 7th career game with 10+ PTS, 10+ REB and 5+ AST.

Noah Clowney had a season-high 17 points off the bench tonight against the Bucks. He has tied his season high with three 3-pointers made.

Michael Porter Jr. logged his third double-double of the season with 12 points and 11 rebounds. It is his 15th time recording at least 10 rebounds as a Net.

Brooklyn gets right back in action after the holiday with a road matchup against the Toronto Raptors on Friday. The North has lost seven of their last eight, including a contest to the Bucks on Monday. They're certainly looking at this one as a "get right" game. The game tips off at 7:30 p.m. EST.

#2567. Timberwolves 113, Thunder 106: Seatbelt Stops the Drivers (Happy Thanksgiving)

Ahead of Thanksgiving, the Minnesota Timberwolves were faced with a challenge: how could they work up an appetite that would let them eat with reckless abandon tomorrow night? As good as the cardio is for getting the stomach going, they had other ideas.

In honor of the most American tradition of overeating and arguments among family, the Wolves decided to challenge the Oklahoma City Thunder with a football game.

This one had everything: injuries, a singular Minnesota defensive talent, and an Oklahoma legend driving himself into trouble.

While we'll get to the first and third items on that list, it's important we start with the most important takeaway from tonight…

Any Thanksgiving needs a very specific menu. We have cornerstone items, favorite recipes that become traditions, and the reluctant inclusions that are only at the table because they have to be. As the holiday dishes are being prepped and baked (I had a friendsgiving last week where I made two roast chickens, potato gratin, mashed potatoes, and an apple pie, and just finished making mac and cheese and apple strudel for my girlfriend's family celebration tomorrow), let's make a menu of our own.

Love it or hate it, we need to have turkey on the table, and we are getting to the point where the team cannot survive without Jaden McDaniels. It's not perfect. Sometimes he has an odd turnover, or he turns down a three for a long midrange.

Well, that was before the last two games. McDaniels has dropped back-to-back 30-point games and is either reaching a new height in his career or in the midst of a leap that will define the player he becomes for the next decade or so. Either way, it's a pretty big moment.

While the focus will understandably be on Jaden's scoring jump – and for good reason – but I want to focus on his playmaking on the ball and on the short roll.

Over his last three, Jaden is averaging 30.3 points, 8.3 rebounds, and five assists. Tonight's four assists came without a single turnover as well.

Looking back on this game, one in which McDaniels outplayed MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander down the stretch, this was the play that stuck out to me. This is what the offense has looked like without Jaden McDaniels and it looked a whole lot like something I've been thinking for a while.

We talk about fit a whole lot in regard to the way teams are built, but we often back seat it to talent comparisons when we try to make historical equivalents. People have been trying to call Anthony Edwards and Jaden McDaniels the new-age Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, but while the aesthetics of a star shooting guard and small forward talking smack and hitting artful middies are there, the actual playstyle isn't.

Especially with the introduction of LaMelo Ball to the mix, I think we need to make a different comparison…

I think these Wolves mirror the early dynasty Golden State Warriors in playstyle. LaMelo Ball (Steph Curry) uses his gravity to draw out trapping defenders, finding the splitting screener rolling to the rim in Jaden McDaniels (Draymond Green), who ultimately dumps it off on the short roll to Rudy Gobert (Javale McGee).

Maybe that's a bit too far, as Gobert would love to have McGee's hands.

No, in all seriousness, Jaden is a far more dominant on-ball player than Green ever really was, but Draymond's playmaking within the high-movement system that the Warriors ran was such an easy boon to push those teams' offense to greatness. If McDaniels can take his more creation-centric role and combine it with the playmaking reads he's been able to make, he will continue to be an All-Star-level player even when Edwards returns and limits his shot diet.

I don't know when mac and cheese became a Thanksgiving food, honestly. I am born and raised in Harlem, New York, so I know that the Abyssinian Church near me always offered it as part of their free plates, but that felt more like "everyone always wants this, so let's just add it to the plate."

And you know what, they were exactly right. I have never been unhappy to see a really crunchy-crusted, soul food baked mac and cheese.

And I have never, never been unhappy to see an Ayo Dosunmu moment.

Ayo has been absolutely unconscious over the past few weeks, but it's his timeliness that has been more impressive than the actual volume of his scoring. 15 points per game is not a massive number – there are 72 players averaging more than that so far this season – but it feels like the Wolves have relied entirely on Dosunmu as fourth quarters hit.

Tonight, it was a singular conversion of a blocked layup to a made three from Ayo that prevented a Thunder comeback from getting a real foothold as the two teams went back and forth.

Just like I don't know just when mac and cheese became a Thanksgiving staple, I don't know when I realized that the Wolves had pulled off another heist the way they had for Nickeil Alexander-Walker. All I know is that I am incredibly happy that it has, and I am filling my plate with a decent chunk of mac and cheese if I want to have an awesome holiday.

I don't want to talk about this, and you don't want to hear it. I don't want to be the one to bring green bean casserole, and you don't want to eat it. It's why I, well, don't bring green bean casserole and why I have never seen anyone enjoy it or eat it.

And yet, every Thanksgiving, there it is, glooping in the corner of the table, filled with cans of string beans and fried onions in sheer defiance of the cornucopia of delicious foods. Believe me, I have made some culinary attrocities, but the way this has become and unavoidable part of the holiday is beyond me.

In the same way, the way that injuries became such a necessary part of the conversation of this wonderful sport is so miserable to me. But, here we are.

Yes, LaMelo Ball, whose value has been discussed alongside the state of his lower body for years, tweaked his ankle on the foot of Isaiah Hartenstein. He headed to the locker room, and did not return for the remainder of the game.

Good news, though. It doesn't seem too bad. Maybe I should give green bean casserole another try.

The Wolves will close out the NBA Cup Group Stage against a Memphis Grizzlies team they faced very recently. A win would mean advancing to the Cup playoffs for the first time in the franchise's history since the event started just a few years ago.

That may not sound important, but it feels pretty massive to us Cupheads.

#2566. Punches and beers fly in wild Thanksgiving Eve brawl at SoFi Stadium between Rams-Packers fans

Apparently, the Los Angeles Rams and Green Bay Packers weren't the only ones throwing their weight around at SoFi Stadium on Thanksgiving Eve.

A massive fight broke out in the stands during the Rams' 26-13 victory Wednesday night, and oddly enough, a Tampa Bay Buccaneers fan appeared to be at the center of it.

In a video posted on X, a man wearing a red Tom Brady Buccaneers jersey and a black hat sticks out like a stop sign in a sea of Rams blue and Packers green. He's seen throwing a punch at someone to his right before the entire section erupts into chaos.

Men and women wearing both Rams and Packers jerseys get involved, with punches flying from seemingly every direction.

Security eventually intervenes as a woman clutching a young child attempts to escape the melee.

Fed-up spectators began showering the combatants with beer. Considering a beer at SoFi Stadium can cost $22, that's an expensive way to express your displeasure.

It's unclear what sparked the altercation or whether anyone was arrested.

There was plenty of fighting on the field, too, where the Rams bullied the Packers at the line of scrimmage, rushing a whopping 47 times for 241 yards, including a career-high 184 from Blake Corum.

The Rams squeezed the life out of Green Bay's offense, possessing the football for 23:45 of the second half and 40:40 overall compared to the Packers' 19:20.

Los Angeles improved to 7-4 with its fifth consecutive victory, climbing back into the NFC playoff picture.

The Rams gave their fans plenty to be thankful for heading into Thanksgiving. Apparently, some were more interested in serving knuckle sandwiches than turkey.

#2563. Diving deeper into Cavs 121-102 loss to Knicks: Even when the stars are at their best, this team isn’t

The Cleveland Cavaliers looked like they could compete with the New York Knicks until they couldn't. Cleveland went into the final quarter with a narrow 85-82 advantage, but then lost the fourth 39-17 to drop this game 121-102.

19 points on 9-of-15 shooting, 8 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 block

Bridges covered up for pretty pedestrian performances from Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns. Bridges provided efficient scoring, was an impactful rebounder, and was good defensively. This all added up to the Knicks winning his minutes by 33.

30 points on 12-of-24 shooting, 4 rebounds, 4 assists, 4 steals, 2 blocks

Mitchell was unstoppable in the first half. His 14 points in the opening quarter and six more in the second put the Cavs in a good position to steal this game. Mitchell seemingly couldn't miss before the break, going 8-for-11 from the field with most of his damage coming at the rim.

The magic went away in the second half. Mitchell scored just 10 points on 4-of-13 shooting in the final two quarters. Cleveland then proceeded to lose those minutes by 15.

The Cavs needed a special performance from Mitchell to defeat the defending champions. They had that in the first half, but not the second.

15 points on 6-of-14 shooting, 12 assists, 7 rebounds, 3 steals, 2 blocks

Hart is a winning player. He does all the little things that championship-level teams need from their supporting cast. Rebounding, additional ball handling, defensive versatility, and ancillary playmaking are attributes you hope to accumulate in your entire supporting cast. Hart provides that as just one player.

Those skills were all on display against the Cavs. Hart rebounded well, forced turnovers, and was a useful facilitator. The Cavs have often decided to cheat off Hart offensively. He didn't make them pay as a shooter, but he used the extra space to find openings for his teammates.

On a night when both teams got similar contributions from their stars, it was the play of the supporting players, like Hart and Jose Alverado (21 points on 8-of-10 shooting), that made all the difference.

5 points on 2-of-8 shooting, 1 rebound, 0 assists

Merrill has had a tough time finding his shot this season. There's many things Merrill does well, but those are mostly muted if the outside shot isn't falling, as was once again the case here.

Head coach Kenny Atkinson has asked a lot out of Merrill this season. He's been consistently forced to guard up a spot or two when he's on the court — particularly when he's been inserted into the starting lineup. That isn't an ideal place for him considering he's undersized for that role, and has been sharing the floor with guards that don't pull their weight defensively.

I don't envy Merrill. He's been continually put into positions to fail this season.

10 points on 5-of-7 shooting, 5 rebounds, 1 assist

Allen is supposed to be a key member of this team, but you wouldn't necessarily know that from watching games like this. The Cavs need Allen to be a force inside as a roller and rebounder with Evan Mobley out of the lineup. He wasn't either of those things, and played with little to no energy, which is why the Cavs lost his minutes by 32.

The Cavs are built around their guards. If that backcourt is going to work on both ends, they need their interior players to consistently show up. They haven't, which is one of the many reasons for the underwhelming start to the season.

The Cavs benefited greatly from Bryant's energy and willingness to be physical. Both of those things stood out on a team that is in desperate need of interior size and presence. It's no coincidence the Cavs played their best basketball of the evening when he was on the court.

28 points on 7-of-19 shooting, 5 assists, 1 rebound

This was a solid night from Harden. He kept the offense moving, took smart shots, and continually forced his way to the line (13-for-14). A poor shooting night from three (1-for-8) kept this from being a great offensive game.

Defensively, the Cavs had some success with hiding him on Towns. Harden held his own in that matchup, resulting in the defense not completely falling apart with him on the floor.

Harden did a good job of forcing his way inside. The offense is in a much better place when he can consistently do that.

Jose Alverado scored as many points off the bench (21) as all five of Cleveland's reserves combined.

This was a bad night from Cleveland's supporting cast, particularly their bench. Tyrese Proctor had just two points on 1-of-6 shooting, Jaylon Tyson went 2-for-8 from the field with four turnovers, and Mario Hezonja registered no points in 10 minutes.

Conversely, New York got key contributions from their role players, including Alverado. He scored 16 of his 21 points in the fourth to help put the Cavs away.

This team makes much more sense on paper than it does on the court. The Cavs have more well-rounded role players than they have had in recent years. This has shown through when they get opportunities to shine. Yet, that may not be what works with this particular core.

Typically, the Cavs are at their best when Mitchell and Harden are playing well, as they were on Wednesday. This formula has been the recipe for their top performances, but the Cavs didn't come close to pulling off the upset because they got next to no help from their supporting cast. No player besides the starting backcourt scored more than 10 points. It's nearly impossible to win games against an elite opponent when your role players add nothing.

Somehow, the Cavs have constructed a team that relies heavily on their guards to be at their best to win alongside a supporting cast that doesn't really fit with how the guards play. That is a problem, and how you get nights like this where Peyton Watson and Mario Hezonja combine to take just five shots from the field.

The Cavs are pot committed to this backcourt both in terms of their recent contract extensions and how they play. Atkinson hasn't indicated that he wants to move away from this isolation- and high pick-and-roll-heavy offense that caters specifically to the two guards. But that style isn't conducive to a team that has struggled to knock down catch-and-shoot threes (36.3%, 16th in the league), doesn't have a versatile defense, and features two bigs that need to be force-fed to be effective offensively.

Koby Altman has built an interesting supporting cast. On paper, it would fit nicely with a team that played like the 2024-25 Cavs. However, this isn't that team. Any hopes of playing that way went out the window when they traded for Harden last winter.

Cleveland has been one of the most inconsistent groups this season. Few teams have as impressive highs and as disappointing lows. Many factors contribute to that, but one of them is that the puzzle pieces don't really fit together. Or at the very least, they don't fit with how they're being used now.

There's no easy fix for this. Getting a team to drastically change how they play 19 games into the season is nearly impossible. At the same time, there isn't an easy way to pivot off either the star or supporting players due to their contracts. It's difficult to see a trade drastically changing the outlook of this team. They're more or less committed to this current group and playstyle. And I'm just not sure what the pathway is to being a legit title contender, which is what you would hope they'd be coming off a run to the Eastern Conference Finals.

Even when the stars are at or near their best, this team isn't.

#2562. Rob Manfred 'can't imagine' MLB team owners will accept new CBA without a salary cap

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred on Wednesday said club owners are not willing to compromise on their push for a salary cap and floor in their ongoing negotiations with the players union on a new collective bargaining agreement. While Manfred noted there was general room for compromise with the MLBPA, that does not extend to the central matter of the capped system owners want.

"I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred said while meeting with the press during the ongoing owners meetings in New York, via the Athletic.

"Thirty clubs are 100% unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made," Manfred said later during a news conference at MLB headquarters. "I'm not in a position to speculate about what happens in the event that we don't achieve our overriding objective, which is to get a cap and floor system that addresses the competitive problem that our fans perceive."

It's possible to parse "can't imagine" as a subtle rhetorical hedge. Additionally, Manfred before he was commissioner was the league's lead negotiator. As such, he's quite familiar with the appearance of unyielding resolve as a tactical implement. Thus, the league has tied every other proposed change to the players' acceptance of a cap and floor, and the players through their union have historically shown zero willingness to accept such a system.

"There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," MLBPA interim head Bruce Meyer said Wednesday in a statement.

"There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries."

In their most recent substantive proposal to the players, MLB pitched a $258.3 million cap and $180.2 million floor on team payrolls, with those limits to be phased in gradually. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor.

The current CBA, which is the accord that governs every aspect of the working relationship between players and clubs in MLB, is set to expire just before midnight on Dec. 1. At that point, the league is expected to lock out the players at the behest of team owners. The lockout will likely not end until a new CBA is agreed to, at least in principle. Owners also locked out the players in 2021, and that lockout lasted 99 days and very nearly ate into the 2022 regular-season schedule.

Rams' Nate Landman, Blake Corum, and Myles Garrett join Michael Irvin and the Netflix broadcast crew for a turkey following Wednesday's win over the Packers on Nov. 25, 2026, in Los Angeles. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

#2558. MLB rumors: Mets to meet with NPB star, plus latest on Ketel Marte, Cubs, Mariners, Nationals, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're one week away from Thanksgiving and the offseason has started to pick up a little bit in Major League Baseball. We've seen an All-Star pitcher sign (Sonny Gray to the Twins) and a trade involving an All-Star (Maikel Garcia to the Mariners). The White Sox also signed a mid-rotation starter while the Red Sox grabbed a first baseman fresh off a World Series title. Is there enough time for a flurry of moves before the owners lock the players out when the CBA expires on Dec. 1?

In theory, there sure is. We can hold out hope, as there has been enough movement to keep belief alive.

It's no secret that the Diamondbacks are willing to trade All-Star second baseman Ketel Marte. A big hurdle might be his 10-and-5 no-trade rights and questions about which teams Marte would approve in a potential deal. Further, the asking price on Arizona's end is "very high," reports FanSided. Still, plenty of teams are said to be interested.

Marte, 33, has five years and $91.75 million left on his deal. He finished third in MVP voting in 2024, was a highly productive All-Star in 2025, but some issues arose in 2026, including several no-shows. He hit .249/.316/.432 (107 OPS+) with 2.5 WAR and some possible clubhouse baggage.

The Mets are planning a Zoom meeting with Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira, reports the New York Post. This won't have an impact on their pursuit of Tarik Skubal, just in case anyone is curious.

Taira, 27, has been one of the top pitchers in Japan's NPB for years. Last season, in 23 starts, he had a 1.36 ERA and 0.96 WHIP with 141 strikeouts in 146 innings. He's had a sub-2.00 ERA four of the last five seasons, with the exception being a 2.40 in 2023.

CBS Sports ranked Taira as the No. 19 free agent available this winter:

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Seibu announced on Oct. 30 that Taira will be posted this offseason.

Because of the expected lockout, international free agents are working under an artificial Dec. 1 deadline to sign, rather than the normal posting window.

For now, the Mets' rotation starts with Nolan McLean and Christian Scott.

The Cubs' main focus is on pitching, as well it should be after having one of the worst pitching staffs in baseball along with one of the best collections of position-player talent. Still, both corner outfielders (Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki) have hit free agency along with catcher Carson Kelly, so they can't just ignore the offense. On that front, the ballclub has "extensively scouted" Teruaki Sato, according to The Athletic.

Sato has played mostly third base, where the Cubs have Alex Bregman, but also has outfield experience and could simply serve as DH. In 143 games last season in NPB, Sato hit .306/.383/.609 with 40 doubles, 39 home runs and 106 RBI. His strikeout numbers are high, but sometimes that's the price to be paid for top-level power.

CBS Sports ranked Sato as the No. 4 free agent this winter:

He will play the entire 2027 season at age 28 and is coming off a .306/.383/.609 slash line with 39 home runs, which won him Japan's first Triple Crown since Munetaka Murakami in 2022. Sato has a similar skill set but is not quite Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll.

After being one of the most disappointing teams in 2026 and having an active general manager, of course the Mariners weren't going to just sit around after one move. Sure enough, Jerry Dipoto told reporters on Wednesday that they are still looking to add a right-handed bat (remember, Randy Arozarena is a free agent) along with a veteran infielder and a left-handed reliever even after acquiring Garcia. And perhaps most importantly, Dipoto insisted that they do have the payroll flexibility to add all of this.

Further, he also said the rotation is set and no other starting pitchers will be moved. So it'll be Logan Gilbert, George Kirby, Bryan Woo, Emerson Hancock and Kade Anderson heading into next season.

Fresh off signing right-handed starter Dustin May, the White Sox are looking to add another starting pitcher "of similar magnitude," reports the Chicago Sun-Times.

Though the White Sox were one of baseball's best stories last season and made the playoffs, the rotation was very thin. Right now, they have Sean Burke, May, Taylor, Davis Martin and Anthony Kay as their top five and are looking to add another of May's ilk. Things are already looking much better.

The Nationals finished third in the majors in runs scored last season, believe it or not. They trailed only the Cubs and Brewers, scoring more than the Dodgers. The problem was that the pitching staff was mostly a mess. As such, it's no surprise they are after starters and The Athletic names three targets: lefty Kris Bubic, righty Brady Singer and Japanese import Kona Takahashi.

Bubic, 29, has battled shoulder and elbow injuries the past two seasons, but the upside was flashed in the first part of 2025. He made the All-Star team and had a 2.55 ERA through 20 starts and 116 ⅓ innings.

The 30-year-old Singer was 6-15 with a 5.85 ERA for the Reds last season in a disaster of a contract year, but he was productive in the previous two seasons.

Takahashi, 29, was 9-7 with a 2.64 ERA, 1.10 WHIP and 118 strikeouts in 143 ⅓ innings in NPB last season.

#2557. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2556. Dillon Brooks gets ejected with 23 seconds left vs. Rockets after getting into it with Kevin Durant

Phoenix Suns guard Dillon Brooks and Houston Rockets forward Kevin Durant exchanged words at the end of Houston's 116-104 win on Wednesday night.

Durant was chippy all night, making sure to deliver extra trash talk against his former team.

With less than 30 seconds left in the game, the Rockets led by 10. In a wild moment, Durant and Brooks weren't really playing; they were just talking to each other near halfcourt while the action continued.

Houston's Fred VanVleet hit a jumper with 23.8 seconds left to make it a 114-102 game in the Rockets' favor. Brooks and Durant were chirping at each other and got in each other's faces.

The referees assessed each player a technical foul. Because Brooks had received a technical foul earlier in the quarter with 4:32 left, he was ejected. VanVleet drained a three and motioned to Brooks; they chirped and were both assessed technicals.

Durant finished the game with 20 points and 10 rebounds. With 46.3 seconds left in the second quarter, the veteran forward drained a 3-pointer. That basket helped him become the fifth player in NBA history to score at least 33,000 points. He joins LeBron James (43,672 and counting), Kareem Abdul-Jabbar (38,387), Karl Malone (36,298) and Kobe Bryant (33,643).

The win moved Houston to 14-5. The Rockets return to action Saturday, hosting the Philadelphia 76ers.

The loss dropped Phoenix to 9-8. The Suns had won four straight before Wednesday's loss, and now turn their attention to taking on the Dallas Mavericks on Friday night.

Castillo, 33, joined the White Sox in a deadline trade with the Seattle Mariners. He struggled badly after the deal, allowing 30 runs in 31 innings, and he finished the season on the injured list with a shoulder issue. Castillo has one year remaining on his contract at $22.75 million, though a $25 million option for 2028 will vest if he throws 150 innings in 2027.

The 29-year-old Martin threw 146 innings with a 3.95 ERA in 2026, but it was a 3.41 ERA in the first half and a 5.12 ERA in the second half. The White Sox kept him at arm's length in the postseason despite running bullpen games almost nightly. Martin allowed two runs in one inning in his only postseason appearance.

Neither Sullivan nor Veliz are significant prospects. For all intents and purposes, the White Sox are attaching Martin to Castillo as a sweetener to get the Rockies to take Castillo's salary. The Rockies are essentially buying Martin, who is under team control through 2030, by taking on the rest of Castillo's contract.

Here now are our trade grades for this two-for-two swap.

Fair or not, I'm going to lump the two Castillo trades together. Chicago stepped out to acquire Castillo at the deadline and absorbed the $30 million or so remaining on his contract to do it. Seranthony Domínguez, who had about $15 million left on his deal, went the other way in the trade, so the White Sox took on about $15 million total, and also gave up a pretty good prospect in Boston Smith.

Four and a half months later, the White Sox had to give up a steady back-end starter in Martin to clear Castillo's money. They ended up saving about $7 million in 2027 in this series of moves, but it cost them Martin and Smith (and Domínguez), and they had to endure 31 awful innings from Castillo. Unless Sullivan or Veliz hit big, the White Sox took a series of Ls here.

Credit to president of baseball operations Chris Getz for acknowledging a mistake with Castillo and acting quickly to unload him. It was costly, though. Martin isn't a star, but cheap back-end starters are very valuable. We'll see what Getz & Co. do with the savings. Presumably they'll invest in more pitching. Having to give up Martin to dump Castillo so soon is a stinker, though. Ouch.

The Rockies need all types of pitching (righty, lefty, starter, reliever, whatever) and it's not often they can convince quality (or even competent) free agents to come to Coors Field. They have to develop their own pitchers or trade for pitching, and in this instance, they took on Castillo's hefty salary to get Martin and his four years of control. Creative, if nothing else.

There is downside potential too. Martin has run below league-average strikeout rates and middling ground ball rates throughout his career. Pitchers who allow a lot of balls in play -- a lot of balls in play in the air -- are a poor match for Coors Field. It's good the Rockies spent and found a way to add controllable pitching. They just might not have picked the best pitcher.

After losing 104 games in 2026, there is no such thing as a bad dart throw for the Rockies. It's unlikely they would have been able to spend the $22.75 million on a free agent (at least not without overpaying), so taking on Castillo to get Martin is the next best thing. I like the thinking, even if I don't love Martin's profile in Coors Field.

#2554. Sean McVay has NSFW reaction to Rams flattening Packers on Thanksgiving Eve

By the time Sean McVay and Matthew Stafford got a good look at what they had left to work with on the sideline Wednesday night, they might as well have been in a garage trying to get a race car back on the track after blowing a tire and snapping a belt.

Oh, and somebody had already borrowed half their tools.

Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay points to his defense during a game against the Green Bay Packers at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., Nov. 25, 2026. Jon SooHoo/UPI/Shutterstock

The Rams went into their game against the Packers without Puka Nacua and Davante Adams, the two receivers Stafford generally looks for when he needs somebody to go make a play. They lost cornerback Jaylen Watson weeks ago.

Then left guard Bill Murray went down. So did right tackle Warren McClendon Jr. Whatever comfort McVay took in having a couple of tight ends to help out his makeshift offensive line lasted only as long as Davis Allen and Tyler Higbee did.

Over on defense, safety Kamren Kinchens got himself thrown out for unnecessary roughness on a hard hit on Packers wide receiver Christian Watson.

Somewhere in all that, McVay and his staff found a way to run the ball down Green Bay's throat for 241 yards in a must-have 26-13 win.

Matthew Stafford of the Los Angeles Rams calls a play against the Green Bay Packers at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Getty Images

And when Stafford needed a receiver, there was second-year wideout Konata Mumpfield, who caught four passes for 69 yards.

Meanwhile, a defense that had every reason to feel as shorthanded as the offense spent most of the night getting itself off the field. Three takeaways. Eleven first downs allowed. All of 244 yards for the Packers, three more than the Rams managed just handing the ball off.

Talk about figuring it out on the fly. Wednesday night and darn near the whole season.

It got McVay thinking about his old college coach, Terry Hoeppner, who had three pieces of advice for him back in the day: Have a plan. Work the plan. Plan for the unexpected.

He's getting tired of the last one, albeit a master at dominating it.

"We've had a lot of that third s––t come to life to plan for the unexpected this year," McVay said.

Consider their five-game winning streak, including Wednesday's win over the Packers, evidence of the Rams' ability to survive and thrive.

By any means necessary. Which sometimes means drawing up formations on the sideline.

Los Angeles Rams running back Blake Corum (24) eludes Green Bay Packers cornerback Brandon Cisse (2) on Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif. Jon SooHoo/UPI/Shutterstock

"The biggest thing is, how do we figure out what's the best way to use the group that we have to play the opponent that we're going against? That was what we felt like it was," McVay said.

Imagine telling McVay beforehand he'd go jumbo against Green Bay, then start losing the very guys who make it possible to play that way. Now imagine telling him the Packers would know exactly what was coming and Corum would still be running through them.
