The NFL is heading into Thanksgiving week, and somehow, all 32 teams are still mathematically alive to make the playoffs. So, every team has that to be thankful for on Thursday.

That said, our first elimination could come this week with the Arizona Cardinals, but the good news for them is that we probably won't see that happen. The Cardinals could theoretically be eliminated by the end of Week 12, but five things would have to happen, including a tie in the Packers-Rams game. For that reason alone, I think the Cards' playoff hopes will survive into Week 13.

Of course, we're not here to talk about teams on the cusp of elimination; we're here to try and figure out who's actually going to make the playoffs this year. To help us figure that out, we had our analytics expert, Stephen Oh, simulate the rest of the 2026 season. There are 109 games left on the regular-season schedule, along with 13 playoff games, and Oh simulated all of them. Not only did he project all eight division winners and the 14 playoff teams, but he also crowned a Super Bowl champion.

With that in mind, let's get to the projections. And just as a reminder, we're projecting what the NFL playoff field will look like at the end of the season. This is NOT the current playoff standings, but you can see those here.

The race for the top seed in the AFC was upended in Week 11 by losses for both the Bengals and Jaguars. BREAKDOWN: The biggest news of the week was Pittsburgh's decision to bench Aaron Rodgers on Tuesday night. This came after the Steelers suffered the ugliest loss of Week 11 in Philadelphia, but despite those two things, our projection model still has them comfortably in the playoffs.

With Rodgers under center, the Steelers were projected to win 9.9 games, but with Rudolph, that number only drops down to 9.7. We have the Texans as their main competition, but Houston only has a 30.2% chance of getting in (The Steelers' playoff chances are at 68.7% with Rudolph, down from 72.4% with Rodgers). The Texans and Steelers actually face each other in Week 13, and that could go a long way toward determining the AFC's final wild card spot. And in the end, the Blazers got some sweet revenge as they defeated the Spurs in NBA Cup group stage action, 116-111, thanks to a dagger triple from Deni Avdija.

#2501. So you missed out on Tarik Skubal: The best starting pitchers still available through free agency, trade

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Mets' splash record signing of ace lefty Tarik Skubal, who was far and away the top free agent available, has of course reset the market in a major way. Those who missed out on Skubal and those aspiring contenders who otherwise have rotation needs may be left wondering: What's next?

Clubs like the Chicago Cubs, Atlanta Braves, San Diego Padres, Los Angeles Dodgers, Chicago White Sox, Tampa Bay Rays, among others, still have options, even if none of them rise to the skyscraping level of Mr. Skubal. Let's explore some possibilities for you, and let's also move beyond just the current class of free agents and name-check some potential trade targets who could buttress a rotation for next season and beyond. Let's jump in.

Yes, Morejon is a reliever at this writing, but his deep repertoire, excellent velocity and stuff make him a compelling transition candidate for next season, even with recent reporting that he wants to stay in the bullpen. Morejon, who sits triple digits, can give some velocity back while working longer outings and still have plenty in the tank to miss bats in the strike zone. And if starting doesn't work, he can go right back to dominating as a reliever. He doesn't turn 28 until February.

While his ERA ballooned last season thanks to some early season struggles, Rogers' underlying performance indicators are still quite strong, specifically his ability to get chase out of the zone and duck quality contact with four pitches (four-seamer, sinker, changeup, sweeper) that light up analytical models. Rogers also has a fifth-pitch cutter and has shown the ability to hammer the strike zone the last two years. He's not a name that leaps readily to mind, but Rogers has a high ceiling and bargain potential.

Peralta, coming off three straight seasons for the Milwaukee Brewers in which he topped 30 starts and 200 strikeouts, wasn't himself with the New York Mets for the first half-plus of 2027. However, after a deadline trade to the Rays, he made some adjustments and re-established himself as a highly useful starter, all the way to ALCS MVP. The market's going to reflect his rediscovered form. The 2027 season will be his age-31 campaign.

He has a full, five-pitch repertoire with elite spin and movement on almost all of those five offerings and boasts an ERA+ of 129 for his career. King turns 32 in May, and he's experienced a gradual decline at the command-and-control level over the past few seasons. As well, his fastball's not beating hitters in the zone like it used to. That's to say, there's risk here, but even if he's beginning his decline phase, King will be a rotation asset for the near- to mid-term.

The 32-year-old righty was reborn last season after a deadline trade to the Braves. Atlanta ramped up his splitter usage and adjusted his slider shape, and in perhaps related matters, Mahle was much more successful at staying away from the heart of the zone. In 54 ⅓ innings after the trade, Mahle ran a sub-2.00 ERA and struck out 48 batters against nine walks. No, he's not going to put up those numbers over the long haul, but his revival makes him an intriguing option.

The big pre-Skubal hot stove news was the San Francisco Giants' reported willingness to listen to offers on ace Logan Webb. Webb, who just recently turned 30, endured a bit of a down 2026 on the run-prevention front, but the overall body of work remains very strong. For his career, the three-time All-Star has a career ERA+ of 115 with three top 10 finishes in the American League Cy Young vote. In three of the past four seasons, he's topped 200 innings. Webb is under contract through 2028.

Will the Rays part with him even though they're the defending American League champs? They're famously comfortable with churning core contributors, and McClanahan is going into his walk year in 2027. McClanahan's long and labored comeback from Tommy John surgery was finally realized this past season, and he turned in a strong age-29 campaign for the Rays. He was pretty much an ace from 2021-23 before the elbow problems took hold.

Teams will pay a lot for a young and controllable starting pitcher with frontline upside, and all of that describes the 27-year-old lefty Detmers. Not eligible for free agency until after the 2028 season, Detmers topped 4.0 WAR this past season and struck out 211 batters in 185 innings. For the Halos, trading him might be an example of selling high, but the pending change in ownership clouds any reading of those particular tea leaves.

Greene has one of the biggest fastballs in the game and a top 10 finish in the NL Cy Young balloting in his recent past. However, he's struggled to stay healthy and realize his potential on a sustained basis – the potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick in 2017. He's signed through 2028 with a club option for 2029, and it may be time for a change of scenery. He's been the subject of trade speculation before, and this winter figures to be no exception.

Yes, deGrom is 38, but going into the final guaranteed year of his contract, he remains capable of being a solid rotation presence for a contender. deGrom reportedly used his full no-trade clause to block a swap to the Braves at the deadline, so it's far from certain whether he'd be willing to approve a deal out of Arlington. That said, such things are always negotiations, and a late-career run at the playoffs might prove tempting for him.

If you were wondering how long it would take for the pitchforks to make an appearance in Toronto, the answer was 20 games. After a promising start, the Maple Leafs have lost four in a row and six of their last seven.

Toronto is now in jeopardy of falling behind in a competitive Atlantic Division. Only the Detroit Red Wings have been worse, and that organization has been a dumpster fire for months now. The Leafs have just a couple weeks to turn things around before Thanksgiving, a key date in the NHL season as the playoff picture begins to solidify.

#2499. Biggest questions on Aaron Rodgers benching: Why did Steelers make abrupt quarterback change?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Less than 48 hours after telling reporters that Aaron Rodgers was still the Steelers' starting quarterback, Mike McCarthy made the decision to bench the future Hall of Fame quarterback for Friday's game against the Broncos. Mason Rudolph will start in place of Rodgers, who will be inactive for the game and was reportedly excused from practice Wednesday in light of his benching.

The Steelers reportedly spent Monday and Tuesday preparing for the Broncos with Rodgers at the helm. That abruptly changed on Tuesday night when McCarthy made the stunning decision following a meeting with other members of Steelers management. Wednesday afternoon saw Rodgers blister McCarthy, who he won a Super Bowl with, in an all-time interview with The Pat McAfee Show.

Here are the big questions we have regarding one of the stories of the year in the NFL.

McCarthy's decision to bench Rodgers was about more than on-field performance.

ESPN's Ian Rapoport said on The Pat McAfee Show that the decision came down to who's calling plays. The Steelers have been running more hurry-up offense in recent weeks. In those situations, the play-calling runs through Rodgers and quarterbacks coach Tom Arth. McCarthy apparently decided that that was no longer sustainable.

Rodgers himself confirmed on McAfee's show that the decision was partly due to play-calling. Rodgers felt that McCarthy shouldn't call plays and accused McCarthy of being late and sleeping through meetings. Rodgers also said that McCarthy admitted that he hadn't watched film of that week's opponent days leading up to games.

Rodgers said that he met with McCarthy this week, expressed his concerns and discussed the play-calling duties. Rodgers said that if changes weren't going to be made, he would rather not be the team's quarterback, which is ultimately what happened.

The situation with Rodgers had been "brewing for a while" and "reached the point of no return" on Tuesday night, according to longtime Steelers beat reporter Gerry Dulac. The Steelers held a series of internal meetings and conversations over the past two days regarding the offense and what needs to change moving forward, per ESPN. One reported change is a more collaborative approach to play calling, which coincides with Rapoport's report.

There had been reports of tension between Rodgers and McCarthy. Cameras caught the two exchanging verbal jabs during Pittsburgh's Week 4 loss to Cleveland. There appeared to be a disconnect between the two in recent weeks over the offense from a philosophical standpoint (Rodgers, for example, often checked out of running plays in lieu of passing plays at the line of scrimmage; McCarthy said during his Monday presser that the Steelers need to run the ball more).

It also goes without saying that Rodgers is not playing his best ball in his final NFL season.

Rodgers, who will turn 43 on Dec. 2, is completing 60.9 percent of his passes this season, the lowest total since his rookie season. During Sunday's loss to the Eagles, Rodgers was sacked five times despite being pressured only eight times. In addition to taking unnecessary sacks, Rodgers missed open receivers multiple times and was inaccurate on several downfield passes.

Rodgers clearly isn't the only issue. The Steelers' offensive line (which suffered a blow in Week 10 when left guard Mason McCormick suffered an ankle injury that is expected to sideline him for the rest of the regular season) has regressed. Pittsburgh's running game has hit a wall, and the Steelers' receiving corps has underwhelmed, especially DK Metcalf, who was ejected from Sunday's loss in the third quarter after committing his second unsportsmanlike conduct penalty of the half.

A breakup probably wasn't going to happen as long as Pittsburgh kept winning. The last two losses were apparently the straws that broke the camel's back.

In 2023, Rudolph was promoted to starting quarterback following an injury to Kenny Pickett and subpar play from Mitch Trubisky. Rudolph took over with the Steelers sitting at 7-7 (having lost three straight games) and on the precipice of missing the playoffs.

Rudolph played brilliantly while leading the Steelers to wins over the Bengals and Seahawks and did enough to help the Steelers edge the Ravens in Baltimore in Week 18 to secure a wild card spot in the playoffs.

A 2018 third-round pick, Rudolph was drafted to potentially serve as Ben Roethlisberger's successor. That never materialized, however, despite Rudolph going 5-3 as Pittsburgh's starter in 2019 after Roethlisberger suffered a season-ending injury. Rudolph was quickly typecast as a game manager and not starter material.

McCarthy, however, spoke glowingly about Rudolph during training camp. At the time, some thought that McCarthy was trying to drum up trade interest in Rudolph. With Tuesday night's announcement, it's clear that McCarthy sees something in Rudolph and wants to give him a chance to run his offense in regular season games.

There are reasons to believe that Rudolph will have another successful stint under center for Pittsburgh. The Steelers' remaining schedule includes only two teams with above .500 records. Pittsburgh's defense has been solid this season (they are seventh in the NFL in fewest points allowed) and its receiving corps appears to be getting better. Hurleman caught six passes and a touchdown Sunday in his season debut. Roman Wilson returned from injury last week, and Michael Pittman is expected to play Friday for the first time since Week 4. The Steelers also have one of the league's better running back duos in Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle.

The Steelers have two young quarterbacks, Will Howard and Drew Allar, who are under contract. Rudolph, however, is slated to enter free agency this offseason. By making this move, McCarthy is essentially giving Rudolph an audition to be Pittsburgh's quarterback in 2027.

If Rudolph plays well and helps lead the Steelers to the playoffs, one would think that the Steelers would re-sign Rudolph this offseason and give him a chance to compete alongside Allar, Howard and whoever the Steelers bring in this offseason. If he doesn't rise to the occasion, the Steelers will likely bring in two quarterbacks this offseason to compete with Howard and Allar.

According to both sides, yes. Rodgers and McCarthy apparently at odds for months. Rodgers acknowldged on Wednesday that he first noticed McCarthy missing meetings, sleeping, etc. shortly after he signed with the team. The two were seen shouting at each other in Cleveland, which was back in Week 4.

Rodgers said that his time with the Steelers is over. The Steelers could retain his rights for the rest of the season, or they could release him, which would give him a chance to finish his career somewhere else.

If he were released, two possible options would be the 49ers and the Packers as a backup to Brock Purdy or Jordan Love. This scenario would give him the opportunity to retire with either his childhood team or the team where he built his NFL legacy. It's also possible that the Patriots and Ravens gives Rodgers a look if he hits the open market.

#2498. NBA injury updates: The latest on Tyrese Haliburton, Anthony Edwards, Kawhi Leonard, Dylan Harper, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Injuries have been one of the defining stories of the young 2026-27 NBA season, and while some teams like the Oklahoma City Thunder are unfortunately months away from relief, others are beginning to see a light at the end of the health tunnel. We're now nearly a month or so out from the early-season wave of losses, and on Friday, ESPN's Shams Charania gave updates on the health of several key absent players. Let's use that as a launching point to check in on a handful of injured stars.

It took Indiana's star point guard a full season to recover from the torn Achilles tendon he suffered in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals, but sadly, his return lasted just four games before he headed back to the sideline. Haliburton was diagnosed with a left hamstring strain in October, and according to ESPN, he will be sidelined for at least the next couple of weeks.

For now, there is no firmer timeline than that, with Pacers coach Rick Carlisle saying in a recent radio interview that he didn't think it was "out of the question" that Haliburton would play in November, but he would not "put a hard date on anything."

Haliburton looked mostly like himself in the four games he played early this season, averaging just under 22 points and 10 assists. The Pacers have fallen to 5-10 and the Eastern Conference's No. 10 seed without him, and they are seemingly aware of the need for reinforcements. The Pacers "clearly are looking at doing something" on the trade market, with an upgrade on the wing viewed as a strong possibility, Jake Fischer said Friday on SiriusXM NBA Radio.

A return to action seems further off for Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards, who had knee surgery in late October. Edwards spoke with reporters Thursday and said he has "no clue" when he'll be able to return to the floor and declined to offer a timetable, per ESPN.

Edwards missed 21 games last year and dealt with a knee issue in the postseason. Despite a hot start, that included a 47-point outburst against the Cavaliers, Edwards continued to experience discomfort in the knee, prompting the team to choose the surgery route rather than have their superstar continue playing through pain.

"It needed to be done in order for me to be able to play without any pain for the next couple years," Edwards said. "But who knows? Maybe in a couple years I might have to get something else. But hopefully not. I think I'll be pretty good."

Led by LaMelo Ball, the Wolves have excelled even in Edwards' absence. At 11-5, Minnesota sits at No. 5 in the Western Conference standings entering their game against the Grizzlies on Saturday.

Leonard has played just twice this season due to knee swelling, but according to Charania, there is optimism that he will return within the next few weeks. Leonard has been dealing with patellar tendinopathy, more commonly known as "jumper's knee," TSN reported on Tuesday. That is the same issue he dealt with throughout his 2019 championship season. SportsNet confirmed that reporting, while noting that swelling is not typically how that injury presents. SportsNet's reporting indicates that the swelling and jumper's knee are separate issues.

The good news on this front is that the reporting to this point indicates that the Raptors do not expect these issues to linger once Leonard returns. Toronto successfully managed Leonard's health through that title season, and is being cautious to start this year as well. However, his absence has certainly been felt as Toronto is in the midst of a six-game losing streak without him.

Meanwhile, the player Leonard was traded for is just about ready to make his Clippers debut. Brandon Ingram is expected to return Monday against the Houston Rockets, according to Charania. Ingram suffered a partially torn Achilles tendon last season, which kept him out of the Clippers' lineup at the start of this year. His absence has been keenly felt in Los Angeles as the Clippers have scuttled to a 4-10 start without him. Los Angeles has both a bottom-eight offense and defense so far this season, so getting Ingram on the court should represent a helpful talent infusion.

San Antonio's second-year star thankfully avoided a major injury when he fell on the court against the Clippers on Thursday. He will, however, miss 1-3 weeks with a left hip rotator strain. Harper was walking without a limp following the injury, per The San Antonio Express-News, a positive sign for his recovery.

The Spurs have the NBA's best record at 13-3, but the story to watch as Harper rests is the performance of former All-Star De'Aaron Fox. Just beginning a four-year max contract, Fox has scored just 23 points in his last three games combined. He's averaging the fewest points and assists of his career since his rookie season. The Spurs had been starting their three high-profile guards -- Fox, Harper and Stephon Castle -- together early in the season. It was working, but with the caveat that that group never played a second without Victor Wembanyama. The Spurs are more than 40 points per 100 possessions better when their MVP candidate is on the floor.

If Fox can't right the ship while Harper is out, that could open the door to San Antonio moving him to the bench upon Harper's return. The Spurs thrived last season with two ball-handlers, two shooters and Wembanyama in their starting lineup. The three guards are working because basically anything works with Wembanyama, but when the competition gets stiffer in the playoffs, it's going to be harder to get away with so little shooting in the starting lineup. That puts the onus on Fox to prove he still belongs in the starting lineup, and bouncing back while Harper is out will be a big part of that.

#2497. What's next for the Mets after record-breaking deal with Tarik Skubal? Biggest needs for 2027

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Mets landed the offseason's best free agent and one of the game's top pitchers Sunday evening. The Mets and two-time Cy Young-winning lefty Tarik Skubal have agreed to a record-shattering nine-year contract worth $450 million. The contract obliterates the previous pitcher records for total guarantee (Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million) and average annual value (Max Scherzer's and Justin Verlander's $43.3 million). A 1-of-1 contract for a 1-of-1 pitcher.

New York's offseason work is not complete, however. It's not close to complete, really. The Mets went 74-88 and disappointed every which way this past season. There are still roster needs to address. Here's what's left for the Mets to do this offseason following the Skubal signing.

Yes, the Mets still need another starter even after signing Skubal. They have an excellent 1-2-3 punch. The depth behind that top three is not great, however. Here is New York's updated rotation depth chart:

Manaea and Senga both pitched so poorly this past season that they were demoted to the bullpen. They shouldn't be counted on as anything more than emergency options at this point in their careers. Thornton had some moments this summer and Tong is not too far removed from being a top prospect, but yeah, the Mets need another starter. Clearly.

After landing Skubal, I suspect the Mets will aim lower than the second tier of free agent starters (Michael King, Freddy Peralta, Trevor Rogers, etc.) to fill out their rotation. A Clay Holmes reunion would make some sense. Others in that class of veterans make sense too. Think Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, Casey Mize, pitchers like that.

Year 1 post-Pete Alonso at first base went worse than anyone could have expected. Jorge Polanco barely played and was terrible when he did play. Jared Young was fine and owner Steve Cohen isn't running near-record payrolls for fine. Alonso led all first basemen with 5.0 WAR for the Orioles. The Mets finished dead last at the position with -0.8 WAR. Yeesh.

Here are the best available free agent first basemen by FanGraphs projected 2027 WAR:

It ain't great. I think the projections on France, who had an excellent season in 2026, are a bit low, but the fact of the matter is he's only had one year in line with the kind of contract he's likely to sign. Perhaps there's a Luis García Jr. trade to be made with the crosstown rival New York Yankees? García's a clunky fit for the Yankees and might be most useful as a trade chip.

The good news is it won't be hard for the Mets to improve at first base. Getting even an average first baseman would represent an enormous upgrade. Now the Mets just have to go out and find that average (or, preferably, better than average) first baseman and improve their lineup. This might be the single biggest item remaining on their offseason to-do list.

The Mets traded away several relievers at the deadline this summer (A.J. Minter, Brooks Raley, Luke Weaver, etc.), which allowed them to audition a few young pitchers down the stretch. Left-hander Nate Lavender in particular stood out and cemented his place in the 2027 bullpen. The bullpen pecking order currently looks something like this:

Williams was at best inconsistent during his first season with the Mets. Another late-inning reliever to share the high-leverage load (someone to replace Weaver, basically) seems essential. You don't want to pay Skubal all that money only to have the bullpen blow his starts, you know? President of baseball operations David Stearns is adept at building bullpens on the cheap. Spending money is OK too.

Assuming the Mets don't go to the top of the market for Adrian Morejon, the best available free agent relievers are battle-tested veterans like Bryan Abreu, JoJo Romero, and Alex Vesia. Abreu is an excellent buy-low candidate after his rocky first half. There is no such thing as too many good relievers. The Mets should continue adding to their bullpen this winter.

The case can be made that Skubal's contract is only the second smartest contract the Mets gave out this weekend. They agreed to an eight-year, $95 million contract with a ninth-year club option with center fielder A.J. Ewing on Saturday. The deal buys out his six years of team control and two free agent years with an option for a third. That's a nifty piece of business.

I would expect the Mets to pursue extensions with McLean and outfielder Carson Benge next, if they haven't already. McLean and Benge both had terrific first full seasons in the big leagues and look like keepers, like players who can be centerpieces for a World Series contender rather than just tag along for the ride. Locking up McLean and/or Benge would be fantastic work.

#2494. ‘Craziest Day in Sports,’ ‘NBA Gotta Mic This Up’ — Hoops Fans Erupt As Dillon Brooks Gets Tossed Out After Heated Face-to-Face Spat With Kevin Durant

Phoenix Suns forward Dillon Brooks was ejected from Wednesday's 116-104 loss to the Houston Rockets after getting into a heated exchange with Kevin Durant in the closing seconds. The confrontation quickly drew reactions online, with fans weighing in on another tense moment between the two.

Brooks already had a technical foul when he and the 16-time All-Star squared up with 23.8 seconds remaining. The second technical sent Brooks to the locker room. Durant stayed in the game and scored Houston's final points on a dunk off an Amen Thompson assist with three seconds left.

BrickCenter posted video of the confrontation, writing that the two "stopped playing MID GAME to trash talk each other."

BGN Hoops had a reaction of its own: "This is what the league is missing. Bring back real rivalries."

One fan replied to BrickCenter's clip, "If you don't like that, you don't like NBA basketballlll."

Another response read, "Looks like this came out of NBA 2K. Love this. Durant has grown on me, but still took the easy way out, unfortunately."

The tension between Brooks and Durant goes back to their days as opponents in the Western Conference. Brooks was still with the Memphis Grizzlies when the two began exchanging words on the court. Their March 30, 2025, meeting between the Rockets and Suns ended with officials throwing Brooks out after an altercation with the two-time NBA Finals MVP.

The two eventually switched teams in a seven-team trade in July 2025. Houston acquired Durant, while Phoenix received Brooks, Jalen Green, and other assets.

Their differences also surfaced online last month. Durant and Suns governor Mat Ishbia exchanged posts after Ishbia revisited Phoenix's decision to acquire KD in 2023. Durant then made an apparent reference to Brooks' DUI arrest, prompting the Suns forward to enter the exchange with an Instagram post of his own.

Brooks posted an Instagram story thanking Ishbia for "cleaning up that stench in the locker room before I came." He did not mention Durant by name, but the post was widely interpreted as a shot at the two-time NBA champion.

The teams had already met earlier in November, with Phoenix taking a 102-99 win on Nov. 7. Durant finished that game 5-for-14 from the field, while Brooks scored 11 points for the Suns.

Another fan wrote, "NBA gotta mic … this up."

One viewer asked, "Craziest day in sports since when?"

A final reaction read, "Me and my ex seeing each other at a bar."

Brooks finished Wednesday's game with 12 points, 6 rebounds and 4 assists in 31 minutes. His premature exit came with Houston holding a 12-point lead, and the Rockets closed out the win without any late drama on the scoreboard.

The confrontation came on a milestone night for Durant, whose second-quarter 3-pointer pushed him to 33,000 career points. He finished with 20 points and 10 rebounds in the Rockets' victory, becoming just the fifth player in NBA history to reach the mark alongside LeBron James, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Karl Malone, and Kobe Bryant.

#2493. Is Tarik Skubal a Hall of Famer? Where new Mets ace stands now and where he could end up

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Mets are signing Tarik Skubal to a monster deal: nine years and $450 million. There's plenty to talk about with this deal, but a fun one for people like me -- especially here in the winter! -- would be glancing at his Hall of Fame case and how it's rounding into shape.

To be clear, Skubal is nowhere close to a Hall of Famer at this point, but that never stops people from throwing around titles like "future Hall of Famer." So, let's look ahead and guess a little bit and wonder if he is, in fact, a future Hall of Famer.

I'm inclined to say yeah, he's headed in that direction. There's a lot more compiling to be done, though.

In parts of seven seasons, Skubal is 66-44 with a 3.02 ERA (138 ERA+), 1.02 WHIP and 1,975 strikeouts against 199 walks in 925 ⅓ innings. He's led the league in pitcher WAR twice, ERA twice, strikeouts once and WHIP once. The two-time All-Star is one of 23 pitchers in history to win multiple Cy Youngs. Only 11 pitchers have ever won three, so if he can grab another one, he'll be in Hall of Fame company.

Some of us will give bonus points for great postseason numbers, and Skubal certainly has those. In three playoff seasons, he's 3-2 with a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts in 50 ⅔ innings.

Still, we're awfully light here on workload and counting stats. Keep in mind that this is obviously a major work in progress and players aren't even eligible for the Hall of Fame until they've logged 10 years of service time. Skubal still has three more to go before this is even a real conversation.

At present, the most statistically similar pitchers are Corbin Burnes, Shane Bieber and a bunch of very good but not Hall-worthy guys. If we set the parameters to the most statistically similar pitchers through age 29, we'll find Kyle Hendricks, Adam Wainwright, Max Fried, Bieber and Burnes as the top five.

Again, that doesn't sound like this pitcher is headed to the Hall of Fame.

Keep in mind, though, that Skubal was a bit of a late bloomer and also had major surgery interrupt his rise. In these last three seasons, he's gone 43-17 with a 2.42 ERA and 655 strikeouts against only 95 walks in 546 innings. He's racked up 17.7 WAR in just three years. Another three like that and he'd be in the ballpark of 40 WAR heading into his age-33 season. Catfish Hunter (40.9) and Jack Morris (43.5) would be within reach.

It is incredibly difficult to predict how a pitcher will age, but with pitchers of Skubal's caliber, there's an excellent track record going into their late 30s. It's reasonable to believe Skubal will remain in his prime through age 35 or so.

Let's say he averages roughly 6.0 WAR per season through age 35 and then averages, say, 2.5 (this is conservative) through the end of his contract. That would give him an additional 43.5 WAR. Add that to his current 22.7 and that gets him to 66.2 WAR through the end of this contract.

No, WAR isn't the only stat that matters, but it's the easy catch-all number to eyeball the Hall of Fame standing.

In the range of 66.2, you'll find Hall of Famers Don Drysdale, John Smoltz, Carl Hubbell, Ed Walsh and Don Sutton, a nice smattering of many different eras of aces. A bit behind the number? Roy Halladay, Bob Feller, Juan Marichal, CC Sabathia and Early Wynn.

Diving beyond WAR, again, Skubal's biggest résumé issue right now is the lack of compiling. With a strikeout artist, you'd like to see him reach 3,000, and he's barely a third of the way there.

Using Bill James' "favorite toy," let's take a look at the career projection. The toy has Skubal finishing with 2,036 strikeouts and gives him a 0% chance to reach 3,000. Of course, it also says that based on his age, he'll play for roughly 4.6 years. He just signed a nine-year deal. I'd be a bit more aggressive, but it isn't difficult to see him falling well short of 3,000 and maybe finishing around 2,500 or so.

Still, given his age and service time, it seems like the best route for Skubal to get to the Hall of Fame would be as a peak candidate rather than a compiler. Another Cy Young or two would certainly help his case.

If Skubal is in his prime for another five years, that would be seven or eight seasons as one of the best pitchers in baseball. That was enough for Sandy Koufax and Dizzy Dean. Félix Hernández is making good progress on getting in. Johan Santana, on the other hand, fell short.

It remains an uphill battle because, well, it's incredibly difficult to make the Hall of Fame. It should be. It's the Hall of Fame!

Without the context behind Skubal's recent surge, it doesn't look like he's headed to Cooperstown at all. He's good enough presently, though, to believe his next several years will put him on track.

Again, my hunch is he'll end up a Hall of Famer.

#2492. As James Harden passes Kobe Bryant on NBA's 50-point game list, Donovan Mitchell says he's underappreciated

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

James Harden is in the midst of his worst scoring season since his second year in Oklahoma City 16 years ago, but the 37-year-old turned back the clock some on Friday night with a 51-point performance in a Cavaliers win over the Pacers.

Harden's vintage scoring night saw him go 15-of-26 from the field and 14-of-14 from the free-throw line in typical Harden fashion for the 26th 50-point game of his career. That moves him into third all-time in NBA history for 50-point games, passing Kobe Bryant and sitting just five behind Michael Jordan.

At 37 years old (and 86 days), Harden is the fourth-oldest player to score 50 points in an NBA game, passing LeBron James on that list and trailing only Bryant, Jordan and Jamal Crawford, who scored 50 at 39 years old.

After the game, Cavaliers' coach Kenny Atkinson offered an eyebrow-raising comment calling Harden "top-10 all-time," which drew immediate pushback from NBA fans, but Harden is an unquestioned Hall of Famer and continues to put his name among the all-time greats on NBA scoring lists.

His co-star in Cleveland, Donovan Mitchell, lamented that Harden doesn't get the appreciation he deserves at this stage of his career, and that he expects, much like Russell Westbrook, that it won't happen until he retires.

"He won't until it's over with," Mitchell said. "I hate it, but that's just the world we live in. We won't appreciate greatness. We didn't appreciate Russ in his latter years until now. It's like, 'Oh man, Russ was this and that.' It's like we forgot he averaged 28, 15 and 16 for a month. It's one of those things where we live in such a negative space. I hate it. At the end of the day, he doesn't care. And for me, seeing that, I don't care. It helps, but at the end of the day, that's just what the world is. It sucks that that's that way, but us in this locker room and guys in this league, we know who he is and we know what he's done for the game. That goes for not just him but a lot of people in this league. We don't appreciate what's in front of us on a consistent basis."

Harden has long been a divisive player among NBA fans. Some have appreciated his ruthless efficiency while others have hated the aesthetics of his mastery of the dark arts of drawing fouls. As Mitchell noted, few players have had as much influence over the game in the last decade-plus as Harden. From his massive stepback 3-pointer to his movement on drives to create contact, so much of Harden's game has made its way into the arsenal of most elite guard scorers.

Fans will debate whether that's a good thing, but his influence is undeniable. As Mitchell said, whenever Harden calls it a career, he will get more appreciation, but there will also be heated debates over his place in NBA history as one of the most divisive stars (from a play-style perspective, at least) of his generation.

#2490. Aaron Rodgers' brother has a theory on why QB was shockingly benched by Steelers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Pittsburgh Steelers made one of the most shocking moves of the NFL season on Tuesday night when they decided to bench Aaron Rodgers in favor of Mason Rudolph for Friday's game against the Broncos.

When the announcement came out at 11:10 p.m. ET, the Steelers didn't offer any reason for the benching, but one person close to Rodgers has a theory on why the QB was benched and that's his brother, Jordan Rodgers.

The younger Rodgers brother believes that Steelers general manager Omar Khan may have played a part in the decision. With the Steelers playing on Friday this week, they held a practice on Tuesday and Aaron took all of the first team reps during that session, which made the decision to bench him so bizarre.

Jordan thinks Steelers general manager Omar Khan may have played a part in decision to bench his brother.

"Remember, yesterday was not a normal Tuesday," Jordan said on Wednesday's edition of ESPN's Get Up. "So there was a practice yesterday where presumably Aaron was the starter for the entire practice, so something had to happen. Him and Mike [McCarthy] have been together so long, the conversations have spanned every aspect of what you could with a head coach and a quarterback, so I don't think that was the issue. To me, this has to be a Omar Khan thing."

It's certainly an interesting theory. As Jordan noted, Aaron spent 13.5 seasons with McCarthy, so the two of them have been through some battles together. Also, McCarthy had declared Rodgers as his starter on Monday when he was asked if there was any thought about benching his quarterback.

As for Khan, Rodgers did seem to take a subtle shot at the front office over the handling of Max Hurleman. The Steelers QB is a big fan of the second-year receiver and he made it clear that he was not happy about the fact that Hurleman didn't get a chance to play until Week 11 (The receiver spent the first 10 weeks of the season on the practice squad).

Hurleman ended up being one of the few bright spots for the Steelers in their 19-16 loss to the Eagles, leading the team with six receptions for 61 yards and his first career touchdown.

"I think it's as much for him as it is for everybody else upstairs making decisions. You know, I think everyone thought before the injury in camp that he was a 53 (roster) guy," Rodgers said of Hurleman. "I know the guys in our room did for sure. So for him to go out there and finally get elevated and go out and play the way he played was not surprising to any of us but great for his confidence and a great reminder for the folks upstairs what kind of player he is."

Aaron was presumably referring to Khan and the Steelers' front office when he mentioned the "Folks upstairs."

It's unclear whether Khan had anything to do with the decision to bench Aaron, but, either way, he deserved much of the blame for how the season is going, according to Jordan.

"This season, the lack of success, to me, is more of an indictment on Omar Khan and how he constructed this roster because they're in the middle of the last dance and rebuild," Jordan said. "And it was a bad combination to be in that spot, but you trade away arguably your two best players in George Pickens and then Joey Porter Jr. on the other side. You got a draft pick in the fourth round as a kick returner (Kaden Wetjen) that can't even return kicks anymore that can't impact the Steelers wide receiver room, there's problems everywhere. So to me, Mason's not solving that this week."

Jordan also said that if you're going to bench Aaron, it doesn't make much sense to give the job to Rudolph.

"I look at this roster and I go, I would've been less surprised waking up hearing Will Howard or Drew Allar was the starter," Jordan said. "If you need a quarterback that's a little younger, that can move around a little bit more, or you're looking to the future, that would make more sense, but their lack of success this year -- and Aaron hasn't played great the last couple weeks -- but there was also a month ago when we're saying, 'He looks like vintage. He's moving around better. He's got three touchdowns in a row for three weeks in a row.'"

Jordan had actually been estranged from Aaron for several years, but at some point over the past few months, the two made up, with Aaron even visiting Jordan last week while his younger brother was working a game as an ESPN announcer.

Among sports fans, Carmelo Anthony is perhaps most synonymous with New York -- both upstate from his incredible year at Syracuse and in New York City, where he starred for the Knicks. But Anthony was raised in Baltimore and is extremely proud of his roots.

So when Baltimore Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey made headlines this week when he said that the thing the city of Baltimore was best at creating was "criminals," Anthony felt compelled to respond. Humphrey was admonished by the Ravens, which sent him home for the week and will hold him out on Sunday against the Carolina Panthers. He also received scathing responses from Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott and many other prominent Baltimore figures.

Anthony joined that group on Friday with an Instagram post that called on Humphrey to go beyond the apology he issued earlier in the week. Anthony wants Humphrey to join him, Scott, and others in the community to find ways to lead by example.

I've been sitting with this one for a couple of days, because Baltimore isn't a talking point to me. It's in my blood. I came up on Myrtle Avenue in West Baltimore. I saw what this city can take fro you. I lost friends to the streets, and I watched people I loved get swallowed by a system that was built to swallow them. I know the reputation. I've heard every joke and every headline my whole life.

So when one of our own stands on our name and says the best thing Baltimore makes is criminals, and then laughs that it'll get cut out, that doesn't get cut out for me. It doesn't get cut out for the kid in Baltimore who heard it. It doesn't get cut out for the mother working two jobs to keep her son off the corner. And it doesn't get cut out for the man who did his time, came home, and is fighting every day to be seen as more than his worst moment.

Marlon, I see the apology. I'll take it, man to man. But Baltimore has been apologized to its whole life. Apologies don't build anything. Presence does. I put my time, energy and resources in Baltimore because I want kids to have somebody who believe in them. That's the job when you wear this city on your chest. You don't get to rep Baltimore on Sundays and talk about it like an outsider on Wednesday.

So let me tell you what Baltimore makes. We make fighters. We make builders. We make people who were counted out from the day they were born and showed up anyway. We make teachers who buy supplies out of their own pockets, coaches who become fathers, artists the whole world copies, and returning citizens who turn their pain into purpose. We make Olympians, Hall of Famers, legends. We make ME. We make Tank Davis.

The Mayor opened a door. Walk through it. And when you do, call me. I'll meet you there. Let's sit with these young boys together and let them hear from two men who wear this city that they are not what anybody says they are.

Baltimore doesn't make criminals. Baltimore makes the ones who make it out. And the ones who come back. #B-MORE.

The overwhelming response to Humphrey's comments in Baltimore has been to highlight the incredible work being done by leaders to improve conditions, decrease violence, and provide mentorship and guidance to young people in the city.

Anthony echoed the mayor's invitation to join in that work in the community and offered to be there right alongside him.

#2488. Why Mets owner Steve Cohen was willing to give Tarik Skubal the most lucrative pitcher contract in MLB history

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Mets have landed two-time Cy Young-winning lefty Tarik Skubal, the offseason's top free agent, with a record-shattering nine-year contract worth $450 million. It far exceeds Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers, which was the previous record guarantee for a pitcher.

Every contract that long and that pricey carries risk and surely makes even the league's wealthiest owner a wee bit queasy. After meeting with Skubal in California last week, though, Mets owner Steve Cohen came away convinced Skubal was his guy and that he would have no issues settling into his new environment.

"He's going to be great for the clubhouse ... I don't have to worry about him pitching in New York," Cohen told the New York Post on Sunday, before the deal went official. "... He's an outstanding individual. He's bright. He's a student of the game. He's very impressive."

The "can he handle New York?" thing tends to get overblown, but it is a real consideration. It's a different market with different demands and you never truly know how a player will handle it until he experiences it. I think Skubal will be more than fine in New York because I don't think you can be as successful as he's been without embracing the spotlight, but I don't know that for certain. No one does.

Skubal has proven his bona fides on the biggest stages. He's been sensational in eight career postseason starts, pitching to a 2.13 ERA with 70 strikeouts in 50 ⅔ innings. All indications are that Skubal is a good teammate who fit in well with the Dodgers following his midseason trade from the Detroit Tigers.

Now 30, Skubal posted a 2.72 ERA in 158 ⅔ innings around his NanoScope elbow procedure this past season. He leads all pitchers with 18.0 WAR over the last three years despite missing time with injury this year.

The Mets went 74-88 and finished in last place in 2026. They were baseball's most disappointing team and signing Skubal is an enormous step toward making sure it doesn't happen again.

The NFL on Wednesday will debut the first Thanksgiving Eve game in league history, and it could feature the return of a superstar defender. Regardless of when it occurs, the All-Pro will soon enter game action for the first time since he tore his ACL and meniscus last year.

"I would say I feel like I've done everything I possibly could to put myself in position to potentially play on Wednesday, but for sure this season," Parsons said on Monday. "And I'll be looking forward to returning to the field."

The Packers could use a lift as they gear up for a run at the NFC North title. If Parsons suits up this week, he could wreak havoc on an injury-riddled Rams offense and guide Green Bay to one of its biggest wins of the year to begin the regular season's final push.

The Kansas City Chiefs were seeking a similar boost from their top running back, Kenneth Walker III, who missed the last two games with a groin injury. As a contender for the league lead in rushing yards per game, Walker has been instrumental in the Chiefs' offensive resurgence in 2026, and the unit will need to fire on all cylinders to keep up with the Buffalo Bills in one of the NFL's biggest blockbuster battles of the year.

Walker returned to practice on Tuesday as a limited participant, but the Chiefs are ruling him out for the holiday showdown.

Below is the latest on all the other injuries that could impact the NFL's Thanksgiving and Thanksgiving Eve slate.

Parsons' potential insertion into Wednesday's lineup would be a boon to the Packers, who in their last outing surrendered 30 points to the typically silent Minnesota Vikings offense. It would also inject life into a roster that will again be without another of its stars, Josh Jacobs. Green Bay's top running back continues to nurse the finger injury he sustained in Week 9, which required surgery. With Jacobs ruled out for the second consecutive game, the rushing attack could remain a non-factor. The run game is historically bleak, as its 3.1 yards per game is on pace to be the worst by any NFL team since 2000.

Ferguson will undergo surgery on the injured ankle that put him on the shelf nearly two months ago. None of those three played in the Rams' 34-6 demolition of the Arizona Cardinals, but the caliber of opponent increases significantly on Wednesday, so the hampered passing attack might not be nearly as impactful this time out.

Kyler Gordon has not played since Nov. 8 and is trending toward another absence, which leaves open a hole at the starting slot cornerback spot, and backup safety Elijah Hicks entered concussion protocol on Tuesday and was promptly ruled out for the Thanksgiving clash with the Detroit Lions. Los Angeles has lost five straight regular-season matchups against Baltimore, including a 30-23 setback at home in 2024. But the Ravens are in disarray themselves, having lost four games in a row after getting off to a 4-1 start. Their top two quarterbacks also were knocked out with injuries -- potentially for the rest of the season -- in their Week 8 setback against the Buffalo Bills.

Returning from a three-game absence due to an ankle injury, two-time NFL MVP Lamar Jackson suffered a dislocated and broken thumb on Baltimore's first offensive play in the loss to Buffalo. The injury required surgery that is expected to keep him sidelined for 6-10 weeks. If the Ravens are out of the playoff picture, it's unlikely they would put Jackson back on the field this year.

Backup Tyler Huntley sustained a season-ending toe injury in that same contest, and undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano started Baltimore's Week 9 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars. The club acquired Jacoby Brissett from the Arizona Cardinals just before that game, and the veteran journeyman will make his Ravens debut on Monday Night Football.

The 33-year-old Brissett threw for 1,719 yards with 10 touchdowns and seven interceptions in eight games with Arizona before being benched in Week 8 and subsequently losing his starting job to Gardner Minshew. Brissett did guide the Cardinals to a season-opening victory over the Chargers, however, throwing for 277 yards and a TD in a 26-14 triumph.

The Ravens, who are fifth in the NFL in rushing with an average of 137.8 yards per game, are 4.5-point favorites over the Chargers in the latest consensus odds for the Week 10 Monday Night Football matchup.

#2484. Predicting MLB's next mega contracts: Paul Skenes, Junior Caminero, James Wood and more in line to get paid

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Baseball has a new highest-paid pitcher. Sunday evening, the New York Mets landed two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal on a record-shattering nine-year contract worth $450 million. Yoshinobu Yamamoto previously held the record for the largest guarantee given to a pitcher at $325 million. Agent Scott Boras came in well above that with Skubal.

This is the fourth straight offseason some sort of contract record was broken. Last offseason, Kyle Tucker set the average annual value record at $60 million. The offseason before that, Juan Soto set the record guarantee at $765 million. The offseason before that, Shohei Ohtani set records every which way with his heavily deferred 10-year, $700 million contract.

Next offseason's free agent class is not robust, and it seems unlikely any contract records will be set, but who knows, really? Add in the uncertainty created by the upcoming collective bargaining agreement and I don't think anyone can confidently say what the next few offseasons will look like, or when contract records will be set.

That won't stop us from speculating, however. Here now are 10 candidates to sign baseball's next mega contract, which we'll loosely define as a contract that makes us stop and say, "oh damn, that's a crazy deal." Sound good? Good. Let's get to it.

Junior Caminero, Rays: Caminero and Hall of Famer Eddie Mathews are the only players in baseball history with two 40-homer seasons before their age-23 seasons. Power pays, always has and always will, and Caminero has power to spare. He is not scheduled to become a free agent until after 2030, when he'll still be only 28 years old. If he doesn't sign a contract extension that would no doubt set new records for his service time level, Caminero will be in line for a Soto-esque deal come free agency, assuming of course he continues hitting home runs at this pace.

Elly De La Cruz, Reds: De La Cruz reportedly rejected what would have been a franchise-record contract last offseason, beating Joey Votto's $225 million extension way back when. Still only 24, De La Cruz just turned in a sensational season, during which he went 30-30 and finished sixth among all players with 6.4 WAR. He is one of those guys who looks like he was put on this Earth for the sole purpose of playing baseball. De La Cruz is an all-around impact player, plus he's a high-energy player who plays with obvious joy. He is three years away from free agency and this is exactly the sort of skill set that gets a record contract.

Paul Skenes, Pirates: You know you've set a high bar when a 4.2 WAR season is considered a disappointment and people spend the summer wondering what's wrong with you. The fact is, though, that Skenes did take a step back in 2026, and he'll have to return to his 2024-25 form to get a mega contract. Plus, he has to stay healthy, which is the unspoken "if" that exists with every pitcher. Skenes will turn only 25 in May and he's three years away from free agency. Even if 2026 proves to be his new normal, he'll get a massive payday as a free agent. And if Skenes rediscovers his 2024-25 form, Skubal's record will almost certainly fall.

Gunnar Henderson, Orioles: A year or two ago Henderson, 25, would have been in the favorites category. He took a step back in 2025, however, and then another step back in 2026. To be sure, a 3.6-WAR season is still very good, but this is becoming a thing with top young Orioles hitters, no? Adley Rutschman regressed from legitimate star to pretty good. Now, Henderson seems to be on the same track. Henderson is only two years away from free agency. If his 2027-28 look more like 2023-24 than 2025-26, then forget it; he'll get a mega contract as a free agent at age 27. Star shortstops reliably get paid handsomely.

Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers and Cam Schlittler, Yankees: This year's Cy Young winners are both five years away from free agency, which puts them at a clear disadvantage in the mega contract race. If they set any records, it will likely be for their service time level with an extension. Otherwise, we're talking about staying healthy and holding this level of performance through 2031 before Misiorowski and Schlittler sign mega deals. The Brewers aggressively lock up their best young players. Based on that, Misiorowski is more likely than Schlittler to sign a record extension for a pitcher this far away from free agency.

James Wood, Nationals: There are very few hitters I would take over Wood for the next five years. He is terrific, with easy power and a discerning eye, and sneaky stolen base ability as well. Wood's outfield defense is not good and might keep him from getting a record contract. Then again, poor defense didn't keep Soto from signing the richest contract ever, and Wood is about the same caliber of hitter. He just turned 24 and he's four years away from free agency. Offense pays more than defense and Wood is going to hit 50 home runs one of these years. If it happens before free agency, all the better for his mega contract pursuit.

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs: Why is the reigning National League MVP a long shot for a mega contract after a 10.6-WAR season? Because the Cubs wisely locked Crow-Armstrong up to a six-year, $115 million extension just before Opening Day. Furthermore, that contract doesn't begin until 2027. The Cubs have PCA locked up through 2032, his age-31 season. It will be difficult, then, for Crow-Armstrong to sign a record contract simply because free agents do not get paid as well when they're in their 30s. No one should reasonably expect 10-WAR seasons every year, but if PCA can continue at an All-Star pace through 2032, then maybe he'll get a record contract. It's not impossible. Just unlikely.

Mason Miller, Padres: No, Miller will not approach Skubal's record, but he is already well-positioned to sign the richest reliever contract in baseball history. The current record is Edwin Díaz's five-year, $102 million deal with the Mets four years ago. I suppose Adrian Morejon, most recently Miller's teammate in San Diego, could break Díaz's record this offseason. Or maybe Jhoan Duran, who will be a free agent next offseason, breaks Díaz's record. As long as he stays healthy and remains this, Miller should break the reliever contract record, whatever it is, when the time comes. He is 28 and three years away from free agency.

Jordan Walker, Cardinals: A bit of a reach, perhaps, but Walker finally arrived as a power-hitting force in 2026, plus he stole 22 bases as well. He's been around so long that it's easy to forget he's still only 24. Walker is on track to become a free agent after 2029, when he'll be only 27, and boy, 27-year-old power hitters are exactly the kind of players who get record contracts. Walker leveled up in 2026. If he levels up again in 2027 and as he gets close to his prime years, he's a sneaky good candidate to get a mega contract down the line.

#2483. Is Stephen Curry the real NBA MVP? It's hard not to think so when you watch the Warriors without him

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's easy to forget because of what Stephen Curry has turned the Golden State Warriors into over the last decade and change, but this is an organization with some pathetic history in its books. So it's really saying something to start registering all-time marks of franchise ineptitude, which is precisely what the Warriors have done over the last week.

After battling admirably in a respectable loss to the Houston Rockets on the night Curry went down with an oblique injury in the first quarter, the Warriors have lost their last four games by 20-plus points for just the second time in franchise history. The only other time this has happened to a Warriors team was in February of 1998, a few months after Latrell Sprewell choked P.J. Carlesimo. The total margin of that four-game losing streak was 104 points.

This current one is even worse. These Warriors have lost their last four by 109 points, and what makes it even more jarring is comparing them to the team that had won eight straight prior to Curry's injury. That 1997-98 team was trash all year, starting 1-14 and finishing with just 19 wins without ever winning more than three straight games.

These Warriors, on the other hand, were starting to look like a legitimate playoff-caliber team. A cynic would say that run of victories came against a softer schedule than what they have faced of late, but that qualification doesn't hold much, if any, water. That eight-game run included wins over the Denver Nuggets, Minnesota Timberwolves, Los Angeles Lakers, Miami Heat and an Orlando Magic team that has immediately gone on to win five of its last six.

Perhaps the Warriors would have lost to the 13-3 San Antonio Spurs even with Curry. Hell, maybe they would've lost to the New Orleans Pelicans, Dallas Mavericks and Memphis Grizzlies, too. That feels unlikely, but who knows? Even with Curry, the Warriors aren't good enough to start checking off scheduled wins. But that's not the point.

The point is how utterly incapable they have looked in losing these games. Not only have they lost each of these last four by at least 20 points, but they've also been held under 100 points in all of them. That's a combination of incompetence that stretches beyond a franchise mark. That hasn't happened to a single other team this century.

Before we try to answer that, let's just agree upfront that Curry has little to no chance of actually winning what would be his third MVP. The Warriors almost certainly won't have a good enough record to put him in real contention. His across-the-board counting stats, even if he were to maintain his torrid early pace, are not going to match those of Luka Dončić or Victor Wembanyama.

The only real chance would be if both of those guys, and likely a bunch of others, failed to meet the 65-game threshold, but the chances of Curry, who has already missed six games and isn't expected to be re-evaluated until around Thanksgiving, making it to 65 games himself already feel next to impossible. He may be past the maximum 17 games-missed mark before he even returns from this injury.

Which is to say, what we're asking here is whether Curry, at 38 years old and in his 18th season, is still the most valuable player in the league (has he always been?), not whether he'll actually win the award, and the answer to that question, at least in its simplest form, could very well lie in his absence. Just look at this team without him.

Admittedly, there's some cherry-picking in those numbers. Curry actually didn't play in one of the wins during that eight-game streak, and the Warriors still beat the Los Angeles Clippers 124-112 with a 122.8 offensive rating behind 37 points from rookie Yaxel Lendeborg.

We're also leaving out the aforementioned game against the Rockets on Nov. 11 in which Curry only played six minutes and the Warriors looked fine, or even good, in testing one of the best teams in the league to its limit. It also must be noted that Golden State lost its first three games of the season and looked every bit like the team many of us predicted would stink, all of which Curry played in.

Still, the general rule applies. The Warriors go as Curry goes. That was true even in the golden years when the on/off splits, even with the likes of Kevin Durant and Klay Thompson still out there, always pointed to Curry as the clear MVP.

"If I didn't have Steph, I would've been like every other NBA coach and lasted a few years [with the Warriors] and then gone and coached somewhere else," Steve Kerr has said, openly admitting that Curry, and Curry alone, has been the difference between a journeyman coaching career and a Hall-of-Fame one.

He's not lying. Have a look at the numbers.

Even if you want to remove the 2019-20 season from the equation, when Durant had defected, Thompson missed the whole year and Curry only played in five games, Kerr is still a below-.500 coach at 74-96 without Curry in the lineup. This is a coach who has had all kinds of great players at his disposal over the years, and still it was always Curry in control of his and the organization's ultimate fate.

This is still the case for the Warriors, who continue to fall off a cliff without Curry. When he's been on the floor this year, they have registered a 59.6 eFG%, which would rank first in the league. When he's off, they fall to 49.1%, which would rank last.

Even the defensive decline we see in Curry's on/off splits can largely be tied back to his offense. Without him, the Warriors are unable to create the same shots and, when their new brand of shots miss far more often, they end up defending in transition on almost 3% more possessions. That's a big deal. It's meant almost five more points per game surrendered to fast breaks over this stretch.

The Warriors have produced an average offensive rating of 103.8 in games Curry hasn't played this year, which would rank as the second-worst mark in the league. All told, they are 26.3 points per 100 possessions better in Curry's minutes this season, per Cleaning The Glass. By comparison, the Lakers drop by 25.5 points per 100 when Dončić sits. Wembanyama is in his own galaxy with this stat, representing a 37.8-point decline in San Antonio when he's off the floor.

It's fair to say Wembanyama means as much to San Antonio's defense, where most of that decline happens, as Curry does to Golden State's offense, and certainly the Lakers falling off by as much as they do offensively, even with Austin Reaves as a legit secondary star, tells you everything you need to know about his impact. All of these guys are MVP players.

But only one, by subjective definition, can be the most valuable, and the simple truth is the Lakers and Spurs are outfitted with far more functional rosters independent of their respective superstars. In Golden State, there is just nowhere else to turn. Nobody to generate any kind of consistent offensive leverage. No gravity. No shot creation.

After the Warriors took that 38-point beating against the Spurs without Curry, the rookie Lendeborg, who had, in total unfairness, been saddled with filling Curry's go-to-scorer shoes, said "it felt helpless out there," and that is exactly what it has looked like since the Curry variable was removed from Golden State's equation.

To be fair, the absence of a player is an imperfect lens through which to view value for a bunch of contextual reasons, not the least of which is how a team like Golden State is designed to play -- a specific, Curry-centric ecosystem not particularly amenable to abrupt adjustments. These players are not as bad as they have looked without Curry over these last four games.

But by the same token, they aren't close to as good as they looked with Curry, either. I always laugh when my dad calls me saying things like, "This Pat Spencer guy can play!" Everyone looks like they can play next to Curry. And then he goes away and suddenly you're wondering how the hell this guy made the Washington Generals look like one of the best teams in the league. Is he some kind of miracle worker?

In a basketball sense, that's not far off. Curry's individual production is already virtually unmatched, but it's his exponential powers, his ability to compound the returns of those around him, that set him apart. It's early, yes. Perhaps the Warriors will figure things out the longer Curry is away. Probably not. But maybe they at least can return to competitive functionality. Until then, however, it's pretty hard to not think Curry is the most valuable player in the league when you watch the Warriors play without him.

#2482. NFL on Thanksgiving cheat sheet: Everything you need to know to impress relatives during three holiday games

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Thanksgiving is finally here, and that means the family gets to gather around the table and share one thing we all know and love …football games with stakes! If we include the Thanksgiving Eve game between the Packers and Rams and the Black Friday game between the Steelers and Broncos, all five Thanksgiving Eve/Day/Black Friday games have major implications for both the AFC and NFC playoff races. Some of the league's best are playing on Turkey Day, so just for you, I've put together a special Thanksgiving plate of matchups to watch for on Thanksgiving Day. Let's hop in and establish some fun!

In this game between two divisional heavyweights, we're going to focus on the trenches when the Lions have the ball. Since adding DT Jeffrey Simmons, the Bears' defense has taken a major leap in efficiency. According to TruMedia, the Bears have the 4th-best Defensive EPA per play and Defensive Success Rate since Week 8, and a large part of that is Jeffrey Simmons lifting the Bears' defense to new heights. What's really stood out is that with Simmons on the field, Bears' defensive coordinator Dennis Allen can really unlock his Rolodex of coverages on 3rd down without resorting to blitzing as much. Before Simmons came around, the Bears had a 39.3% blitz rate on 3rd down, and when they didn't blitz, their 43.2% pressure rate was 15th in the NFL. Since adding Simmons, their blitz rate on third down has dropped to 25.7%, while their pressure rate without blitzing has risen to 46.2%. With Simmons on the field, Allen can use those blitz looks to scheme up 1v1 chances for Simmons, or force teams to show attention to him that frees up his teammates.

Take this play against the Saints as an example. It's 3rd and 4, and the Bears line up in a BOSS (Big On Same Side) front, meaning three of their defensive linemen (including Simmons) are lined up on the defense's right, and LB TJ Edwards is lined up over the right guard. In this moment, the Saints are forced to slide the protection to the three defensive linemen and leave the right guard to block Edwards. At the snap, Allen changes the picture, dropping Edwards and giving Simmons a 1v1. Simmons wins instantly and forces Shough out of the pocket and into a pass short of the sticks.

This will be Simmons and the Bears' biggest test since the trade, as they face a Lions offense that has been hitting all the right notes. Since their last loss in week four, the Lions are fourth in the NFL in Offensive Success Rate, fifth in EPA per play and fifth in points per drive. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing has done a really good job of mixing in his own unique flavors to the Detroit offense, but what I really think has helped the most is the offensive line stability and growth. Penei Sewell has fully settled in at left tackle, Christian Mahogany has taken back over at left guard after a suspension and center Juice Scruggs has rebounded from his rough play early in the season to provide stability after starter Cade Mays got hurt. Petzing has gotten creative with his pass protection around Goff (see: the Minnesota game), but the step up in pass pro is due to the overall quality of the OL and some impressive blocks by Jahmyr Gibbs and Sione Vaki.

Against the Bucs, Goff and the Lions absolutely ripped passes down the seams of the defense, and the pass protection did their job to let those chunk plays happen. This one is a five-out play, where all five eligible receivers are out into the passing concept if Vaki doesn't get a blitzer. Look at how pristine this pocket is. Mahogany takes his man and deposits him across the formation as well.

This game is going to be all about trench warfare, as the good Lord intended. There's definitely going to be a lot of points, but when you watch this game as you sit down for your first plate of food, keep an eye on the offensive line for the Lions as they try to handle the Jeffrey Simmons problem.

This one doesn't quite have the same juice we might've thought it would coming into the season — it doesn't even have the same juice we thought it would a month ago. But it's a rivalry game nonetheless, and for the Cowboys it's a chance to stay alive in their hopes of winning the division. These teams have played before this season, and while some of the faces might look different, the objective for Dallas remains the same:

"Run the ball." - Georgia Tech head coach Brent Keypic.twitter.com/yFuipSdv3a

Since the win against the Eagles, the Cowboys have run for over 100 yards twice in four games, and since Week 8 Dallas is fifth in EPA per designed rushing attempt (which excludes scrambles) and rushing Success Rate. Part of this emergence has been the offensive line play, which came into the season as a strength and has weathered injuries to get better at the right time. But the other part of it is Brian Schottenheimer getting a little more creative with his run schemes. Through the first seven weeks of the season, Dallas felt like their offense was static. Since Week 8, their motion rate at the snap has ticked up, and it especially has jumped up in the run game. The motion usage and creativity were on display when Kavontae Turpin ran in a 22-yard touchdown against the Titans. Turpin is lined up in the backfield, and the RB goes in orbit motion around him. Then, Dallas runs pin and pull to get their linemen in space against cornerbacks. Advantage: Dallas.

Tyler Guyton, Tyler Smith and Cooper Beebe all had killer blocks on this Turpin TD run off pin n pull. #Cowboys pic.twitter.com/9HTr0OqWoR

Philadelphia is coming off one of their best performances against the run, holding the Steelers to their lowest success rate on designed carries since the first game of the season. What was most impressive about the performance was their tackling, especially by the linebacker group. Pittsburgh's offense relies heavily on yards after the catch and yards after contact, and in their game against the Eagles, they only had one tackle avoided on rushing attempts and 1.80 yards after contact per carry. The Eagles rely heavily on their linebackers to flow fast to the ball in the run game; living in light run boxes requires your linebackers to be real players.

Outside of Zack Baun, it hasn't always been perfect, but LB Jeremiah Trotter Jr. might've played one of his best career games. He was decisive and fast, filling the run and making a bunch of splash plays in space.

Heck of a game for Jeremiah Trotter Jr. Sure helps when the #Steelers don't block you on half their runs.Reminds me of another #54. Fred Warner in the '23 opener when he dominated all game. Ground game doesn't stand a chance with LBs running free. pic.twitter.com/U7H2gPQaZZ

Second-year LB Jihaad Campbell hasn't been as consistent, but even he had his flashes on Sunday. If you're looking to watch something, anything during this game, look at how the Cowboys run the ball against an Eagles front coming off a really good performance.

The nightcap might be the most anticipated game of the Thanksgiving Day festivities, as we get another battle between two of the best QBs of the 2020s. Kansas City heads to Buffalo in a game that could also decide home-field advantage in the AFC. The biggest matchup is obviously going to be which defense can slow down the opposing QB, but for this one I'm choosing to focus on the Bills' defense, which is playing sound football, going up against a now-multifaceted Kansas City offense.

Very slowly, the Chiefs' passing game has rounded into form since their week seven debacle against the Seahawks. Since Week 8, the Chiefs are fifth in the NFL in Success Rate and fourth in the NFL in EPA per play, but if you just take their passing offense since adding WR Josh Downs, the number goes to a 52.6% Passing Success Rate and their EPA per pass has jumped up from 0.17 to 0.22. What Downs has given the Chiefs is another savvy route runner who easily finds holes in zones and creates separation when the Chiefs need him to. Downs is third on the Chiefs in targets since being traded to Kansas City, and you can feel his presence on the field when finding holes in zones.

This was a fun play for Downs that highlights his ability to find holes in zone coverage and make himself available. The Cardinals are running Cover 6, with the Cover 2 corner to Downs' side. Kansas City is running a Sail concept, with Downs running the "sail" part of the route. Instead of running into the coverage, Downs sits and finds the hole between the two defenders as the go route clears the outside cornerback. Results in an easy first down for the Chiefs.

3rd and Josh Downs, this time in KC. Downs made a couple of these plays, out routes settling into holes of zones from the slot. He and the emergence of Cyrus Allen have given the Chiefs offense more layers pic.twitter.com/rzk4xinRFH

On the flip side, the Bills' defense hasn't allowed a touchdown on 43 straight possessions, one shy of an NFL record set in 2019 by the New England Patriots. Yes, the offenses they've played haven't been super impressive, but what they've done to get their secondary turned around is pretty notable. Through the first seven weeks, the Bills were a Cover 3 and Quarters team, asking their DBs to match and communicate as routes were being passed off. Since week 8, they've played much more Cover 2 as their changeup to Cover 3, meaning fewer guys have to run and match and more guys using physicality at the line of scrimmage and driving on routes quickly.

I think this fits more of the personnel that the Bills have. I've always loved CB Christian Benford in more of a physical, press alignment to get eyes and hands on the receiver, and rookie CB Davison Igbinosun is tailor-made for that style of football. The trade for S Amani Hooker gives them a playmaker on the back end, and everything is tied together much more. Again, this is against the Dolphins, but this is good work by the Bills, rotating into an inverted Cover 2.

One of the coverage changeups the Bills have leaned into has been Tampa 2 invert/non traditional Tampa like the one here, with Bishop in the flat (cloud) and Igbinosun as a deep half player. This particular one is also paired with a creeper pressure pic.twitter.com/mXe1L6F2HN

In a season where there's so much parity, having Bills-Chiefs be a massive game feels right. Both teams are angling for the top seed in a loaded conference, with offenses that are peaking at the right time. It's the perfect ending to an awesome day of football. Happy Thanksgiving, y'all.
